posts.title: American Music Tourism Act of 2025
posts.label: 📌 Presented to President
posts.summary:
American Music Tourism Act of 2025
This bill directs the National Travel and Tourism Office (NTTO) of the Department of Commerce to promote tourism to music-related and sports attractions.
The bill requires NTTO to promote domestic and international travel and tourism to U.S. music festivals, concert venues, and other music-related attractions and locations. The bill also expands NTTO's current mandate to facilitate sports and recreation events and activities to include the promotion of international travel and tourism to such activities in the United States.
NTTO must report its activities and findings to Congress within one year after the bill's enactment and, thereafter, every two years.
posts.summaryLabel: Congressional Research Service, Introduced in Senate
posts.meta: Commerce, Science, and Transportation Committee · Sen. Marsha Blackburn (R-TN)
posts.whatsNext: President has 10 days (Sundays excepted): sign, veto, or it becomes law unsigned (pocket veto if adjournment prevents return)

aiSummaries.text: The American Music Tourism Act of 2025 would direct the National Travel and Tourism Office, part of the Department of Commerce, to promote tourism to music and sports attractions. The office would be required to encourage both domestic and international travel to U.S. music festivals, concert venues, and other music-related places. It would also expand its existing work on sports and recreation so that it promotes international travel to those events and activities in the United States. The office must report its activities and findings to Congress within one year of the bill becoming law, and then every two years after that.

posts.title: Kay Hagan Tick Reauthorization Act
posts.label: 📌 Presented to President
posts.summary:
Kay Hagan Tick Reauthorization Act
This bill reauthorizes through FY2030 activities of the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention to address vector-borne diseases (e.g., diseases spread by bites from ticks or mosquitoes). These activities include (1) a national strategy, (2) grants for regional centers of excellence, and (3) cooperative agreements with state, local, and tribal health departments to increase capacity for preventing and responding to vector-borne diseases.

aiSummaries.text: This bill extends, through fiscal year 2030, the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention's work on diseases spread by insect and tick bites, such as those carried by ticks or mosquitoes. That work covers three main efforts: creating a national plan to deal with these diseases, giving grants to regional centers of excellence, and entering into cooperative agreements with state, local, and tribal health departments. The goal of these agreements is to help those departments better prevent and respond to vector-borne diseases.

posts.title: Billion Dollar Boondoggle Act of 2025
posts.label: 📌 Presented to President
posts.summaryLabel: Congressional Research Service, Introduced in Senate
posts.committee: Small Business and Entrepreneurship Committee, Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee
posts.meta: Small Business and Entrepreneurship Committee, Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee · Sen. Joni Ernst (R-IA)
posts.whatsNext: President has 10 days (Sundays excepted): sign, veto, or it becomes law unsigned (pocket veto if adjournment prevents return)

aiSummaries.text:
The Billion Dollar Boondoggle Act of 2025 would require the Office of Management and Budget (OMB) to gather information from federal agencies about federally funded projects that are running badly behind schedule or going far over budget, and then report on them to Congress.

Under the bill, OMB must issue guidance telling agencies to send it information each year about projects that are either more than five years behind schedule or have spent at least $1 billion more than their original cost estimate.

For each of these projects, agencies must report a description of the project, any changes to its original scope, and both the original and current expected completion dates. They must also report the original and current cost estimates, adjusted for inflation, along with explanations for any delays or cost increases. Finally, they must report any award, incentive fee, or other bonus given for the project and the reason for it.

OMB must then prepare an annual report for Congress that includes all of this information and post the report on its website.

posts.title: Ratepayer Protection Act
posts.label: 🗳️ Motion to proceed filed
posts.summary:
Ratepayer Protection Act
The bill requires state utility regulators and nonregulated utilities to consider implementing a standard to hold certain large-load customers responsible for the costs associated with any generation, transmission, or distribution upgrade of electric service necessary to serve such customers. A large-load customer means a non-residential electric consumer that enters, or requests to enter, an agreement concerning the sale of electric energy primarily to operate information technology infrastructure and related systems pertaining to data storage and computational applications and services (e.g., data centers) that have a peak electric demand of 100 megawatts or more at a single site or campus.
Specifically, the bill requires states to consider implementing a federal standard for large-load customers. The standard must require rates charged by electric utilities for providing electric service to a large-load customer to be designed to recover from the large-load customer the full, incremental cost of any generation, transmission, or distribution upgrade necessary to serve such customer. This rate must include the costs that would be incurred if the large-load customer terminates an agreement with the electric utility pertaining to the sale of electric energy or otherwise ceases the purchase of energy from the electric utility.
Under the standard, an electric utility must require the large-load customer to provide to the utility financial assurances or contributions to cover the cost of any generation, transmission, or distribution upgrade that is necessary to serve the load of a large-load customer before the utility makes any generation, transmission, or distribution upgrade.
posts.summaryLabel: Congressional Research Service, Reported to House
posts.meta: Energy and Commerce Committee · Rep. Gabe Evans (R-CO)
posts.whatsNext: The Senate votes on taking it up (the motion can be withdrawn)

aiSummaries.text:
This bill asks state utility regulators and nonregulated utilities to consider a standard that makes large electricity users pay for the power system upgrades needed to serve them. The "large-load customers" it covers are non-residential customers, such as data centers, that buy electricity mainly to run computing and data storage operations and have a peak demand of 100 megawatts or more at a single site or campus.

Under the proposed standard, the rates a utility charges these customers would have to be set so that the customer covers the full added cost of any new power generation, transmission, or distribution upgrade needed to serve it. The rates would also have to cover the costs the utility would still face if the customer ends its agreement or stops buying power from that utility.

The standard would also require utilities to collect financial assurances or contributions from the large-load customer before they build any generation, transmission, or distribution upgrade needed to serve that customer.

posts.title: Southcentral Foundation Land Transfer Act of 2025
posts.label: ✅🏛️ Passed Senate (unanimous consent)
posts.summary:
Southcentral Foundation Land Transfer Act of 2025
This bill directs the Department of Health and Human Services (HHS) to convey approximately 3.4 acres in Anchorage, Alaska, to the Southcentral Foundation (SCF) for use in connection with health and social services programs.
The conveyance must be made by warranty deed. The conveyance may not (1) require any consideration (such as payment) from the SCF for the property; (2) impose any obligation, term, or condition on the SCF relating to that property; or (3) allow for any U.S. reversionary interest in the property.
HHS must be accorded any easement or access to the property as may be reasonably necessary to satisfy any retained obligation or liability of HHS.
The bill prohibits the SCF from being liable for certain environmental contamination that occurred on or before the date on which the property is conveyed to the SCF. In turn, HHS may not be liable for any contamination that occurred after the date that the SCF controlled, occupied, and used the property.
posts.summaryLabel: Congressional Research Service, Reported to House
posts.committee: Indian Affairs Committee, Energy and Commerce Committee, Natural Resources Committee
posts.meta: Indian Affairs Committee, Energy and Commerce Committee, Natural Resources Committee · Rep. Nicholas Begich (R-AK)
posts.whatsNext: Presidential review (±10 days)

aiSummaries.text:
The Southcentral Foundation Land Transfer Act of 2025 would require the Department of Health and Human Services (HHS) to transfer about 3.4 acres of land in Anchorage, Alaska, to the Southcentral Foundation (SCF). The land would be used for the foundation's health and social service programs.

The land must be transferred through a warranty deed, which is a document that gives the buyer a guarantee of clear ownership. The transfer cannot require the SCF to pay anything for the property. It also cannot place any duty, term, or condition on the SCF about the land, and it cannot give the federal government a right to take the property back later.

HHS would keep whatever easement or access rights to the property it reasonably needs to meet any obligation or liability it still has.

The SCF would not be held responsible for environmental contamination that happened on or before the date the land is transferred to it. In the same way, HHS would not be responsible for contamination that happened after the SCF began controlling, occupying, and using the property.

posts.title: To authorize the Secretary of the Army to convey to the State of North Carolina a certain parcel of real property located at Fort Bragg, North Carolina, on which the State shall construct a veterans’ State home, and for other purposes.
posts.label: ✅🏛️ Passed Senate (unanimous consent)
posts.summary:
This bill authorizes the Department of the Army to transfer, without compensation or other consideration, all right, title, and interest to a specified 20-acre parcel of land on Fort Bragg to the State of North Carolina for the purpose of constructing a state home under the jurisdiction of the North Carolina Department of Military and Veterans Affairs. (A state home is a home established by a state for veterans who are disabled by age, disease, or otherwise and are incapable of earning a living because of such disability. The term also includes a home that furnishes nursing home care for veterans.)
Specifically, the bill authorizes the conveyance of a 20-acre parcel of land situated on the Fort Bragg Training Area in Harnett County, North Carolina, that is commonly referred to as Parcel 3B.
The State of North Carolina must cover all costs to carry out the conveyance.
If the Department of the Army determines the property is not being used for activities related to a state home, all right, title, and interest in the property may revert to the United States.
posts.summaryLabel: Congressional Research Service, Introduced in House
posts.meta: Armed Services Committee · Rep. Richard Hudson (R-NC)
posts.whatsNext: Presidential review (±10 days)

aiSummaries.text:
This bill lets the Army give a 20-acre piece of land on Fort Bragg, known as Parcel 3B, to the State of North Carolina for free. The land is in Harnett County, on the Fort Bragg Training Area. The state plans to use it to build a state home for veterans, and the home would be run by the North Carolina Department of Military and Veterans Affairs.

A state home is a home set up by a state for veterans who are disabled by age, illness, or some other cause and cannot earn a living because of that disability. The term also covers a home that provides nursing home care for veterans.

North Carolina has to pay all the costs of carrying out the transfer.

If the Army decides the land is not being used for activities related to the state home, the land can go back to the United States.

posts.title: America's National Churchill Museum National Historic Landmark Act
posts.label: ✅🏛️ Passed Senate (unanimous consent)
posts.summary:
America's National Churchill Museum National Historic Landmark Act
This bill designates the America’s National Churchill Museum, including the Winston Churchill Memorial, located at Westminster College in Fulton, Missouri, as the America’s National Churchill Museum National Historic Landmark. (Former British Prime Minister Winston Churchill gave a speech titled The Sinews of Peace, also widely known as the Iron Curtain Speech, at the college in 1946.)
The bill permits the Department of the Interior to enter into cooperative agreements with public and private entities for the purposes of protecting historic resources at the landmark and providing educational and interpretive facilities for the public. Interior may provide technical and financial assistance to partner entities.
The bill also directs Interior to conduct a special resource study to evaluate the national significance of the landmark and to determine the suitability and feasibility of designating it as a unit of the National Park System. The study must consider alternatives to that designation for the preservation, protection, and interpretation of the landmark, and must include cost estimates associated with identified alternatives.
posts.summaryLabel: Congressional Research Service, Introduced in House
posts.meta: Natural Resources Committee · Rep. Robert Onder (R-MO)
posts.whatsNext: Presidential review (±10 days)

aiSummaries.text:
This bill would designate the America's National Churchill Museum, including the Winston Churchill Memorial at Westminster College in Fulton, Missouri, as the America's National Churchill Museum National Historic Landmark. The college is the place where former British Prime Minister Winston Churchill gave his 1946 speech "The Sinews of Peace," also widely known as the Iron Curtain Speech.

The bill allows the Department of the Interior to make cooperative agreements with public and private groups. These agreements would aim to protect the historic features of the landmark and to provide educational and interpretive facilities for the public. Interior may also give technical and financial help to these partner groups.

The bill also requires Interior to carry out a special resource study. This study would evaluate how nationally important the landmark is and whether it would be suitable and feasible to make it a unit of the National Park System. The study must look at other options for preserving, protecting, and explaining the landmark, and it must include cost estimates for those options.

posts.title: Common Cents Act
posts.label: ✅🏛️ Passed Senate (unanimous consent)
posts.summary:
Common Cents Act
This bill ends the production of the penny for general circulation, requires rounding to an amount divisible by five for the payment or transfer of cash, and allows the nickel to be composed of different material.
The Department of the Treasury must stop producing the penny, except to meet collector needs. The penny shall continue to be legal tender.
Any person selling goods or services in a cash transaction, entering into other transfers of cash, or paying cash wages to an employee must round the payment up or down in accordance with the bill.
The bill also allows Treasury to discontinue the minting for circulation of any coin if Treasury follows procedures as outlined by the bill, including providing notice and a briefing to Congress.
The Federal Reserve Board must periodically report on a strategic plan for the acceptance of penny orders and deposits at commercial coin terminals that provide services under agreements with Federal Reserve banks.
Finally, the bill allows for a different material composition of the nickel. In addition to being made from an alloy of copper and nickel, the nickel may also be clad with an inner core of zinc and an outer layer of nickel.
posts.summaryLabel: Congressional Research Service, Introduced in House
posts.committee: Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs Committee, Financial Services Committee
posts.meta: Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs Committee, Financial Services Committee · Rep. Lisa McClain (R-MI)
posts.whatsNext: Presidential review (±10 days)

aiSummaries.text:
The Common Cents Act would stop the U.S. Treasury from making new pennies for everyday circulation, though the Treasury could still make them to meet the needs of coin collectors. Pennies would remain legal money.

Under the bill, anyone who sells goods or services for cash, makes other cash transfers, or pays employees in cash would have to round the amount up or down so it can be divided evenly by five. This rounding rule would apply to those cash payments and transfers.

The bill also lets the Treasury stop making any coin for circulation, but only if it follows the steps set out in the bill. Those steps include giving notice to Congress and providing it a briefing.

The Federal Reserve Board would have to report regularly on a strategic plan for accepting penny orders and deposits at commercial coin terminals that offer services under agreements with Federal Reserve banks.

Finally, the bill would allow the nickel to be made from a different material. Besides the current copper and nickel alloy, a nickel could be made with an inner core of zinc and an outer layer of nickel.

posts.title: Accelerating Access to Critical Therapies for ALS Reauthorization Act of 2026
posts.label: ✅🏛️ Passed Senate (voice vote)
posts.summary:
Accelerating Access to Critical Therapies for ALS Reauthorization Act of 2026
This bill reauthorizes through FY2031 and revises programs that support research and development of drugs and other therapies to address amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (also known as ALS or Lou Gehrig's disease) and other neurodegenerative diseases.
The bill reauthorizes
grants from the National Institutes of Health (NIH) for scientific research on investigational drugs to prevent or treat ALS for individuals not otherwise eligible for clinical trials,
grants from the Food and Drug Administration (FDA) for research and development of therapies to prevent and treat ALS and other neurodegenerative diseases, and
a Public-Private Partnership including the FDA and NIH that supports development and regulatory review of treatments for neurodegenerative diseases.
Also, the NIH, in considering renewal of its grants, must assess available information on the safety and efficacy of the investigational drugs. It must also require grantees to promptly report serious and unexpected adverse events associated with their investigational drugs.
Additionally, the FDA must publish a plan describing actions it will take over a five-year period to foster development of safe and effective drugs, and facilitate access to investigational drugs, that treat ALS and other rare neurodegenerative diseases. The FDA must also publish a report describing the actions it has taken under the plan.
posts.summaryLabel: Congressional Research Service, Reported to House
posts.meta: Energy and Commerce Committee · Rep. Mike Quigley (D-IL)
posts.whatsNext: Presidential review (±10 days)

aiSummaries.text:
This bill extends several federal programs through fiscal year 2031 that fund research and development of drugs and other treatments for amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS, also called Lou Gehrig's disease) and other brain-related diseases that get worse over time.

Three programs are renewed. The National Institutes of Health (NIH) can keep giving grants for research on experimental drugs to prevent or treat ALS for people who can't otherwise join clinical trials. The Food and Drug Administration (FDA) can keep giving grants to develop therapies for ALS and other neurodegenerative diseases. A public-private partnership involving the FDA and NIH can also keep supporting the development and regulatory review of treatments for these diseases.

The bill adds some safety requirements. When the NIH decides whether to renew one of these grants, it must review the available information on how safe and effective the experimental drug is. It must also require grant recipients to report serious and unexpected side effects promptly.

The FDA must publish a five-year plan describing what it will do to encourage the development of safe and effective drugs for ALS and other rare neurodegenerative diseases, and to make experimental drugs easier to access. Afterward, it must publish a report on the actions it has taken under that plan.

posts.title: Making America's Food Safer Act
posts.label: ✅🏛️ Passed Senate with amendment (unanimous consent)
posts.summary:
Making America's Food Safer Act
This bill expands the Food and Drug Administration’s (FDA’s) authority to require the destruction of unsafe imported foods, share food safety information, and make use of food facility audit information.
Specifically, the bill authorizes the FDA to order the destruction, without the opportunity for export, of any item that (1) is refused import into the United States; (2) violates federal law regulating food, drugs, medical devices, cosmetics, and tobacco products; and (3) presents a significant public health concern. Before issuing a destruction order, the FDA must provide an item’s owner or consignee with appropriate due process, including notice and an opportunity to appear. If an order is issued, the item’s owner or consignee must destroy it within 90 days at their own cost.
The bill also generally authorizes the FDA to share unredacted food safety information with state, local, tribal, and territorial authorities, including information related to foodborne illness tracking, recalls and outbreaks, and other topics. During a food safety incident, the FDA may disclose certain commercial information that is otherwise protected from disclosure.
Finally, the bill expands the FDA’s third-party audit system to make domestic food facilities eligible for voluntary audits. (Foreign facilities are eligible under current law.) The bill also authorizes the FDA to use audit results and related certifications to analyze risks and prioritize regulatory activities (e.g., inspections) to protect public health. (This information is currently used to determine whether specific food, or food from a specific facility, is eligible for import.)
posts.summaryLabel: Congressional Research Service, Reported to Senate
posts.committee: Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee
posts.meta: Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee · Sen. Tommy Tuberville (R-AL)
posts.whatsNext: To the House (if and when it takes it up)

aiSummaries.text:
The Making America's Food Safer Act lets the Food and Drug Administration (FDA) order that certain imported products be destroyed instead of sent back out of the country. This applies to an item that has been refused entry into the United States, breaks federal rules covering food, drugs, medical devices, cosmetics, or tobacco products, and poses a significant risk to public health. Before issuing such an order, the FDA must give the item's owner or buyer fair notice and a chance to appear and respond. If the order is issued, the owner or buyer has 90 days to destroy the item at their own expense.

The bill also lets the FDA share food safety information more broadly with state, local, tribal, and territorial governments. This covers information about tracking foodborne illness, recalls, and outbreaks, along with other food safety topics. The information shared is not blacked out. During a food safety emergency, the FDA may also release certain business information that would normally be kept private.

Finally, the bill extends the FDA's voluntary third-party audit program to domestic food facilities, which are now eligible to take part. Foreign food facilities already qualify under current law. The FDA may also use the results of these audits and related certifications to assess risks and decide where to focus its work, such as inspections, to protect public health. Currently, this audit information is used to decide whether particular food, or food from a particular facility, can be imported.

posts.title: Modernizing Access to Our Public Oceans Act
posts.label: 📜✍️ Signed by Pres. Trump
posts.summary:
Modernizing Access to Our Public Oceans Act
This act directs the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA) to standardize and publish geospatial data related to public recreational use of federal waterways (e.g., boating and fishing).
Under the act, NOAA must consult with relevant stakeholders (including state and local governments, Indian tribes, and Native Hawaiian organizations) to develop and adopt standards for the coordination and dissemination of geospatial data relating to fishing restrictions and recreational vessels' use of federal waterways, including the exclusive economic zone of the United States (EEZ). (The EEZ generally includes waters between 3 and 200 miles seaward from the U.S. coastline.)
Within four years after the act is enacted, NOAA must provide geographic information system data on a public website that identifies and describes the locations where and conditions under which certain recreational activities are restricted in federal waterways. Specifically, the website must identify (1) locations where fishing restrictions are imposed, (2) areas in the EEZ with restrictions on specified recreational vessel types, and (3) federally protected areas (e.g., National Marine Sanctuaries). NOAA must also continue to provide digitized navigation information related to the EEZ and make the information available on the website to the extent practicable.
The act allows NOAA to coordinate and partner with nonfederal entities to carry out this act. It also directs NOAA to work with other federal agencies to ensure compatibility and interoperability among federal databases with respect to collecting and disseminating geospatial data related to the public outdoor recreational use of the EEZ.
posts.summaryLabel: Congressional Research Service, Public Law
posts.meta: Commerce, Science, and Transportation Committee · Sen. Ted Cruz (R-TX)
posts.whatsNext: Takes effect (on enactment unless the text sets other dates)

aiSummaries.text:
The Modernizing Access to Our Public Oceans Act tells the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA) to create standard, public map-based information about where people can boat and fish in federal waters.

NOAA must work with state and local governments, Indian tribes, Native Hawaiian organizations, and other interested groups to set standards for gathering and sharing this location data. The data covers fishing restrictions and where certain recreational boats may go in federal waters, including the exclusive economic zone of the United States. That zone generally covers waters from 3 to 200 miles out from the U.S. coast.

Within four years of the act becoming law, NOAA must publish this information on a public website. The website must show where fishing is restricted and under what conditions, which areas of the exclusive economic zone limit certain types of recreational boats, and which places are federally protected, such as National Marine Sanctuaries. NOAA must also keep sharing digital navigation information about that zone on the site, as far as is practical.

The act lets NOAA partner with outside groups to carry this out. It also requires NOAA to work with other federal agencies so their databases are compatible and can share recreational ocean-use data smoothly.

posts.title: Protect College Sports Act of 2026
posts.label: ⏱️ Cloture invoked (74-25)
posts.summary:
Protect College Sports Act of 2026
This bill establishes requirements for name, image, or likeness (NIL) agreements for college student athletes and provides a limited antitrust exemption for schools and conferences to pool and sell certain college sports media rights. The requirements address elements of the court-approved agreement to settle In re College Athlete NIL Litigation (i.e., House settlement).
First, the bill statutorily prohibits institutions, conferences, or interstate intercollegiate athletic associations (e.g., the National Collegiate Athletic Association [NCAA]) from restricting student athletes from entering NIL agreements (subject to specified limitations). Students must report to their institution NIL compensation greater than $600.
The bill requires agents to register with a state and caps agent endorsement contract fees at 5%.
The bill also provides student athletes with one transfer without losing athletic eligibility and restricts football personnel from becoming the head football coach at a different institution during the same season.
Further, the bill prohibits institutions, conferences, or specified entities acting for the benefit of an institution from providing athletes with compensation that circumvents the limit on sharing revenue with student athletes established under the House settlement. The bill also makes the limit permanent and provides for an annual inflation adjustment.
The bill generally prohibits Division I conferences from reducing the number of varsity or Olympic sports teams that a member institution must sponsor. Specifically, large institutions ($80 million or more in annual athletics revenue) must offer and maintain at least as many grant-in-aid opportunities and roster spots for sports that do not generate positive net revenue as the institution provided during academic year 2024-25. The bill provides for a waiver of this requirement under certain circumstances of financial hardship and the requirements expire nine years after the enactment of the bill.
Additionally, the bill establishes (subject to specified conditions) a limited antitrust exemption for institutions or conferences that form joint agreements to transfer their sports telecasting rights to a third party. Such an agreement requires participation from at least 75% of the institutions in the Football Bowl Subdivision.
posts.summaryLabel: Congressional Research Service, Reported to Senate
posts.meta: Commerce, Science, and Transportation Committee · Sen. Ted Cruz (R-TX)
posts.whatsNext: Senate floor vote (up to 30 hours of consideration remain)

aiSummaries.text:
The Protect College Sports Act of 2026 sets rules for how college athletes can earn money from their name, image, or likeness (NIL) and gives schools and conferences a limited legal exemption to pool and sell certain sports TV and media rights. Many of its requirements follow up on a court-approved settlement in a lawsuit known as the House settlement.

Under the bill, colleges, conferences, and national athletic associations such as the NCAA generally cannot stop student athletes from signing NIL deals, though some limits apply. Students must report to their school any NIL pay greater than $600. Agents who work with athletes must register with a state, and their fees under endorsement contracts are capped at 5%.

The bill also makes some changes to athletes' eligibility and coaching. Student athletes can transfer one time without losing their eligibility to compete. Football personnel are barred from becoming the head football coach at a different school during the same season.

To prevent schools from getting around the House settlement, the bill bans payments to athletes that are designed to avoid the limit on revenue sharing with athletes. That limit becomes permanent and will rise each year to keep pace with inflation.

For Division I conferences, the bill generally stops them from cutting the number of varsity or Olympic sports teams that member schools must sponsor. Large schools, defined as those with $80 million or more in annual athletics revenue, must keep offering at least as many scholarships and roster spots in sports that do not bring in positive net revenue as they did in the 2024-25 academic year. A waiver is available in certain serious financial hardship cases. These requirements expire nine years after the bill is enacted.

Finally, the bill creates a limited antitrust exemption, subject to certain conditions, that lets schools or conferences jointly agree to transfer their sports broadcast rights to a third party. Such an agreement must include at least 75% of the schools in the Football Bowl Subdivision.

posts.title: Indian Health Service Emergency Claims Parity Act
posts.label: 📋 Reported by committee
posts.note: Indian Affairs, without amendment, S. Rept. 119-152
posts.summary:
Indian Health Service Emergency Claims Parity Act
This bill extends from 72 hours to 15 days the time period to notify the Purchased/Referred Care (PRC) program of emergency medical care received from a non-Indian Health Service (IHS) medical provider or at a non-IHS medical facility. This bill does not apply to individuals who are elderly or disabled, who continue to have a 30-day notification requirement for emergency services.
The IHS provides medical and dental services directly to American Indian and Alaska Native patients whenever possible. The PRC program pays for medical or dental care that is provided away from an IHS or tribal health care facility. The PRC program must be notified of requests for authorization of payment for health care services from a non-IHS provider.
Currently in emergency cases, the patient, an individual on behalf of the patient, or the medical care provider must, within 72 hours after the beginning of treatment for the condition or after admission to a health care facility, notify a PRC authorizing official of the need for the emergency medical care. This bill instead allows the patient, other individual, or provider to notify PRC within 15 days of the treatment or admission.
posts.summaryLabel: Congressional Research Service, Introduced in Senate
posts.meta: Indian Affairs Committee · Sen. Mike Rounds (R-SD)
posts.whatsNext: Floor scheduling (leadership decides if and when it gets a vote)

aiSummaries.text:
This bill gives more time to notify the Indian Health Service's Purchased/Referred Care (PRC) program about emergency medical care that an American Indian or Alaska Native patient receives from a provider or facility outside the IHS system. Right now, that notice must be given within 72 hours after treatment begins or after the patient is admitted. Under the bill, the patient, someone acting for the patient, or the care provider would have 15 days instead.

The bill does not change the rule for people who are elderly or disabled. They would still need to give notice within 30 days for emergency services.

The IHS provides medical and dental care directly to American Indian and Alaska Native patients whenever it can. The PRC program pays for care delivered away from an IHS or tribal health facility, and it must be notified when payment is requested for care from a non-IHS provider.

posts.title: Critical Infrastructure Manufacturing Feasibility Act
posts.label: ✅🏛️ Passed Senate (unanimous consent)
posts.summary:
Critical Infrastructure Manufacturing Feasibility Act
This bill requires the Department of Commerce to study and report on products that are in high demand across the critical infrastructure sectors. Critical infrastructure sectors are those whose assets, systems, and networks are vital to national security, the economy, public health or safety, or any combination of those matters.
The study must (1) identify the products in high demand across those sectors that are being imported due to manufacturing, material, or supply chain constraints; and (2) analyze the costs, benefits, and feasibility of manufacturing those products in the United States.
posts.summaryLabel: Congressional Research Service, Introduced in House
posts.committee: Commerce, Science, and Transportation Committee, Energy and Commerce Committee
posts.meta: Commerce, Science, and Transportation Committee, Energy and Commerce Committee · Rep. Mariannette Miller-Meeks (R-IA)
posts.whatsNext: Presidential review (±10 days)

aiSummaries.text:
This bill asks the Department of Commerce to study products that are in high demand across the sectors the country depends on most, such as national security, the economy, public health, and public safety. These are called critical infrastructure sectors.

The study has two parts. First, it must identify which in-demand products in those sectors are being brought in from other countries because of problems with manufacturing, materials, or supply chains. Second, it must look at what it would cost and gain, and how practical it would be, to make those products in the United States.

posts.title: Romance Scam Prevention Act
posts.label: ✅🏛️ Passed Senate (unanimous consent)
posts.summary:
Romance Scam Prevention Act
This bill requires online dating service providers (i.e., mobile applications or websites) to provide users with a fraud ban notification if the user has established an account with the service and received a message through the service from a banned user of the service.
The fraud ban notification must include (1) the username or other profile identifier of the banned user and the most recent time when the user who is receiving the notification sent or received a message through the service to or from the banned user, (2) a statement that the banned user may have been using a false identity or attempting to defraud other users, (3) a statement that the user should not send cash (or another form of currency) or personal financial information to another user, (4) information about avoiding online fraud (e.g., a link to another website or a disclosure) and (5) contact information for the provider's customer service department.
The bill provides for enforcement of these requirements by the Federal Trade Commission and state attorneys general.
posts.summaryLabel: Congressional Research Service, Introduced in House
posts.meta: Energy and Commerce Committee · Rep. David Valadao (R-CA)
posts.whatsNext: Presidential review (±10 days)

aiSummaries.text:
This bill, called the Romance Scam Prevention Act, requires online dating services, whether they run as phone apps or websites, to warn users about possible scammers. If a user has an account and has received a message through the service from someone who has since been banned, the service must send that user a fraud ban notification.

The notification must include the banned user's username or other profile identifier, and the most recent time the notified user sent or received a message to or from that person. It must also say that the banned user may have been using a fake identity or trying to defraud people. It must tell the user not to send cash, another form of currency, or personal financial information to anyone on the service. It must give information about avoiding online fraud, such as a link to another website or a disclosure. Finally, it must provide contact information for the service's customer service department.

The Federal Trade Commission and state attorneys general would be responsible for enforcing these requirements.

posts.title: Vicksburg National Military Park Boundary Modification Act
posts.label: ✅🏛️ Passed Senate (unanimous consent)
posts.summary:
Vicksburg National Military Park Boundary Modification Act
This bill directs the Department of the Interior to convey approximately 7 acres of specified land (in two parcels) within the Vicksburg National Military Park to Mississippi for an interpretive center.
The conveyed land must facilitate public access to the park, may not be used in a manner that adversely impacts the park's resources or visitor experience, and remains subject to any use restriction that Interior determines is appropriate.
Interior must convey the land by quitclaim deed and without consideration, such as payment. Upon the conveyance of the land, Interior must modify the park's boundary to exclude the land.
posts.summaryLabel: Congressional Research Service, Reported to House
posts.meta: Natural Resources Committee · Rep. Bennie Thompson (D-MS)
posts.whatsNext: Presidential review (±10 days)

aiSummaries.text:
The Vicksburg National Military Park Boundary Modification Act would require the Department of the Interior to transfer about 7 acres of land, in two separate parcels, within Vicksburg National Military Park to the State of Mississippi so that a interpretive center can be built there.

The land has to be used in a way that helps the public reach the park. It cannot be used in any way that harms the park's resources or the experience of visitors. Interior may also place any use restrictions it considers appropriate on the land.

The land must be transferred by quitclaim deed, and the state does not have to pay for it. Once the transfer is complete, Interior must change the park's boundary so that the land is no longer part of the park.

posts.title: Reversionary Interest Conveyance Act
posts.label: ✅🏛️ Passed Senate (unanimous consent)
posts.summary:
Reversionary Interest Conveyance Act
This bill directs the Bureau of Land Management (BLM) to offer to sell the reversionary interest of the United States in approximately 8.43 acres of land in Sacramento, California, as generally depicted on a specified map dated November 7, 2022. Within two years of receiving a request from the owner of the land, the BLM must offer the reversionary interest and convey the reversionary interest to the buyer upon payment. The payment must be in an amount that is at least the fair market value of the reversionary interest. The buyer must also pay all costs related to the applicable conveyance of the reversionary interest, including all surveys, appraisals, and other administrative costs.
The bill subjects the conveyance to valid existing rights.
The proceeds from the sale must be deposited into Federal Land Disposal Account.
posts.summaryLabel: Congressional Research Service, Introduced in House
posts.committee: Energy and Natural Resources Committee, Natural Resources Committee
posts.meta: Energy and Natural Resources Committee, Natural Resources Committee · Rep. Doris Matsui (D-CA)
posts.whatsNext: Presidential review (±10 days)

aiSummaries.text:
The Reversionary Interest Conveyance Act would require the Bureau of Land Management (BLM) to offer to sell the United States' reversionary interest in about 8.43 acres of land in Sacramento, California. The land is shown on a map dated November 7, 2022. A reversionary interest is the government's right to get the land back under certain conditions.

If the owner of the land asks, the BLM must make the offer within two years of receiving the request. Once the buyer pays, the BLM must transfer the reversionary interest to them. The price must be at least the fair market value of that interest. The buyer also has to cover all costs of the transfer, including surveys, appraisals, and other administrative expenses.

The sale is subject to valid existing rights, meaning any rights that already legally apply to the land still hold. The money from the sale must be deposited into the Federal Land Disposal Account.

aiSummaries.text:

The goal is to help the public learn about and appreciate the history of George Catlett Marshall, Jr., who led the U.S. Army as Chief of Staff during World War II and later served as Secretary of State, president of the American Red Cross, and Secretary of Defense.

posts.title: Modernizing Access to Our Public Oceans Act
posts.label: 📌 Presented to President
posts.summary:
Modernizing Access to Our Public Oceans Act
This bill directs the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA) to publish geospatial data related to public recreational use of federal waterways (e.g., boating and fishing).
Under the bill, NOAA must consult with relevant stakeholders (including state and local governments, Indian tribes, and Native Hawaiian organizations) to develop and adopt standards for the coordination and dissemination of geospatial data relating to fishing restrictions and recreational vessels' use of federal waterways, including the exclusive economic zone of the United States (EEZ). (The EEZ generally includes waters between 3 and 200 miles seaward from the U.S. coastline.)
Within four years after the bill is enacted, NOAA must provide geographic information system data on a public website that identifies and describes the locations where and conditions under which certain recreational activities are restricted in federal waterways. Specifically, the website must identify (1) locations where fishing restrictions are imposed, (2) areas in the EEZ with restrictions on specified recreational vessel types, and (3) federally protected areas (e.g., National Marine Sanctuaries). NOAA must also continue to provide digitized navigation information related to the EEZ and make the information available on the website to the extent practicable.
The bill allows NOAA to coordinate and partner with nonfederal entities to carry out this bill. It also directs NOAA to work with other federal agencies to ensure compatibility and interoperability among federal databases with respect to collecting and disseminating geospatial data related to the public outdoor recreational use of the EEZ.
posts.summaryLabel: Congressional Research Service, Passed Senate
posts.meta: Commerce, Science, and Transportation Committee · Sen. Ted Cruz (R-TX)
posts.whatsNext: President has 10 days (Sundays excepted): sign, veto, or it becomes law unsigned (pocket veto if adjournment prevents return)

aiSummaries.text:
This bill asks the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA) to make it easier for the public to find out where they can boat and fish in federal waters. It covers the exclusive economic zone of the United States, the ocean area that generally runs from 3 to 200 miles out from the coastline.

NOAA would first need to consult with groups that have a stake in this, including state and local governments, Indian tribes, and Native Hawaiian organizations. Together they would develop and adopt standards for sharing map-style location data about fishing restrictions and where certain recreational boats may go in federal waters.

Within four years of the bill becoming law, NOAA must post this location data on a public website. The website would show where fishing is restricted, which areas of the exclusive economic zone limit particular types of recreational boats, and which federally protected areas exist, such as National Marine Sanctuaries. NOAA would also keep providing digital navigation information about the zone and make it available on the site as far as is practical.

The bill lets NOAA team up with outside organizations to carry out this work. It also directs NOAA to work with other federal agencies so their databases fit together and can share information about outdoor recreation in the zone.

posts.title: A bill to take certain Federal land in the State of California into trust for the benefit of the Shingle Springs Band of Miwok Indians, and for other purposes.
posts.label: 📋 Reported by committee
posts.note: Indian Affairs, without amendment, S. Rept. 119-149
posts.summary:
Shingle Springs Band of Miwok Indians Land Transfer Act of 2025
This bill takes approximately 265 acres of specified lands in El Dorado County, California, into trust for the benefit of the Shingle Springs Band of Miwok Indians.
The bill revokes a specified public land order and administratively transfers the land from the Forest Service to the Department of the Interior. (In the public land order, the land was designated for use by the Forest Service as an experiment station.)
The bill directs Interior to take the following lands into trust for the benefit of the tribe: (1) approximately 80 acres of federal land managed by Interior's Bureau of Land Management (which includes the land transferred from the Forest Service), and (2) approximately 185 acres of fee land held by the tribe. These combined lands, approximately 265 acres, shall be part of the tribe's reservation. Further, the bill prohibits gaming on the land taken into trust.
posts.summaryLabel: Congressional Research Service, Introduced in Senate
posts.meta: Indian Affairs Committee · Sen. Alex Padilla (D-CA)
posts.whatsNext: Floor scheduling (leadership decides if and when it gets a vote)

aiSummaries.text:
This bill would place about 265 acres of land in El Dorado County, California, into trust for the Shingle Springs Band of Miwok Indians. Under the bill, the land would become part of the tribe's reservation.

The bill first cancels a specific public land order that had set aside the land for use by the Forest Service as an experiment station. It then moves that land from the Forest Service to the Department of the Interior.

The land being placed in trust comes from two sources. About 80 acres are federal land managed by the Interior Department's Bureau of Land Management, which includes the land transferred from the Forest Service. The other 185 acres are land the tribe already owns outright.

The bill also prohibits gaming on the land taken into trust.

posts.title: Protect College Sports Act of 2026
posts.label: 🗳️ Motion to proceed filed
posts.summary:
Protect College Sports Act of 2026
This bill establishes requirements for name, image, or likeness (NIL) agreements for college student athletes and provides a limited antitrust exemption for schools and conferences to pool and sell certain college sports media rights. The requirements address elements of the court-approved agreement to settle In re College Athlete NIL Litigation (i.e., House settlement).
First, the bill statutorily prohibits institutions, conferences, or interstate intercollegiate athletic associations (e.g., the National Collegiate Athletic Association [NCAA]) from restricting student athletes from entering NIL agreements (subject to specified limitations). Students must report to their institution NIL compensation greater than $600.
The bill requires agents to register with a state and caps agent endorsement contract fees at 5%.
The bill also provides student athletes with one transfer without losing athletic eligibility and restricts football personnel from becoming the head football coach at a different institution during the same season.
Further, the bill prohibits institutions, conferences, or specified entities acting for the benefit of an institution from providing athletes with compensation that circumvents the limit on sharing revenue with student athletes established under the House settlement. The bill also makes the limit permanent and provides for an annual inflation adjustment.
The bill generally prohibits Division I conferences from reducing the number of varsity or Olympic sports teams that a member institution must sponsor. Specifically, large institutions ($80 million or more in annual athletics revenue) must offer and maintain at least as many grant-in-aid opportunities and roster spots for sports that do not generate positive net revenue as the institution provided during academic year 2024-25. The bill provides for a waiver of this requirement under certain circumstances of financial hardship and the requirements expire nine years after the enactment of the bill.
Additionally, the bill establishes (subject to specified conditions) a limited antitrust exemption for institutions or conferences that form joint agreements to transfer their sports telecasting rights to a third party. Such an agreement requires participation from at least 75% of the institutions in the Football Bowl Subdivision.

aiSummaries.text:
The Protect College Sports Act of 2026 sets rules for how college athletes can earn money from their name, image, or likeness (NIL) and gives schools and conferences a limited legal exemption to pool and sell certain sports TV and media rights. Many of its requirements follow up on a court-approved settlement in a lawsuit known as the House settlement.

Under the bill, colleges, conferences, and national athletic associations such as the NCAA generally cannot stop student athletes from signing NIL deals, though some limits apply. Students must report to their school any NIL pay greater than $600. Agents who work with athletes must register with a state, and their fees under endorsement contracts are capped at 5%.

The bill also makes some changes to athletes' eligibility and coaching. Student athletes can transfer one time without losing their eligibility to compete. Football personnel are barred from becoming the head football coach at a different school during the same season.

To prevent schools from getting around the House settlement, the bill bans payments to athletes that are designed to avoid the limit on revenue sharing with athletes. That limit becomes permanent and will rise each year to keep pace with inflation.

For Division I conferences, the bill generally stops them from cutting the number of varsity or Olympic sports teams that member schools must sponsor. Large schools, defined as those with $80 million or more in annual athletics revenue, must keep offering at least as many scholarships and roster spots in sports that do not bring in positive net revenue as they did in the 2024-25 academic year. A waiver is available in certain serious financial hardship cases. These requirements expire nine years after the bill is enacted.

Finally, the bill creates a limited antitrust exemption, subject to certain conditions, that lets schools or conferences jointly agree to transfer their sports broadcast rights to a third party. Such an agreement must include at least 75% of the schools in the Football Bowl Subdivision.

posts.title: To amend the Mineral Leasing Act for Acquired Lands to make that Act applicable to hardrock minerals.
posts.label: 📋 Reported by committee
posts.note: Energy and Natural Resources, without amendment, without written report
posts.summary:
This bill specifies that all federally acquired lands are eligible to be considered for hardrock mineral leasing under the Mineral Leasing Act for Acquired Lands (MLAAL). The bill defines the term hardrock mineral to (1) include deposits of minerals found in sedimentary or other rocks, base metals, precious metals, industrial minerals, and precious and semi-precious gemstones; and (2) exclude deposits of coal, oil, oil shale, gas, sodium, potassium, sulfur, or mineral materials subject to disposition under the Materials Act of 1947.
By way of background, hardrock minerals are not currently listed under the MLAAL as deposits subject to a lease, while mineral resources such as coal, phosphate, oil, gas, gilsonite, and sulfur are listed. As a result, federal lands may be leased for mining hardrock minerals only if the federal lands were acquired under a statute, such as the Weeks Act, that specifically authorizes the land to be used for hardrock mineral leasing.

posts.committee: Energy and Natural Resources Committee, Natural Resources Committee
posts.meta: Energy and Natural Resources Committee, Natural Resources Committee · Rep. Pat Fallon (R-TX)

aiSummaries.text:
This bill would make all federally acquired lands eligible for hardrock mineral leasing under the Mineral Leasing Act for Acquired Lands (MLAAL). "Hardrock minerals" would cover mineral deposits found in sedimentary or other rocks, including base metals, precious metals, industrial minerals, and precious and semi-precious gemstones. It would not cover coal, oil, oil shale, gas, sodium, potassium, sulfur, or mineral materials that are handled under the Materials Act of 1947.

Right now, hardrock minerals are not on the MLAAL's list of resources that can be leased, while things like coal, phosphate, oil, gas, gilsonite, and sulfur are. Because of this, federal land can be leased for hardrock mining only if it was acquired under a law, such as the Weeks Act, that specifically allows hardrock mineral leasing on that land.

posts.title: To require the Secretary of Agriculture to convey the Pleasant Valley Ranger District Administrative Site to Gila County, Arizona.

posts.note: Energy and Natural Resources, without amendment, without written report
posts.summary:
This bill directs the Forest Service to convey specified property to Gila County, Arizona, upon the county's submission of a written request for such conveyance. The property, identified as the Gila County Area, consists of approximately 232.9 acres of National Forest System land located in the Tonto National Forest in Arizona.
The county must use the land for the purposes of serving and supporting veterans. If any land conveyed under this bill ceases to be used for such purpose, all right, title, and interest in and to the land shall revert to the United States, at the discretion of the Forest Service.
The conveyance must be made with a quitclaim deed and without consideration (value, such as payment, provided in exchange for the property).
The Forest Service must not be required to provide any covenant or warranty for the land and improvements conveyed to the county under such conveyance.
As a condition of the conveyance, the county must pay all the costs associated with the conveyance, including any (1) surveys, (2) environmental analysis or resource survey required under federal law, and (3) analysis required to comply with certain provisions of the National Historic Preservation Act.

aiSummaries.text:
This bill would require the Forest Service to transfer about 232.9 acres of National Forest System land in the Tonto National Forest in Arizona, known as the Gila County Area, to Gila County. The transfer would happen once the county submits a written request for it.

The county must use the land to serve and support veterans. If the county stops using it for that purpose, ownership of the land goes back to the United States, if the Forest Service chooses to take it back.

The land would be transferred by quitclaim deed, which gives the county whatever interest the federal government holds without any guarantees about the property. The county pays nothing for the land. The Forest Service does not have to promise anything about the land or the buildings on it.

As a condition of the transfer, the county must pay all costs of completing it. These include surveys, any environmental analysis or resource survey required under federal law, and any analysis needed to meet certain requirements of the National Historic Preservation Act.

posts.title: Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act of 2026
posts.label: 📌 Presented to President
posts.summary:
Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act of 2026
This bill imposes a variety of sanctions, tariffs, and prohibitions related to Russia, extends an Iran-related sanctions law, and expands a tax deduction for teacher expenses to include early childhood educators.
For example, under the bill, the President must impose visa- and property-blocking sanctions on specified persons (individuals and entities) such as the Russian president and certain Russian military commanders. The President must also increase the rate of duty up to 100% ad valorem (i.e., relative to the value) on all goods imported into the United States from a country that was among the five largest importers of Russian-origin crude oil or natural gas if such country knowingly makes new purchases of such products after enactment of the bill.
The bill prohibits (1) the export, reexport, or in-country transfer to or in Russia of any U.S.-produced energy or energy product; (2) U.S. persons from making new investments in Russia or purchasing Russian sovereign debt; and (3) trading the securities of Russian government-owned, -controlled, or -affiliated entities on U.S. national securities exchanges.
The bill extends through 2031 the Iran Sanctions Act of 1996, which requires the President, with some exceptions, to impose sanctions on certain persons engaged in specified transactions related to Iran's energy sector or Iran's efforts to acquire or develop certain weapons.
The bill expands eligibility for federal tax deductions of certain educator expenses to early childhood educators providing educational or childcare services to those under age 6.
posts.summaryLabel: Congressional Research Service, Passed Senate
posts.meta: Ways and Means Committee · Rep. Jimmy Panetta (D-CA)
posts.whatsNext: President has 10 days (Sundays excepted): sign, veto, or it becomes law unsigned (pocket veto if adjournment prevents return)

aiSummaries.text:
This bill sets up a range of sanctions and trade restrictions aimed at Russia, extends an existing law that punishes certain dealings with Iran, and widens a tax break for teachers so that it also covers some early childhood educators.

On Russia, the President must block visas and property of named individuals and organizations, including the Russian president and certain Russian military commanders. The President must also be able to raise tariffs on goods coming into the United States from a country that was among the five largest buyers of Russian crude oil or natural gas, up to 100% of the goods' value, if that country knowingly makes new purchases of those products after the bill becomes law.

The bill also bans three things: exporting or moving U.S.-made energy products to or within Russia, American individuals and companies making new investments in Russia or buying Russian government debt, and trading the stocks of Russian government-owned, controlled, or affiliated companies on U.S. stock exchanges.

The bill extends the Iran Sanctions Act of 1996 through 2031. That law requires the President, with some exceptions, to impose sanctions on certain people who take part in specified deals involving Iran's energy sector or its efforts to get or develop certain weapons.

Finally, the bill extends a federal tax deduction for certain educator expenses to early childhood educators who provide educational or childcare services to children under age 6.

posts.title: Ratepayer Protection Act
posts.label: ✅🏛️ Passed House with amendment (417-3)
posts.summary:
Ratepayer Protection Act
The bill requires state utility regulators and nonregulated utilities to consider implementing a standard to hold certain large-load customers responsible for the costs associated with any generation, transmission, or distribution upgrade of electric service necessary to serve such customers. A large-load customer means a non-residential electric consumer that enters, or requests to enter, an agreement concerning the sale of electric energy primarily to operate information technology infrastructure and related systems pertaining to data storage and computational applications and services (e.g., data centers) that have a peak electric demand of 100 megawatts or more at a single site or campus.
Specifically, the bill requires states to consider implementing a federal standard for large-load customers. The standard must require rates charged by electric utilities for providing electric service to a large-load customer to be designed to recover from the large-load customer the full, incremental cost of any generation, transmission, or distribution upgrade necessary to serve such customer. This rate must include the costs that would be incurred if the large-load customer terminates an agreement with the electric utility pertaining to the sale of electric energy or otherwise ceases the purchase of energy from the electric utility.
Under the standard, an electric utility must require the large-load customer to provide to the utility financial assurances or contributions to cover the cost of any generation, transmission, or distribution upgrade that is necessary to serve the load of a large-load customer before the utility makes any generation, transmission, or distribution upgrade.
posts.summaryLabel: Congressional Research Service, Reported to House
posts.meta: Energy and Commerce Committee · Rep. Gabe Evans (R-CO)
posts.whatsNext: To the Senate (if and when it takes it up)

aiSummaries.text:
This bill asks state utility regulators and nonregulated utilities to consider a standard that makes large electricity users pay for the power system upgrades needed to serve them. The "large-load customers" it covers are non-residential customers, such as data centers, that buy electricity mainly to run computing and data storage operations and have a peak demand of 100 megawatts or more at a single site or campus.

Under the proposed standard, the rates a utility charges these customers would have to be set so that the customer covers the full added cost of any new power generation, transmission, or distribution upgrade needed to serve it. The rates would also have to cover the costs the utility would still face if the customer ends its agreement or stops buying power from that utility.

The standard would also require utilities to collect financial assurances or contributions from the large-load customer before they build any generation, transmission, or distribution upgrade needed to serve that customer.

posts.title: Civil Preparedness for Agroterrorism Exercise Act of 2026
posts.label: ✅🏛️ Passed House (voice vote)
posts.summary:
Civil Preparedness for Agroterrorism Exercise Act of 2026
This bill requires the Department of Homeland Security (DHS), within four years after the bill’s enactment, to conduct an exercise to enhance collective domestic prevention, response, and recovery regarding acts of agroterrorism (i.e., terrorism targeting or threatening agriculture and food systems of vital importance to national security, public health, or safety). The scenario in the exercise must involve agroterrorists transporting and deploying in the United States a biological agent (e.g., microorganism or infectious substance) capable of harming critical agriculture and food operations and must address how relevant public and private entities can coordinate to develop preparedness and mitigate widespread disruption.
Within 180 days after completion of the exercise, DHS must submit to Congress an after-action report including the findings of the exercise, plans for incorporating lessons learned into future operations, and recommended legislative actions.
posts.summaryLabel: Congressional Research Service, Introduced in House
posts.committee: Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee, Homeland Security Committee
posts.meta: Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee, Homeland Security Committee · Rep. Dale Strong (R-AL)
posts.whatsNext: To the Senate (if and when it takes it up)

aiSummaries.text:
This bill would require the Department of Homeland Security to run a practice exercise within four years of the bill becoming law. The exercise would prepare the country to prevent, respond to, and recover from agroterrorism, meaning attacks aimed at farming and food systems that are vital to national security, public health, or safety.

The practice scenario must involve people who carry out such attacks bringing a biological agent, such as a microorganism or infectious substance, into the United States and using it to harm important farm and food operations. The exercise must also look at how public agencies and private businesses can work together to get ready and limit widespread disruption.

Within 180 days after the exercise is finished, the Department of Homeland Security must send Congress a report. That report must include what the exercise found, plans for using those lessons in future work, and suggested laws to pass.

posts.title: Retire through Ownership Act
posts.label: ✅🏛️ Passed House (401-14)
posts.summary:
Retire through Ownership Act
This bill allows the fiduciary of an Employee Stock Ownership Plan (ESOP) to rely on a valuation provided by an independent valuation expert or business appraiser in determining the fair market value of the plan's securities if the securities are not traded on a national securities exchange (i.e., not publicly traded) and the expert or appraiser follows specified methodologies.
In general, ESOPs are defined contribution pension plans where employees accrue shares of their employers' stock in individual accounts as part of their compensation. After separating from employment or retiring, employees receive the cash value of their shares.
Under the bill, an independent expert or appraiser must adhere to the methodology established under the Internal Revenue Service Ruling 59-60, which prescribes the factors a professional business appraiser should consider in forming a valuation of the stock for a closely held business.

posts.meta: Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee · Sen. Roger Marshall (R-KS)

aiSummaries.text:
The Retire through Ownership Act lets the trustee of an Employee Stock Ownership Plan (ESOP) rely on a valuation from an independent valuation expert or business appraiser when setting the fair market value of plan stock that is not publicly traded. The expert or appraiser must follow the methods set out in the bill.

ESOPs are retirement plans in which employees earn shares of their employer's stock in individual accounts as part of their pay. When an employee leaves the job or retires, they receive the cash value of those shares.

Under the bill, the independent expert or appraiser must use the approach in Internal Revenue Service Ruling 59-60. That ruling lists the factors a professional business appraiser should consider when valuing stock in a closely held business.

aiSummaries.text:
The Billion Dollar Boondoggle Act of 2025 would require the Office of Management and Budget (OMB) to gather information from federal agencies about federally funded projects that are running badly behind schedule or going far over budget, and then report on them to Congress.

Under the bill, OMB must issue guidance telling agencies to send it information each year about projects that are either more than five years behind schedule or have spent at least $1 billion more than their original cost estimate.

For each of these projects, agencies must report a description of the project, any changes to its original scope, and both the original and current expected completion dates. They must also report the original and current cost estimates, adjusted for inflation, along with explanations for any delays or cost increases. Finally, they must report any award, incentive fee, or other bonus given for the project and the reason for it.

OMB must then prepare an annual report for Congress that includes all of this information and post the report on its website.

posts.title: Protect College Sports Act of 2026
posts.label: 🗳️ Motion to proceed filed
posts.summary:
Protect College Sports Act of 2026
This bill establishes requirements for name, image, or likeness (NIL) agreements for college student athletes and provides a limited antitrust exemption for schools and conferences to pool and sell certain college sports media rights. The requirements address elements of the court-approved agreement to settle In re College Athlete NIL Litigation (i.e., House settlement).
First, the bill statutorily prohibits institutions, conferences, or interstate intercollegiate athletic associations (e.g., the National Collegiate Athletic Association [NCAA]) from restricting student athletes from entering NIL agreements (subject to specified limitations). Students must report to their institution NIL compensation greater than $600.
The bill requires agents to register with a state and caps agent endorsement contract fees at 5%.
The bill also provides student athletes with one transfer without losing athletic eligibility and restricts football personnel from becoming the head football coach at a different institution during the same season.
Further, the bill prohibits institutions, conferences, or specified entities acting for the benefit of an institution from providing athletes with compensation that circumvents the limit on sharing revenue with student athletes established under the House settlement. The bill also makes the limit permanent and provides for an annual inflation adjustment.
The bill generally prohibits Division I conferences from reducing the number of varsity or Olympic sports teams that a member institution must sponsor. Specifically, large institutions ($80 million or more in annual athletics revenue) must offer and maintain at least as many grant-in-aid opportunities and roster spots for sports that do not generate positive net revenue as the institution provided during academic year 2024-25. The bill provides for a waiver of this requirement under certain circumstances of financial hardship and the requirements expire nine years after the enactment of the bill.
Additionally, the bill establishes (subject to specified conditions) a limited antitrust exemption for institutions or conferences that form joint agreements to transfer their sports telecasting rights to a third party. Such an agreement requires participation from at least 75% of the institutions in the Football Bowl Subdivision.
posts.summaryLabel: Congressional Research Service, Reported to Senate
posts.meta: Commerce, Science, and Transportation Committee · Sen. Ted Cruz (R-TX)
posts.whatsNext: The Senate votes on taking it up (the motion can be withdrawn)

aiSummaries.text:
The Protect College Sports Act of 2026 sets rules for how college athletes can earn money from their name, image, or likeness (NIL) and gives schools and conferences a limited legal exemption to pool and sell certain sports TV and media rights. Many of its requirements follow up on a court-approved settlement in a lawsuit known as the House settlement.

Under the bill, colleges, conferences, and national athletic associations such as the NCAA generally cannot stop student athletes from signing NIL deals, though some limits apply. Students must report to their school any NIL pay greater than $600. Agents who work with athletes must register with a state, and their fees under endorsement contracts are capped at 5%.

The bill also makes some changes to athletes' eligibility and coaching. Student athletes can transfer one time without losing their eligibility to compete. Football personnel are barred from becoming the head football coach at a different school during the same season.

To prevent schools from getting around the House settlement, the bill bans payments to athletes that are designed to avoid the limit on revenue sharing with athletes. That limit becomes permanent and will rise each year to keep pace with inflation.

For Division I conferences, the bill generally stops them from cutting the number of varsity or Olympic sports teams that member schools must sponsor. Large schools, defined as those with $80 million or more in annual athletics revenue, must keep offering at least as many scholarships and roster spots in sports that do not bring in positive net revenue as they did in the 2024-25 academic year. A waiver is available in certain serious financial hardship cases. These requirements expire nine years after the bill is enacted.

Finally, the bill creates a limited antitrust exemption, subject to certain conditions, that lets schools or conferences jointly agree to transfer their sports broadcast rights to a third party. Such an agreement must include at least 75% of the schools in the Football Bowl Subdivision.

aiSummaries.text:
The Prison Staff Safety Enhancement Act requires the Department of Justice and its agencies to look closely at incidents where people in federal prison sexually harass or sexually assault Bureau of Prisons staff, and to respond to them. The Department of Justice must also set national standards aimed at preventing these incidents, reducing them, and punishing them when they happen. These standards cover harassment and assault by incarcerated people against correctional officers and other Bureau of Prisons employees.

The act also requires the Bureau of Prisons to fully carry out the recommendations made by the Justice Department's Inspector General. Those recommendations come from a report evaluating how well the Bureau of Prisons has been handling sexual harassment and sexual assault committed by inmates against staff.
