posts.title: Science of Reading Act of 2026
posts.label: ✅🏛️ Passed House with amendment (voice vote)
posts.summary:
Science of Reading Act of 2026
This bill revises the Comprehensive Literacy State Development (CLSD) grant program to prioritize literacy instruction that is aligned to the science of reading.
Under the bill, science of reading is defined as an interdisciplinary body of evidence-based research about reading and issues related to reading and writing that (1) identifies instruction in phonemic awareness, phonics, vocabulary, fluency, comprehension, and writing as essential components to skilled reading; (2) demonstrates the importance of background knowledge, oral language, the connection between reading and writing, and strong writing instruction; (3) explains why some students have difficulty with reading and writing; and (4) does not use a three-cueing model. Three-cueing model means an instructional approach or model that (1) uses meaning drawn from context, pictures, or syntax as the primary basis for teaching word recognition; or (2) teaches visual memory as the primary basis for word recognition.
Current law authorizes competitive CLSD grants to state educational agencies (SEAs) and, through them, competitive subgrants to local educational agencies for the development and implementation of a comprehensive literacy instruction plan, professional development, and other activities. Eligible early childhood education programs may also receive subgrants for early literacy services.
The bill (1) specifies that comprehensive literacy instruction for CLSD grants does not include the use of a three-cueing model, and (2) requires the Department of Education and SEAs to prioritize awarding CLSD grants and subgrants for evidence-based activities that are aligned to the science of reading.
posts.summaryLabel: Congressional Research Service, Reported to House
posts.meta: Education and Workforce Committee · Rep. Erin Houchin (R-IN)
posts.whatsNext: To the Senate (if and when it takes it up)

aiSummaries.text:
The Science of Reading Act of 2026 changes a federal literacy grant program so that its money goes first to reading instruction based on the science of reading. Under the bill, the science of reading is a body of evidence-based research about reading and writing. It treats phonemic awareness, phonics, vocabulary, fluency, comprehension, and writing as essential parts of becoming a skilled reader. It also stresses the importance of background knowledge, oral language, the link between reading and writing, and strong writing instruction, and it explains why some students struggle with reading and writing.

The bill also rules out a "three-cueing" approach. That is a teaching method that relies mainly on guessing a word from its surrounding context, pictures, or sentence structure, or that relies mainly on visual memory of whole words. Under the bill, comprehensive literacy instruction supported by these grants cannot use this approach.

The grant program currently lets the Department of Education and state education agencies give competitive grants and subgrants to local school districts and, in some cases, early childhood programs. These funds support literacy plans, teacher training, and related activities. The bill requires the Department and state agencies to give priority to grants and subgrants for activities that are aligned with the science of reading.

posts.title: Providing for congressional disapproval under chapter 8 of title 5, United States Code, of the rule issued by the Environmental Protection Agency relating to the "California State Nonroad Engine Pollution Control Standards; Commercial Harbor Craft Regulations; Notice of Decision".
posts.label: ✅🏛️ Passed House (214-208)
posts.summary:
This joint resolution revokes the partial authorization granted to the California Air Resources Board (CARB) to amend its Commercial Harbor Craft regulation. Among other elements, the amendments proposed by CARB and partially authorized by the Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) create new emission standards and compliance dates depending on vessel category and engine model year and expand the types of vessels covered by the regulation (e.g. commercial fishing boats). (Under the Clean Air Act, the EPA may authorize California to adopt and enforce standards relating to the control of emissions from nonroad vehicles or engines if those standards meet certain requirements.)
Specifically, the joint resolution nullifies the EPA authorization decision titled California State Nonroad Engine Pollution Control Standards; Commercial Harbor Craft Regulations; Notice of Decision.
posts.summaryLabel: Congressional Research Service, Introduced in House
posts.meta: Energy and Commerce Committee · Rep. James Gallagher (R-CA)
posts.whatsNext: To the Senate (if and when it takes it up)

aiSummaries.text:
This measure cancels the partial permission that the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency had given to the California Air Resources Board to update its rules for commercial harbor craft, which are boats used for work in ports and harbors. The rule changes the state wanted would set new pollution limits and compliance deadlines that depend on the type of vessel and the year its engine was made, and would also apply to more kinds of boats, such as commercial fishing boats.

The background is that under the federal Clean Air Act, the EPA can let California adopt and enforce its own standards for controlling emissions from nonroad vehicles and engines, but only if those standards meet certain requirements. The resolution specifically cancels the EPA decision titled "California State Nonroad Engine Pollution Control Standards; Commercial Harbor Craft Regulations; Notice of Decision," which is the action that had granted the partial authorization.

posts.title: PROOF Act
posts.label: ✅🏛️ Passed House (217-207)
posts.summary:
Preventing Rip-offs and Obtaining Oversight of Funds Act or the PROOF Act
This bill requires states to provide such information as the Department of Justice (DOJ) may require for the purpose of investigating or prosecuting alleged fraud committed with regard to certain federally funded programs.
Programs covered by this requirement include:
Medicaid,
Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program (SNAP),
Temporary Assistance for Needy Families (TANF),
certain federal payments and grants to state governments related to the coronavirus response, and
any other program to which funds are made available to states and identified by DOJ as vulnerable to fraud.
A federal agency may only use such information for law enforcement purposes related to fraud and may not disclose it for any unrelated administrative or commercial purpose.
DOJ must annually report to Congress on the number of requests for information issued to state agencies under this bill, the programs with respect to which such requests were made, and the number of fraud investigations initiated and convictions secured using the information obtained.
posts.summaryLabel: Congressional Research Service, Introduced in House
posts.meta: Judiciary Committee · Rep. Jefferson Van Drew (R-NJ)
posts.whatsNext: To the Senate (if and when it takes it up)

aiSummaries.text:
The PROOF Act would require states to give the Department of Justice whatever information it asks for when investigating or prosecuting suspected fraud in certain federally funded programs. These programs include Medicaid, the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program (SNAP), Temporary Assistance for Needy Families (TANF), certain federal payments and grants to states related to the coronavirus response, and any other program that receives funds for states and that the Justice Department identifies as vulnerable to fraud.

Federal agencies could use this information only for law enforcement purposes connected to fraud. They could not share it for unrelated administrative or commercial purposes.

Each year, the Justice Department would have to report to Congress on how many requests it sent to state agencies under the bill, which programs those requests involved, and how many fraud investigations were started and how many convictions were obtained using the information.

posts.title: Stopping Political Discrimination in Disaster Assistance Act
posts.label: ✅🏛️ Passed House (voice vote)
posts.summary:
Stopping Political Discrimination in Disaster Assistance Act
This bill prohibits discrimination on the basis of political affiliation by the Federal Emergency Management Agency (FEMA) and other participating entities (i.e., public or private entities providing or receiving assistance) in carrying out federal major disaster or emergency relief and assistance activities.
Current law requires FEMA and other participating entities to provide federal major disaster or emergency relief and assistance without discrimination on the basis of race, color, religion, nationality, sex, age, disability, English proficiency, or economic status. The bill adds political affiliation to the classes protected under this requirement.
posts.summaryLabel: Congressional Research Service, Introduced in House
posts.committee: Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee, Transportation and Infrastructure Committee
posts.meta: Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee, Transportation and Infrastructure Committee · Rep. Scott Perry (R-PA)
posts.whatsNext: To the Senate (if and when it takes it up)

aiSummaries.text:
This bill would stop the Federal Emergency Management Agency (FEMA) and other groups involved in disaster aid from treating people differently based on their political party or political views. It covers any public or private group that gives or receives help during federal major disaster or emergency relief efforts.

The bill adds political affiliation to a list of characteristics that already cannot be used to deny disaster help. Under current law, aid must be provided without discrimination based on race, color, religion, nationality, sex, age, disability, English proficiency, or economic status. With this bill, political affiliation would be added to that list.

posts.title: Protect College Sports Act of 2026
posts.label: ⏱️ Cloture invoked (on taking up the bill) (74-24)
posts.summary:
Protect College Sports Act of 2026
This bill establishes requirements for name, image, or likeness (NIL) agreements for college student athletes and provides a limited antitrust exemption for schools and conferences to pool and sell certain college sports media rights. The requirements address elements of the court-approved agreement to settle In re College Athlete NIL Litigation (i.e., House settlement).
First, the bill statutorily prohibits institutions, conferences, or interstate intercollegiate athletic associations (e.g., the National Collegiate Athletic Association [NCAA]) from restricting student athletes from entering NIL agreements (subject to specified limitations). Students must report to their institution NIL compensation greater than $600.
The bill requires agents to register with a state and caps agent endorsement contract fees at 5%.
The bill also provides student athletes with one transfer without losing athletic eligibility and restricts football personnel from becoming the head football coach at a different institution during the same season.
Further, the bill prohibits institutions, conferences, or specified entities acting for the benefit of an institution from providing athletes with compensation that circumvents the limit on sharing revenue with student athletes established under the House settlement. The bill also makes the limit permanent and provides for an annual inflation adjustment.
The bill generally prohibits Division I conferences from reducing the number of varsity or Olympic sports teams that a member institution must sponsor. Specifically, large institutions ($80 million or more in annual athletics revenue) must offer and maintain at least as many grant-in-aid opportunities and roster spots for sports that do not generate positive net revenue as the institution provided during academic year 2024-25. The bill provides for a waiver of this requirement under certain circumstances of financial hardship and the requirements expire nine years after the enactment of the bill.
Additionally, the bill establishes (subject to specified conditions) a limited antitrust exemption for institutions or conferences that form joint agreements to transfer their sports telecasting rights to a third party. Such an agreement requires participation from at least 75% of the institutions in the Football Bowl Subdivision.
posts.summaryLabel: Congressional Research Service, Reported to Senate
posts.meta: Commerce, Science, and Transportation Committee · Sen. Ted Cruz (R-TX)
posts.whatsNext: Senate votes on taking up the bill (up to 30 hours on the motion first)

aiSummaries.text:
The Protect College Sports Act of 2026 sets rules for how college athletes can earn money from their name, image, or likeness (NIL) and gives schools and conferences a limited legal exemption to pool and sell certain sports TV and media rights. Many of its requirements follow up on a court-approved settlement in a lawsuit known as the House settlement.

Under the bill, colleges, conferences, and national athletic associations such as the NCAA generally cannot stop student athletes from signing NIL deals, though some limits apply. Students must report to their school any NIL pay greater than $600. Agents who work with athletes must register with a state, and their fees under endorsement contracts are capped at 5%.

The bill also makes some changes to athletes' eligibility and coaching. Student athletes can transfer one time without losing their eligibility to compete. Football personnel are barred from becoming the head football coach at a different school during the same season.

To prevent schools from getting around the House settlement, the bill bans payments to athletes that are designed to avoid the limit on revenue sharing with athletes. That limit becomes permanent and will rise each year to keep pace with inflation.

For Division I conferences, the bill generally stops them from cutting the number of varsity or Olympic sports teams that member schools must sponsor. Large schools, defined as those with $80 million or more in annual athletics revenue, must keep offering at least as many scholarships and roster spots in sports that do not bring in positive net revenue as they did in the 2024-25 academic year. A waiver is available in certain serious financial hardship cases. These requirements expire nine years after the bill is enacted.

Finally, the bill creates a limited antitrust exemption, subject to certain conditions, that lets schools or conferences jointly agree to transfer their sports broadcast rights to a third party. Such an agreement must include at least 75% of the schools in the Football Bowl Subdivision.

posts.title: Midnight Rules Relief Act of 2025
posts.label: 📋 Reported by committee
posts.note: Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs, without amendment, without written report
posts.summary:
Midnight Rules Relief Act of 2025
This bill allows Congress to disapprove multiple regulations under one joint resolution of disapproval if the regulations were submitted for review during a portion of the final year of a President's term.
Under current law, the Congressional Review Act generally provides for a period of additional review during the succeeding Congress for regulations that were submitted during the last 60 legislative days of the prior Congress. However, each joint resolution may disapprove of only one regulation.
posts.summaryLabel: Congressional Research Service, Introduced in Senate
posts.committee: Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee
posts.meta: Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee · Sen. Ron Johnson (R-WI)
posts.whatsNext: Floor scheduling (leadership decides if and when it gets a vote)

aiSummaries.text: This bill would let Congress reject several regulations at once with a single joint resolution, as long as those regulations were sent for review during part of a President's final year in office. Right now, under the Congressional Review Act, regulations submitted during the last 60 legislative days of a Congress can get an extra review period in the next Congress, but each joint resolution can only reject one regulation.

posts.title: To require the Commissioner of U.S. Customs and Border Protection to link together applications of family members throughout the NEXUS application process, and for other purposes.
posts.label: 📋 Reported by committee
posts.note: Homeland Security, H. Rept. 119-828
posts.summary:
This bill requires U.S. Customs and Border Protection (CBP) to link the applications of family members (parents, legal guardians, children, grandparents, grandchildren, and siblings residing within a single household) throughout the NEXUS application process (an expedited border inspections program between the United-States and Canada).
CBP must permit a family member to schedule NEXUS interviews for all linked family members and may provide linked family members the option to participate in joint interviews.
CBP may exempt from the interview process a child under 14 years of age who is linked to an eligible family member.
posts.summaryLabel: Congressional Research Service, Introduced in House
posts.meta: Homeland Security Committee · Rep. Timothy Kennedy (D-NY)
posts.whatsNext: Floor scheduling (leadership decides if and when it gets a vote)

aiSummaries.text:
This bill would require U.S. Customs and Border Protection (CBP) to connect the NEXUS applications of family members who live together in one household. Covered relatives include parents, legal guardians, children, grandparents, grandchildren, and siblings. NEXUS is a program that speeds up border crossings between the United States and Canada.

Under the bill, CBP must let one family member schedule NEXUS interviews for all of the linked family members. CBP may also offer linked family members the option of attending a joint interview together.

CBP may skip the interview for a child under 14 who is linked to an eligible family member.

posts.title: To require the Administrator of the Transportation Security Administration of the United States to develop guidelines to improve returning citizens' access to the Transportation Worker Identification Credential program, to assist individuals in custody of Federal, State, and local prisons in pre-applying or preparing applications for Transportation Worker Identification Credential cards, and to assist individuals requesting an appeal or waiver of preliminary determination of ineligibility, and for other purposes.
posts.label: 📋 Reported by committee
posts.note: Homeland Security, H. Rept. 119-827
posts.summary:
This bill directs the Transportation Security Administration (TSA) to develop guidelines to improve access to a Transportation Worker Identification Credential (TWIC) for prisoners prior to their release.
Specifically, TSA must develop guidelines to assist individuals in federal, state, and local prisons in (1) pre-applying or preparing an application for a TWIC card; and (2) requesting an appeal or waiver of a preliminary determination of ineligibility for a TWIC card.
As background, a TWIC card is required by the Maritime Transportation Security Act for workers who need access to secure areas of U.S. maritime facilities and vessels. TSA conducts a background check to determine a person’s eligibility and issues the credential.
posts.summaryLabel: Congressional Research Service, Introduced in House
posts.meta: Homeland Security Committee · Rep. Troy Carter (D-LA)
posts.whatsNext: Floor scheduling (leadership decides if and when it gets a vote)

aiSummaries.text:
This bill asks the Transportation Security Administration (TSA) to create guidelines that make it easier for people in prison to get a Transportation Worker Identification Credential (TWIC) before they are released. Under the bill, the guidelines would help people in federal, state, and local prisons do two things: start or prepare their TWIC application ahead of time, and ask for an appeal or waiver if they receive a preliminary decision that they are not eligible for the card.

Some background helps explain why this matters. The Maritime Transportation Security Act requires a TWIC card for workers who need access to secure areas of U.S. ports, maritime facilities, and vessels. To decide whether someone qualifies, TSA runs a background check and then issues the credential if the person is eligible.

posts.title: Northern Border Security Enhancement and Review Act
posts.label: 📋 Reported by committee
posts.note: Homeland Security, H. Rept. 119-830
posts.summary:
Northern Border Security Enhancement and Review Act
This bill requires the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) to regularly perform a threat analysis of the northern U.S. border.
The analysis must be performed every two years and include terroristic and criminal threats, improvements needed to prevent terrorism and reduce criminal activity, and whether preclearance and advance inspection operations at northern ports of entry could prevent terrorists from entering in the United States.
DHS must (1) update its northern border strategy after performing each threat analysis, and (2) provide a classified briefing to Congress. If DHS determines no update is required, DHS must notify Congress.
U.S. Customs and Border Protection’s Air and Marine Operations (AMO) must develop performance measures to assess the AMO’s effectiveness at securing the northern border between ports of entry in air and maritime environments.
posts.summaryLabel: Congressional Research Service, Introduced in House
posts.meta: Homeland Security Committee · Rep. Nicholas Langworthy (R-NY)
posts.whatsNext: Floor scheduling (leadership decides if and when it gets a vote)

aiSummaries.text:
The Northern Border Security Enhancement and Review Act requires the Department of Homeland Security to review threats along the northern U.S. border every two years. Each review must look at terrorist and criminal threats, identify improvements needed to prevent terrorism and reduce crime, and assess whether preclearance and advance inspection operations at northern ports of entry could help keep terrorists from entering the United States.

After each review, the Department must update its northern border strategy and give Congress a classified briefing. If the Department decides no update is needed, it must tell Congress that instead.

The bill also requires U.S. Customs and Border Protection's Air and Marine Operations to create performance measures. These measures will be used to judge how well the office secures the northern border between official ports of entry, both in the air and at sea.

posts.title: EMRTAI Authorization Act of 2026
posts.label: 📋 Reported by committee
posts.note: Energy and Commerce, H. Rept. 119-821
posts.summary:
Environmental Monitoring and Remediation Technology Assessment Initiative Authorization Act of 2026 or the EMRTAI Authorization Act of 2026
This provides statutory authority for an initiative within the Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) that recovers critical materials from contaminated sites.
A critical material means (1) any non-fuel mineral, element, substance, or material that the Department of Energy determines has a high risk of a supply chain disruption and serves an essential function in energy technologies; and (2) any critical mineral. A critical mineral means any mineral, element, substance, or material designated as critical by the U.S. Geological Survey.
Under the program, the EPA must investigate, evaluate, and support processes, methods, and systems which may be used to identify sources of critical materials at contaminated sites and recover such critical materials from those sites. In carrying out the program, the EPA may provide assistance (e.g., awards) to persons, nonprofit organizations, and state, local, and tribal government entities.
The bill prohibits the EPA from providing assistance (1) in an amount that exceeds $10 million in any fiscal year in the aggregate; or (2) to any person, nonprofit organization, or government entity, in an amount that exceeds $3 million.
The bill terminates the program after 10 years.
posts.summaryLabel: Congressional Research Service, Introduced in House
posts.meta: Energy and Commerce Committee · Rep. August Pfluger (R-TX)
posts.whatsNext: Floor scheduling (leadership decides if and when it gets a vote)

aiSummaries.text:
The EMRTAI Authorization Act of 2026 creates a program within the Environmental Protection Agency to recover critical materials from contaminated sites. It applies to two kinds of materials: any non-fuel mineral, element, substance, or material that the Department of Energy determines has a high risk of supply chain disruption and serves an essential function in energy technologies, and any mineral designated as critical by the U.S. Geological Survey.

Under the program, the EPA must investigate, evaluate, and support methods and systems that can find where these critical materials are at contaminated sites and recover them. The EPA may provide assistance, such as awards, to individuals, nonprofit organizations, and state, local, and tribal governments to carry out this work.

The law sets spending limits. The EPA may not provide more than $10 million in assistance in any fiscal year in total, and it may not give any single person, nonprofit organization, or government entity more than $3 million.

The program ends after 10 years.

posts.title: CHARM Act
posts.label: 📋 Reported by committee
posts.note: Energy and Commerce, H. Rept. 119-820
posts.summary:
Coordinating and Harnessing America’s Recovery of Minerals Act or the CHARM Act
This bill requires the Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) to establish and carry out a national strategy for recovering critical minerals from discarded materials. Critical minerals are defined as any mineral, element, substance, or material designated as critical by the U.S. Geological Survey because it is essential to U.S. economic or national security, has a vulnerable supply chain, and serves an essential function in manufacturing a product.
The EPA must report to Congress every two years on its actions, plans, and recommendations relating to the national strategy.
posts.summaryLabel: Congressional Research Service, Introduced in House
posts.meta: Energy and Commerce Committee · Rep. Gary Palmer (R-AL)
posts.whatsNext: Floor scheduling (leadership decides if and when it gets a vote)

aiSummaries.text:
This bill, the Coordinating and Harnessing America's Recovery of Minerals Act (the CHARM Act), would require the Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) to create and carry out a national plan for recovering critical minerals from discarded materials. Critical minerals are those the U.S. Geological Survey has labeled as critical because they are essential to the nation's economy or security, their supply chains are vulnerable, and they play an essential role in making a product.

The EPA would also have to report to Congress every two years on what it has done, what it plans to do, and what it recommends regarding this national strategy.

aiSummaries.text:

The first bill would create a National Fraud Enforcement Division within the Department of Justice. The second would make it easier for federal law enforcement and state agencies to share information in order to detect, investigate, and prosecute fraud in certain federal programs, while also protecting individual privacy.

posts.title: American Music Tourism Act of 2025
posts.label: ✅🏛️ Passed House (voice vote)
posts.summary:
American Music Tourism Act of 2025
This bill directs the National Travel and Tourism Office (NTTO) of the Department of Commerce to promote tourism to music-related and sports attractions.
The bill requires NTTO to promote domestic and international travel and tourism to U.S. music festivals, concert venues, and other music-related attractions and locations. The bill also expands NTTO's current mandate to facilitate sports and recreation events and activities to include the promotion of international travel and tourism to such activities in the United States.
NTTO must report its activities and findings to Congress within one year after the bill's enactment and, thereafter, every two years.

The office would be required to encourage both domestic and international travel to U.S. music festivals, concert venues, and other music-related places. It would also expand its existing work on sports and recreation so that it promotes international travel to those events and activities in the United States. posts.title: Fostering the Use of Technology to Uphold Regulatory Effectiveness in Supervision Act
posts.label: ✅🏛️ Passed House with amendment (417-7)
posts.summary:
Fostering the Use of Technology to Uphold Regulatory Effectiveness in Supervision Act
This bill requires specified federal financial agencies to assess their technological capabilities and procurement practices.
Specifically, agencies (the Federal Reserve Board, the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau, the Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation, the Department of the Treasury, the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency, the Financial Crimes Enforcement Network, the Federal Housing Finance Agency, and the National Credit Union Administration) must assess the technology used by the agency and its capabilities to conduct real-time supervisory assessments of entities over which the agency has supervisory authority.
Additionally, the agencies must assess the applicable procurement rules and protocols when acquiring or developing new technological systems and identify any opportunities to streamline these procedures.
Every five years, these agencies must report to specified congressional committees. Among other topics, the report must contain an overview of the technology used in supervisory assessments and any anticipated upgrades, a description of procurement practices, an overview of the agency’s technology development workforce, and details regarding data sharing procedures.
posts.summaryLabel: Congressional Research Service, Reported to House
posts.meta: Financial Services Committee · Rep. Marlin Stutzman (R-IN)
posts.whatsNext: To the Senate (if and when it takes it up)

aiSummaries.text:
The Fostering the Use of Technology to Uphold Regulatory Effectiveness in Supervision Act would require several federal financial agencies to examine their technology and how they buy it. The agencies covered are the Federal Reserve Board, the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau, the Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation, the Department of the Treasury, the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency, the Financial Crimes Enforcement Network, the Federal Housing Finance Agency, and the National Credit Union Administration.

Each agency would have to review the technology it uses now and whether that technology lets it carry out real-time supervisory checks on the entities it oversees.

The agencies would also have to review the rules and procedures they follow when they acquire or build new technology systems, and identify any ways to make those procedures more efficient.

Every five years, each agency would report to the specified congressional committees. The reports would cover, among other things, the technology used in supervisory checks and any planned upgrades, how the agency buys technology, the make-up of its workforce that develops technology, and how it shares data.

Load Forecasting Enhancement Act
This bill requires the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission (FERC) to establish regional boards to study and recommend best practices for electric load forecasting, which is the process of predicting the demand for electricity at a particular time. It also requires states to consider adopting the recommendations.
Specifically, the bill directs FERC to establish regional boards to study electric load forecasting, chair the boards, and run them jointly with each state public utility commission in the regions. The boards must (1) study issues relevant to identifying best practices for electric load forecasting that enhance the reliability and affordability of electric service to customers, and (2) identify such best practices. FERC must make recommendations to Congress for the consistent use across states of such best practices by electric utilities.
The bill also modifies provisions under the Public Utility Regulatory Policies Act to require state public utility commissions to consider adopting those recommendations.
It also modifies the Energy Policy and Conservation Act to make federal assistance for state energy conservation plans contingent upon the plan including procedures and programs to improve the accuracy, oversight, and transparency to stakeholders of the forecasting of electric loads by electric utilities.

posts.meta: Energy and Commerce Committee · Rep. Troy Balderson (R-OH)

FERC would create these boards and chair them, running each one jointly with the state utility commissions in its region. The boards would study the issues involved in good forecasting, identify best practices, and then FERC would recommend to Congress how those practices could be used consistently across states by electric utilities.

The bill would also change the Public Utility Regulatory Policies Act so that state utility commissions must consider adopting those recommendations.

In addition, the bill would change the Energy Policy and Conservation Act so that federal help for state energy conservation plans depends on those plans including steps to make electric load forecasting by utilities more accurate, more closely overseen, and more transparent to stakeholders.

posts.title: End Tax Penalties on American Hostages Act
posts.label: ✅🏛️ Passed House with amendment (voice vote)
posts.summary:
End Tax Penalties on American Hostages Act
This bill extends certain federal tax deadlines for U.S. nationals who are unlawfully or wrongfully detained abroad or held hostage abroad and their spouses. The bill also allows for an abatement and refund of additional taxes, interest, and penalties assessed to such individuals for failing to meet a federal tax deadline during a period of detention.
Specifically, under the bill, the time period during which a U.S. national is unlawfully or wrongfully detained abroad or held hostage abroad is disregarded in determining certain federal tax deadlines, including deadlines for
filing a return for and paying federal income, estate, gift, employment, or excise taxes;
a tax credit or refund claim; and
the determination, assessment, and collection of additional taxes, interest, or penalties.
The bill requires the Department of State and the Department of Justice to annually provide the Internal Revenue Service (IRS) with lists to identify U.S. nationals who qualify for an extension.
The bill also requires the IRS to (1) abate and refund additional taxes, interest, and penalties assessed for any tax year ending during a period of detention for which an extension of a federal tax deadline is permitted; and (2) establish a program allowing U.S. nationals unlawfully or wrongfully detained abroad or taken hostage abroad (or their spouse or dependent) to claim a refund of additional taxes, interest, and penalties assessed for any tax year ending during a period of detention from 2021 to the bill’s enactment date.
posts.summaryLabel: Congressional Research Service, Reported to House
posts.meta: Ways and Means Committee · Rep. Claudia Tenney (R-NY)
posts.whatsNext: To the Senate (if and when it takes it up)

aiSummaries.text:
This bill gives tax relief to U.S. citizens who are wrongfully detained or held hostage in another country, along with their spouses. While someone is held, that time is not counted when deadlines for federal tax matters are figured. These deadlines include those for filing and paying income, estate, gift, employment, and excise taxes, for claiming a tax credit or refund, and for the IRS to determine, assess, and collect additional taxes, interest, or penalties.

The State Department and the Justice Department would each year send the IRS lists of people who qualify for these extensions.

The bill also requires the IRS to cancel and refund any extra taxes, interest, and penalties charged for a tax year that ended while a person was detained, as long as the deadline extension applies. In addition, the IRS would set up a program that lets detained or hostage-held Americans, or their spouses or dependents, ask for refunds of such extra charges for tax years ending during a detention from 2021 until the bill becomes law.

posts.title: Protecting Taxpayers from Ghost Preparers Act
posts.label: ✅🏛️ Passed House with amendment (voice vote)
posts.summary:
Protecting Taxpayers from Ghost Preparers Act
This bill limits the amount of time the Internal Revenue Service (IRS) has to assess taxes related to fraudulent or false federal tax returns where there is no intent by the taxpayer to evade taxes.
As background, the IRS generally has three years from the date that a tax return is filed (statute of limitations) to assess taxes owed by the taxpayer for the tax year. However, if a false or fraudulent tax return is filed with the intent to evade tax (fraud exception), then the IRS may assess taxes at any time. In Murrin v. Commissioner the U.S. Tax Court held (and the U.S. Court of Appeals for the Third Circuit affirmed) that the fraud exception applies when a tax return preparer places false or fraudulent entries on a tax return without the taxpayer’s knowledge. In contrast, the U.S. Court of Federal Claims held in BASR Partnership v. Commissioner that the fraud exception only applies if the taxpayer intends to evade taxes.
The bill limits the fraud exception to cases in which the taxpayer intends to evade taxes.
posts.summaryLabel: Congressional Research Service, Passed House
posts.meta: Ways and Means Committee · Rep. Nicole Malliotakis (R-NY)
posts.whatsNext: To the Senate (if and when it takes it up)

aiSummaries.text:
The Protecting Taxpayers from Ghost Preparers Act would limit how long the Internal Revenue Service (IRS) can go back to collect taxes from a fraudulent or false federal tax return when the taxpayer did not intend to evade taxes.

Normally, the IRS has three years from the date a tax return is filed to assess the taxes owed for that tax year. But if a false or fraudulent return is filed with the intent to evade taxes, the IRS can assess taxes at any time. Courts have disagreed about what counts as this exception. In Murrin v. Commissioner, the U.S. Tax Court, with the U.S. Court of Appeals for the Third Circuit agreeing, ruled that the exception applies when a tax return preparer puts false or fraudulent entries on a return without the taxpayer knowing. In BASR Partnership v. Commissioner, the U.S. Court of Federal Claims ruled that the exception applies only if the taxpayer intended to evade taxes.

The bill would settle this disagreement by limiting the fraud exception to cases where the taxpayer intends to evade taxes.

posts.title: Directing the President, pursuant to section 5(c) of the War Powers Resolution, to remove United States Armed Forces from hostilities with Iran.
posts.label: ✅🏛️ Passed House (220-204)
posts.summary:
This concurrent resolution directs the President to remove U.S. Armed Forces from hostilities against Iran unless explicitly authorized by a declaration of war or a congressional authorization for use of military force against Iran.
Elements of the U.S. Armed Forces needed to defend the United States, an ally, or a partner from imminent attack are not covered by this requirement provided the President complies with a specified provision of the War Powers Resolution. (The provision generally requires the President to remove U.S. Armed Forces from hostilities no more than 60 days after the President notifies or is required to notify Congress of such involvement, unless Congress authorizes such use. For more information on the War Powers Resolution, see CRS In Focus 13134.)
posts.summaryLabel: Congressional Research Service, Introduced in House
posts.meta: Foreign Affairs Committee · Rep. Seth Moulton (D-MA)
posts.whatsNext: To the Senate (if and when it takes it up)

aiSummaries.text:
This measure tells the President to pull U.S. military forces out of fighting against Iran, unless Congress has approved that fighting through a declaration of war or a specific authorization for the use of military force against Iran.

There is an exception. Forces needed to defend the United States, an ally, or a partner from an attack that is about to happen can stay, as long as the President follows a certain part of the War Powers Resolution. That part generally requires the President to withdraw forces from fighting within 60 days after notifying Congress of the military involvement, or after being required to do so, unless Congress authorizes the use of force.

posts.title: Providing for congressional disapproval under chapter 8 of title 5, United States Code, of the rule submitted by the Environmental Protection Agency relating to "California State Nonroad Engine Pollution Control Standards; Ocean-Going Vessels At-Berth; Notice of Decision".
posts.label: ✅🏛️ Passed House (216-211)
posts.summary:
This joint resolution revokes the authorization granted to the California Air Resources Board (CARB) to amend its Ocean-Going Vessels At-Berth Regulation. Among other elements, the amendment proposed by CARB and authorized by the Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) expanded auxiliary engine emissions reductions requirements to include additional categories of ocean-going vessels. (Under the Clean Air Act, the EPA may authorize California to adopt and enforce standards relating to the control of emissions from nonroad vehicles or engines if those standards meet certain requirements.)
Specifically, the joint resolution nullifies the EPA authorization decision titled California State Nonroad Engine Pollution Control Standards; Ocean-Going Vessels At-Berth; Notice of Decision.
posts.summaryLabel: Congressional Research Service, Passed House
posts.meta: Energy and Commerce Committee · Rep. Vince Fong (R-CA)
posts.whatsNext: To the Senate (if and when it takes it up)

aiSummaries.text:
This measure cancels the permission that the federal Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) gave to California's Air Resources Board (CARB) to change its rules for ocean-going ships docked at port. Those rules require the ships' auxiliary engines, which run power and other systems while the ship is in port, to produce fewer emissions. The change CARB proposed, and the EPA approved, widened these requirements to cover more types of ocean-going vessels.

Under the federal Clean Air Act, the EPA can allow California to set and enforce its own standards for emissions from nonroad vehicles and engines, as long as those standards meet certain conditions. The measure specifically cancels the EPA decision titled "California State Nonroad Engine Pollution Control Standards; Ocean-Going Vessels At-Berth; Notice of Decision."

posts.title: Tyler’s Law
posts.label: ✅🏛️ Passed House (voice vote)
posts.summary:
Tyler’s Law
This bill requires the Department of Health and Human Services (HHS) to complete, within one year after the bill’s enactment, a study on how frequently Medicare-participating hospital emergency departments test for fentanyl in patients experiencing an overdose, the costs associated with such testing, and how such testing may impact patients.
Within six months after the study’s completion and based on its results, HHS must issue guidance regarding (1) whether hospital emergency departments should implement fentanyl testing as a routine procedure for patients experiencing an overdose, (2) how to ensure clinicians know which substances they are testing for in routine drug tests, and (3) how fentanyl testing may affect the future risk of overdose and other health outcomes.
posts.summaryLabel: Congressional Research Service, Introduced in House
posts.meta: Energy and Commerce Committee · Rep. Ted Lieu (D-CA)
posts.whatsNext: To the Senate (if and when it takes it up)

aiSummaries.text:
The Tyler's Law bill would require the Department of Health and Human Services to carry out a study, to be finished within one year of the bill becoming law. The study would look at how often hospital emergency departments that take Medicare patients test people for fentanyl when they come in with an overdose, what that testing costs, and how it might affect patients.

Within six months after the study is finished, and based on what it finds, HHS would have to issue guidance on three things. The first is whether emergency departments should make fentanyl testing a standard part of care for overdose patients. The second is how to make sure doctors and other clinicians know which substances a routine drug test is looking for. The third is how fentanyl testing might affect a patient's future risk of overdose and other health outcomes.

posts.title: Whistleblower Protection Act of 2025
posts.label: ✅🏛️ Passed House with amendment (424-0)
posts.summary:
Whistleblower Protection Act of 2025
This bill expands existing whistleblower protections for employees of federal contractors or grant recipients to apply to all contracts and grants funded by the Department of Housing and Urban Development (HUD) regardless of the date of execution.
Current law protects employees of federal contractors or grant recipients from a reprisal (i.e., discharge, demotion, or discrimination) for disclosing evidence to Congress or another appropriate official of certain misconduct involving federal contracts, grants, or funds. This provision currently applies only to contracts and grants signed or modified after the law took effect in 2013. The bill expands these protections to apply to HUD contracts and grants signed before the law was enacted.
posts.summaryLabel: Congressional Research Service, Reported to House
posts.committee: Oversight and Government Reform Committee, Financial Services Committee
posts.meta: Oversight and Government Reform Committee, Financial Services Committee · Rep. Monica De La Cruz (R-TX)
posts.whatsNext: To the Senate (if and when it takes it up)

aiSummaries.text:
This bill would extend whistleblower protections to more workers who are employed under contracts and grants funded by the Department of Housing and Urban Development (HUD). Under current law, employees of federal contractors and grant recipients are protected from being fired, demoted, or otherwise discriminated against for reporting certain misconduct involving federal contracts, grants, or funds to Congress or another appropriate official. However, these protections only cover contracts and grants that were signed or changed after the law took effect in 2013.

The bill would remove that date limit for HUD-funded work. Its protections would apply to HUD contracts and grants signed before the law was enacted, as well as those signed afterward.

posts.title: Tyler’s Law
posts.label: 📋 Reported by committee
posts.note: Energy and Commerce, H. Rept. 119-817
posts.summary:
Tyler’s Law
This bill requires the Department of Health and Human Services (HHS) to complete, within one year after the bill’s enactment, a study on how frequently Medicare-participating hospital emergency departments test for fentanyl in patients experiencing an overdose, the costs associated with such testing, and how such testing may impact patients.
Within six months after the study’s completion and based on its results, HHS must issue guidance regarding (1) whether hospital emergency departments should implement fentanyl testing as a routine procedure for patients experiencing an overdose, (2) how to ensure clinicians know which substances they are testing for in routine drug tests, and (3) how fentanyl testing may affect the future risk of overdose and other health outcomes.
posts.summaryLabel: Congressional Research Service, Introduced in House
posts.meta: Energy and Commerce Committee · Rep. Ted Lieu (D-CA)
posts.whatsNext: Floor scheduling (leadership decides if and when it gets a vote)

aiSummaries.text:
The Tyler's Law bill would require the Department of Health and Human Services to carry out a study, to be finished within one year of the bill becoming law. The study would look at how often hospital emergency departments that take Medicare patients test people for fentanyl when they come in with an overdose, what that testing costs, and how it might affect patients.

Within six months after the study is finished, and based on what it finds, HHS would have to issue guidance on three things. The first is whether emergency departments should make fentanyl testing a standard part of care for overdose patients. The second is how to make sure doctors and other clinicians know which substances a routine drug test is looking for. The third is how fentanyl testing might affect a patient's future risk of overdose and other health outcomes.

posts.title: Modernizing Access to Our Public Oceans Act
posts.label: ✅🏛️ Passed House (voice vote)
posts.summary:
Modernizing Access to Our Public Oceans Act
This bill directs the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA) to publish geospatial data related to public recreational use of federal waterways (e.g., boating and fishing).
Under the bill, NOAA must consult with relevant stakeholders (including state and local governments, Indian tribes, and Native Hawaiian organizations) to develop and adopt standards for the coordination and dissemination of geospatial data relating to fishing restrictions and recreational vessels' use of federal waterways, including the exclusive economic zone of the United States (EEZ). (The EEZ generally includes waters between 3 and 200 miles seaward from the U.S. coastline.)
Within four years after the bill is enacted, NOAA must provide geographic information system data on a public website that identifies and describes the locations where and conditions under which certain recreational activities are restricted in federal waterways. Specifically, the website must identify (1) locations where fishing restrictions are imposed, (2) areas in the EEZ with restrictions on specified recreational vessel types, and (3) federally protected areas (e.g., National Marine Sanctuaries). NOAA must also continue to provide digitized navigation information related to the EEZ and make the information available on the website to the extent practicable.
The bill allows NOAA to coordinate and partner with nonfederal entities to carry out this bill. It also directs NOAA to work with other federal agencies to ensure compatibility and interoperability among federal databases with respect to collecting and disseminating geospatial data related to the public outdoor recreational use of the EEZ.
posts.summaryLabel: Congressional Research Service, Passed Senate
posts.meta: Commerce, Science, and Transportation Committee · Sen. Ted Cruz (R-TX)
posts.whatsNext: Presidential review (±10 days)

aiSummaries.text:
This bill asks the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA) to make it easier for the public to find out where they can boat and fish in federal waters. It covers the exclusive economic zone of the United States, the ocean area that generally runs from 3 to 200 miles out from the coastline.

NOAA would first need to consult with groups that have a stake in this, including state and local governments, Indian tribes, and Native Hawaiian organizations. Together they would develop and adopt standards for sharing map-style location data about fishing restrictions and where certain recreational boats may go in federal waters.

Within four years of the bill becoming law, NOAA must post this location data on a public website. The website would show where fishing is restricted, which areas of the exclusive economic zone limit particular types of recreational boats, and which federally protected areas exist, such as National Marine Sanctuaries. NOAA would also keep providing digital navigation information about the zone and make it available on the site as far as is practical.

The bill lets NOAA team up with outside organizations to carry out this work. It also directs NOAA to work with other federal agencies so their databases fit together and can share information about outdoor recreation in the zone.

posts.title: Prison Staff Safety Enhancement Act
posts.label: 📌 Presented to President
posts.summary:
Prison Staff Safety Enhancement Act
This bill establishes requirements for the Department of Justice (DOJ) and component agencies to assess and respond to incidents of sexual harassment and sexual assault by incarcerated individuals against Bureau of Prisons (BOP) staff.
Specifically, the bill requires DOJ to adopt national standards for the prevention, reduction, and punishment of sexual harassment and sexual assault by incarcerated individuals against correctional officers or other employees of the BOP.
Additionally, the bill requires the BOP to fully implement the recommendations of the DOJ Inspector General contained in the report titled Evaluation of the Federal Bureau of Prisons’ Efforts to Address Sexual Harassment and Sexual Assault Committed by Inmates Toward Staff.
posts.summaryLabel: Congressional Research Service, Introduced in Senate
posts.meta: Judiciary Committee · Sen. Marsha Blackburn (R-TN)
posts.whatsNext: President has 10 days (Sundays excepted): sign, veto, or it becomes law unsigned (pocket veto if adjournment prevents return)

aiSummaries.text:
The Prison Staff Safety Enhancement Act is meant to better protect staff at federal prisons from sexual harassment and sexual assault by people who are incarcerated. It covers the Department of Justice and the agencies under it, requiring them to look closely at these incidents and respond to them.

Under the bill, the Department of Justice must set national standards for preventing, reducing, and punishing sexual harassment and sexual assault by incarcerated people against correctional officers and other employees of the Bureau of Prisons.

The bill also requires the Bureau of Prisons to fully carry out the recommendations made by the Department of Justice's Inspector General. Those recommendations come from a report evaluating how well the Bureau of Prisons has been handling sexual harassment and sexual assault committed by inmates against staff.

posts.title: Indian Health Service Emergency Claims Parity Act
posts.label: ✅🏛️ Passed House (voice vote)
posts.summary:
Indian Health Service Emergency Claims Parity Act
This bill extends from 72 hours to not less than 15 days the time period to notify the Purchased/Referred Care (PRC) program of emergency medical care received from a non-Indian Health Service (IHS) medical provider or at a non-IHS medical facility. This bill does not apply to individuals who are elderly or disabled, who continue to have a 30-day notification requirement for emergency services.
The IHS provides medical and dental services directly to American Indian and Alaska Native patients whenever possible. The PRC program pays for medical or dental care that is provided away from an IHS or tribal health care facility. The PRC program must be notified of requests for authorization of payment for health care services from a non-IHS provider.
Currently in emergency cases, the patient, an individual on behalf of the patient, or the medical care provider must, within 72 hours after the beginning of treatment for the condition or after admission to a health care facility, notify a PRC authorizing official of the need for the emergency medical care. This bill instead allows the patient, other individual, or provider to notify PRC not less than 15 days of the treatment or admission.
posts.summaryLabel: Congressional Research Service, Introduced in House
posts.committee: Energy and Commerce Committee, Natural Resources Committee
posts.meta: Energy and Commerce Committee, Natural Resources Committee · Rep. Mike Kennedy (R-UT)
posts.whatsNext: To the Senate (if and when it takes it up)

aiSummaries.text:
This bill gives more time to notify the Indian Health Service's Purchased/Referred Care (PRC) program about emergency medical care received outside IHS. The PRC program pays for care that IHS or tribal health facilities don't provide directly, so it has to be told about emergency care from a non-IHS provider or facility.

Right now, the patient, someone acting for the patient, or the care provider must notify a PRC authorizing official within 72 hours after treatment begins or after the patient is admitted. Under this bill, they would instead have at least 15 days from the treatment or admission to give that notice.

The longer deadline does not apply to elderly or disabled individuals. For them, the current 30-day notification requirement for emergency services remains in place.

posts.title: Safe Beaches, Safe Swimmers Act
posts.label: ✅🏛️ Passed House with amendment (voice vote)
posts.summary:
Safe Beaches, Safe Swimmers Act
This bill establishes requirements to ensure an adequate staff of lifeguards at swimming areas and swimming beaches managed by the National Park Service, the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service, the Bureau of Land Management, or the Bureau of Reclamation that are typically monitored by federally employed lifeguards during normal seasonal operating hours.
If the Department of the Interior determines there is a staffing shortage of lifeguards that will leave a swimming area or beach unmonitored by federally employed lifeguards during normal seasonal operating hours, Interior may enter into an agreement with local government agencies to provide lifeguards. Interior must ensure that a local government agency providing lifeguard services is reimbursed for all reasonable costs it incurred in carrying out the agreement.
The bill does not apply to short-term staffing shortages caused by temporary absences, such as an employee taking annual or sick leave.
posts.summaryLabel: Congressional Research Service, Reported to House
posts.meta: Natural Resources Committee · Rep. Jennifer Kiggans (R-VA)
posts.whatsNext: To the Senate (if and when it takes it up)

aiSummaries.text:
The Safe Beaches, Safe Swimmers Act would require the government to keep enough lifeguards on duty at federally managed swimming areas and beaches that are normally watched by federal lifeguards during their regular seasonal hours. These areas are managed by the National Park Service, the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service, the Bureau of Land Management, or the Bureau of Reclamation.

If the Department of the Interior finds that a shortage of federal lifeguards would leave one of these swimming areas or beaches without a lifeguard during its normal season, the department may make an agreement with local government agencies to provide lifeguards instead. The department must pay the local agency back for all reasonable costs it incurs under that agreement.

The bill does not cover short-term shortages caused by temporary absences, such as an employee taking annual or sick leave.

posts.title: Common Cents Act
posts.label: ✅🏛️ Passed House (voice vote)
posts.summary:
Common Cents Act
This bill ends the production of the penny for general circulation, requires rounding to an amount divisible by five for the payment or transfer of cash, and allows the nickel to be composed of different material.
The Department of the Treasury must stop producing the penny, except to meet collector needs. The penny shall continue to be legal tender.
Any person selling goods or services in a cash transaction, entering into other transfers of cash, or paying cash wages to an employee must round the payment up or down in accordance with the bill.
The bill also allows Treasury to discontinue the minting for circulation of any coin if Treasury follows procedures as outlined by the bill, including providing notice and a briefing to Congress.
The Federal Reserve Board must periodically report on a strategic plan for the acceptance of penny orders and deposits at commercial coin terminals that provide services under agreements with Federal Reserve banks.
Finally, the bill allows for a different material composition of the nickel. In addition to being made from an alloy of copper and nickel, the nickel may also be clad with an inner core of zinc and an outer layer of nickel.

posts.meta: Financial Services Committee · Rep. Lisa McClain (R-MI)

aiSummaries.text:
The Common Cents Act would stop the U.S. Treasury from making new pennies for everyday circulation, though the Treasury could still make them to meet the needs of coin collectors. Pennies would remain legal money.

Under the bill, anyone who sells goods or services for cash, makes other cash transfers, or pays employees in cash would have to round the amount up or down so it can be divided evenly by five. This rounding rule would apply to those cash payments and transfers.

The bill also lets the Treasury stop making any coin for circulation, but only if it follows the steps set out in the bill. Those steps include giving notice to Congress and providing it a briefing.

The Federal Reserve Board would have to report regularly on a strategic plan for accepting penny orders and deposits at commercial coin terminals that offer services under agreements with Federal Reserve banks.

Finally, the bill would allow the nickel to be made from a different material. Besides the current copper and nickel alloy, a nickel could be made with an inner core of zinc and an outer layer of nickel.

posts.title: Legislative Branch Agencies Clarification Act
posts.label: ✅🏛️ Passed House (voice vote)
posts.summary:
Legislative Branch Agencies Clarification Act
This bill revises the procedures for appointing and removing the Librarian of Congress, the Director of the Government Publishing Office (GPO), and the Register of Copyrights. The bill also establishes an Office of Inspector General within the Copyright Office and requires GPO to establish a human management system.
Specifically, the bill requires the Librarian of Congress and the Director of GPO to be appointed by a bipartisan congressional commission, based on procedures outlined by the bill and without regard to political affiliation. (Currently, these positions are appointed by the President with the advice and consent of the Senate.) The Librarian of Congress and the Director of GPO may only be removed from office by a majority vote of the majority and minority leaders of the House of Representatives and the Senate.
Additionally, the bill requires the Librarian of Congress and the Director of GPO to each appoint a deputy within a set time frame and outlines related procedures.
The bill removes the Library of Congress's (LOC's) supervisory authority over the Copyright Office and instead transfers those powers directly to the Register of Copyrights. LOC and other legislative agencies may provide support services to the Copyright Office.
The bill requires the Register of Copyrights to be (1) a U.S. citizen with a background and experience in copyright law, and (2) appointed by the President with the advice and consent of the Senate. (Currently, the Register is appointed by the Librarian.) Before the President makes the appointment, the chair and ranking minority member of each specified committee must jointly recommend three individuals whom the President may consider in making the appointment. The bill limits the term of office for the Register to 10 years, but the individual may be reappointed.
The bill requires subordinate officers and employees of the Copyright Office to be appointed by the Register. Further, the bill requires the Register (instead of the Librarian) to appoint the three administrative judges of the Copyright Royalty Board.
The bill also establishes an Office of Inspector General within the Copyright Office to, among other duties, conduct and supervise audits and investigations (excluding incidents involving violence and personal property) relating to the Copyright Office. The Register must appoint an Inspector General to head this office without regard to political affiliation. The Register may remove or transfer the Inspector General with prior congressional notification.
The bill also requires GPO to establish and maintain a human capital management system and outlines the requirements for the system.
posts.summaryLabel: Congressional Research Service, Introduced in House
posts.committee: Oversight and Government Reform Committee, Judiciary Committee, House Administration
posts.meta: Oversight and Government Reform Committee, Judiciary Committee, House Administration · Rep. H. Griffith (R-VA)
posts.whatsNext: To the Senate (if and when it takes it up)

aiSummaries.text:
This bill changes how three legislative branch agencies are run: the Library of Congress, the Government Publishing Office (GPO), and the Copyright Office. It changes who picks the heads of these agencies and who can remove them, and it sets up new internal oversight and staffing rules.

Right now, the Librarian of Congress and the GPO Director are nominated by the President and confirmed by the Senate. Under the bill, a bipartisan congressional commission would appoint them instead, using procedures set out in the bill and without regard to political affiliation. These two officials could only be removed by a majority vote of the majority and minority leaders of the House and the Senate. The Librarian and the Director would each also have to appoint a deputy within a set time frame, following related procedures the bill lays out.

The bill also takes the Copyright Office out from under the Library of Congress. Authority that the Library now holds over the Copyright Office would move directly to the Register of Copyrights. The Library and other legislative agencies could still provide support services to the Copyright Office.

Under the bill, the Register of Copyrights would have to be a U.S. citizen with background and experience in copyright law, and would be appointed by the President with the advice and consent of the Senate. Today, the Librarian makes that appointment. Before the President chooses, the chair and ranking minority member of each specified committee would jointly recommend three people for consideration. The Register would serve a 10-year term and could be reappointed. The Register would also appoint the Copyright Office's subordinate officers and employees, and would take over the Librarian's role in appointing the three administrative judges of the Copyright Royalty Board.

The bill creates an Office of Inspector General within the Copyright Office to conduct and supervise audits and investigations of the office, though incidents involving violence and personal property are excluded. The Register would appoint the Inspector General without regard to political affiliation and could remove or transfer that person only after giving prior notice to Congress.

Finally, the bill requires GPO to set up and maintain a human capital management system, and it spells out what that system must include.

posts.title: Stop Secret Spending Act of 2025
posts.label: 📜✍️ Signed by Pres. Trump
posts.summary:
Stop Secret Spending Act of 2025
This bill expands a requirement for federal agencies to report expenditures on the USAspending.gov website to include other transaction agreement expenditures. (Other transaction agreements, or OTAs, are contractual instruments other than standard procurement contracts, grants, or cooperative agreements; they are exempt from many federal procurement laws and regulations).
Under current law, federal agencies must report expenditures on federal awards to USAspending.gov with the term federal award defined as federal grants, loans, cooperative agreements, contracts, and certain other types of expenditures. This bill expands the definition of federal award to include expenditures under OTAs, and therefore such expenditures must be included on the USAspending.gov website.
The Department of the Treasury must ensure that data relating to OTAs are automatically transmitted to the website and a centralized view of this data is available on the website. Treasury must also annually post on the USAspending.gov website a report that includes (1) the total amount of federal spending on federal awards for which data has not been posted on the website, and (2) the reason why such spending data was not posted.
For 10 years after enactment, the Office of Inspector General of specified federal agencies must periodically submit to Congress and make publicly available a report assessing the agency's spending data and use of data standards.
posts.summaryLabel: Congressional Research Service, Introduced in House
posts.meta: Oversight and Government Reform Committee · Rep. Barry Moore (R-AL)
posts.whatsNext: Takes effect (on enactment unless the text sets other dates)

aiSummaries.text:
This bill requires federal agencies to report their spending on other transaction agreements, a type of contract that falls outside standard procurement, grant, and cooperative agreement rules, to the USAspending.gov website. Currently, the reporting requirement covers federal grants, loans, cooperative agreements, contracts, and certain other expenditures, but not these agreements. Once this bill passes, spending under these agreements will count as federal awards and must appear on the site.

The Department of the Treasury must make sure data on these agreements is sent to the website automatically and that a single, central view of this data is available there. Each year, Treasury must also post a report on the site showing the total amount of federal spending on federal awards whose data has not been posted, along with the reason it was not posted.

For 10 years after the law is enacted, the Office of Inspector General of specified federal agencies must regularly send Congress a report evaluating the agency's spending data and its use of data standards. These reports must also be made available to the public.

posts.title: Doug LaMalfa Federal Disaster Tax Relief Certainty Act
posts.label: 📜✍️ Signed by Pres. Trump
posts.summary:
Doug LaMalfa Federal Disaster Tax Relief Certainty Act
This act extends the federal tax deduction for qualified disaster-related personal casualty losses and the exclusion from gross income of qualified wildfire relief payments.
Under current law, unreimbursed personal casualty losses arising in a qualified disaster area (qualified disaster-related personal casualty losses) are deductible (as an itemized tax deduction or as part of the standard tax deduction) if such losses exceed $500 per casualty. A qualified disaster area is an area with respect to which a major disaster has been declared during the period beginning in 2020 and ending 60 days after July 4, 2025, if the incident period begins on or after December 28, 2019, and on or before July 4, 2025.
The act extends the federal tax deduction for qualified disaster-related personal casualty losses by defining a qualified disaster area as an area with respect to which a major disaster has been declared if the incident period begins on or after December 28, 2019, and before January 1, 2027.
The act provides that the exclusion from gross income of qualified wildfire relief payments applies to such payments attributable to forest or range fires declared a federal disaster after 2014 and before 2027, regardless of when such payments are received. (Currently, qualified wildfire relief payments attributable to forest or range fires declared a federal disaster after 2014 and received after 2019 and before 2026 may be excluded from gross income.)
The act also provides statutory authority for several related tax rules.
posts.summaryLabel: Congressional Research Service, Public Law
posts.committee: Finance Committee, Ways and Means Committee
posts.meta: Finance Committee, Ways and Means Committee · Rep. W. Steube (R-FL)
posts.whatsNext: Takes effect (on enactment unless the text sets other dates)

aiSummaries.text:
The Doug LaMalfa Federal Disaster Tax Relief Certainty Act extends two federal tax benefits for people affected by disasters.

The first benefit covers personal property losses from disasters. Under current law, if you lose property in a qualified disaster area and are not reimbursed, you can deduct those losses, either as an itemized deduction or as part of the standard deduction, as long as each loss is more than $500. A qualified disaster area is one where a major disaster has been declared, with the incident period starting in the window that currently runs through 60 days after July 4, 2025. The act extends this so that an area counts if its incident period begins on or after December 28, 2019, and before January 1, 2027.

The second benefit covers wildfire relief payments. These payments can currently be left out of your taxable income if they relate to forest or range fires declared federal disasters after 2014 and are received after 2019 and before 2026. The act extends this exclusion to payments tied to fires declared federal disasters after 2014 and before 2027, no matter when the payments are received.

The act also gives statutory authority to several related tax rules.

posts.title: Ratepayer Protection Act
posts.label: 📋 Reported by committee
posts.note: Energy and Commerce, as amended, H. Rept. 119-814
posts.summary:
Ratepayer Protection Act
The bill requires state utility regulators and nonregulated utilities to consider implementing a standard to hold certain large-load customers responsible for the costs associated with any generation, transmission, or distribution upgrade of electric service necessary to serve such customers. A large-load customer means a non-residential electric consumer that enters, or requests to enter, an agreement concerning the sale of electric energy primarily to operate information technology infrastructure and related systems pertaining to data storage and computational applications and services (e.g., data centers) that have a peak electric demand of 100 megawatts or more at a single site or campus.
Specifically, the bill requires states to consider implementing a federal standard for large-load customers. The standard must require rates charged by electric utilities for providing electric service to a large-load customer to be designed to recover from the large-load customer the full, incremental cost of any generation, transmission, or distribution upgrade necessary to serve such customer. This rate must include the costs that would be incurred if the large-load customer terminates an agreement with the electric utility pertaining to the sale of electric energy or otherwise ceases the purchase of energy from the electric utility.
Under the standard, an electric utility must require the large-load customer to provide to the utility financial assurances or contributions to cover the cost of any generation, transmission, or distribution upgrade that is necessary to serve the load of a large-load customer before the utility makes any generation, transmission, or distribution upgrade.
posts.summaryLabel: Congressional Research Service, Reported to House
posts.meta: Energy and Commerce Committee · Rep. Gabe Evans (R-CO)
posts.whatsNext: Floor scheduling (leadership decides if and when it gets a vote)

aiSummaries.text:
This bill asks state utility regulators and nonregulated utilities to consider a standard that makes large electricity users pay for the power system upgrades needed to serve them. The "large-load customers" it covers are non-residential customers, such as data centers, that buy electricity mainly to run computing and data storage operations and have a peak demand of 100 megawatts or more at a single site or campus.

Under the proposed standard, the rates a utility charges these customers would have to be set so that the customer covers the full added cost of any new power generation, transmission, or distribution upgrade needed to serve it. The rates would also have to cover the costs the utility would still face if the customer ends its agreement or stops buying power from that utility.

The standard would also require utilities to collect financial assurances or contributions from the large-load customer before they build any generation, transmission, or distribution upgrade needed to serve that customer.

posts.title: Civil Preparedness for Agroterrorism Exercise Act of 2026
posts.label: 📋 Reported by committee
posts.note: Homeland Security, H. Rept. 119-813
posts.summary:
Civil Preparedness for Agroterrorism Exercise Act of 2026
This bill requires the Department of Homeland Security (DHS), within four years after the bill’s enactment, to conduct an exercise to enhance collective domestic prevention, response, and recovery regarding acts of agroterrorism (i.e., terrorism targeting or threatening agriculture and food systems of vital importance to national security, public health, or safety). The scenario in the exercise must involve agroterrorists transporting and deploying in the United States a biological agent (e.g., microorganism or infectious substance) capable of harming critical agriculture and food operations and must address how relevant public and private entities can coordinate to develop preparedness and mitigate widespread disruption.
Within 180 days after completion of the exercise, DHS must submit to Congress an after-action report including the findings of the exercise, plans for incorporating lessons learned into future operations, and recommended legislative actions.
posts.summaryLabel: Congressional Research Service, Introduced in House
posts.meta: Homeland Security Committee · Rep. Dale Strong (R-AL)
posts.whatsNext: Floor scheduling (leadership decides if and when it gets a vote)

aiSummaries.text:
This bill would require the Department of Homeland Security to run a practice exercise within four years of the bill becoming law. The exercise would prepare the country to prevent, respond to, and recover from agroterrorism, meaning attacks aimed at farming and food systems that are vital to national security, public health, or safety.

The practice scenario must involve people who carry out such attacks bringing a biological agent, such as a microorganism or infectious substance, into the United States and using it to harm important farm and food operations. The exercise must also look at how public agencies and private businesses can work together to get ready and limit widespread disruption.

Within 180 days after the exercise is finished, the Department of Homeland Security must send Congress a report. That report must include what the exercise found, plans for using those lessons in future work, and suggested laws to pass.
