posts.title: End Tax Penalties on American Hostages Act
posts.label: 📋 Reported by committee
posts.note: Ways and Means, as amended, H. Rept. 119-797
posts.summary:
End Tax Penalties on American Hostages Act
This bill extends certain federal tax deadlines for U.S. nationals who are unlawfully or wrongfully detained abroad or held hostage abroad and their spouses. The bill also allows for an abatement and refund of additional taxes, interest, and penalties assessed to such individuals for failing to meet a federal tax deadline during a period of detention.
Specifically, under the bill, the time period during which a U.S. national is unlawfully or wrongfully detained abroad or held hostage abroad is disregarded in determining certain federal tax deadlines, including deadlines for
filing a return for and paying federal income, estate, gift, employment, or excise taxes;
a tax credit or refund claim; and
the determination, assessment, and collection of additional taxes, interest, or penalties.
The bill requires the Department of State and the Department of Justice to annually provide the Internal Revenue Service (IRS) with lists to identify U.S. nationals who qualify for an extension.
The bill also requires the IRS to (1) abate and refund additional taxes, interest, and penalties assessed for any tax year ending during a period of detention for which an extension of a federal tax deadline is permitted; and (2) establish a program allowing U.S. nationals unlawfully or wrongfully detained abroad or taken hostage abroad (or their spouse or dependent) to claim a refund of additional taxes, interest, and penalties assessed for any tax year ending during a period of detention from 2021 to the bill’s enactment date.
posts.summaryLabel: Congressional Research Service, Reported to House
posts.meta: Ways and Means Committee · Rep. Claudia Tenney (R-NY)
posts.whatsNext: Floor scheduling (leadership decides if and when it gets a vote)

aiSummaries.text:
This bill gives tax relief to U.S. citizens who are wrongfully detained or held hostage in another country, along with their spouses. While someone is held, that time is not counted when deadlines for federal tax matters are figured. These deadlines include those for filing and paying income, estate, gift, employment, and excise taxes, for claiming a tax credit or refund, and for the IRS to determine, assess, and collect additional taxes, interest, or penalties.

The State Department and the Justice Department would each year send the IRS lists of people who qualify for these extensions.

The bill also requires the IRS to cancel and refund any extra taxes, interest, and penalties charged for a tax year that ended while a person was detained, as long as the deadline extension applies. In addition, the IRS would set up a program that lets detained or hostage-held Americans, or their spouses or dependents, ask for refunds of such extra charges for tax years ending during a detention from 2021 until the bill becomes law.

posts.title: Safe Cloud Storage Act
posts.label: 📋 Reported by committee
posts.note: Judiciary, as amended, H. Rept. 119-804
posts.summary:
Safe Cloud Storage Act
This bill limits the civil and criminal liability of vendors that contract with law enforcement agencies to provide digital storage services (e.g., cloud-based storage) for storing, maintaining, and processing child sexual abuse material (CSAM) in investigations of online child sexual exploitation.
Under current law, the National Center for Missing & Exploited Children (NCMEC) receives reports of online child sexual exploitation via its CyberTipline, evaluates and prioritizes the reports, and refers the reports to law enforcement agencies to investigate. Currently, federal law limits the liability of vendors that contract directly with the NCMEC to store and transfer CSAM. However, federal law does not limit the liability of vendors that contract with law enforcement agencies to assist in investigations.
This bill establishes liability protections for vendors that contract with federal, state, and local law enforcement agencies to store, maintain, and process CSAM in investigations of online child sexual exploitation. Specifically, the bill prohibits a civil claim or criminal charge in federal or state court against such a vendor, so long as the vendor has not engaged in intentional misconduct or negligent conduct, acted with malice or reckless disregard, or acted for a purpose unrelated to its contractual duties.
The bill requires vendors to comply with cybersecurity requirements for CSAM that is stored, maintained, or processed. The bill also requires vendors to comply with storage requirements for CSAM that is retained as evidence.
posts.summaryLabel: Congressional Research Service, Reported to House
posts.meta: Judiciary Committee · Rep. Laurel Lee (R-FL)
posts.whatsNext: Floor scheduling (leadership decides if and when it gets a vote)

aiSummaries.text:
This bill protects companies that provide digital storage, such as cloud storage, to law enforcement agencies from being sued or criminally charged for storing, maintaining, and processing child sexual abuse material while helping investigate online child sexual exploitation. The protection covers federal, state, and local agencies and applies in federal or state court.

Right now, the National Center for Missing & Exploited Children receives reports of online child sexual exploitation through its CyberTipline, reviews and prioritizes them, and passes them to law enforcement for investigation. Federal law already limits the liability of companies that contract directly with the Center to store and transfer this material. It does not offer the same limits to companies that contract with law enforcement agencies to help with investigations.

The protection does not apply in every case. A company can still be sued or charged if it engaged in intentional misconduct or negligent conduct, acted with malice or reckless disregard, or acted for a purpose unrelated to its contract.

The bill also requires these companies to follow cybersecurity rules for the material they store, maintain, or process. When the material is kept as evidence, they must also follow specific storage rules.

posts.title: Congressional Records Protection Act of 2026
posts.label: 📋 Reported by committee
posts.note: Judiciary, as amended, H. Rept. 119-805
posts.summary:
Congressional Records Protection Act of 2026
This bill generally prohibits the government from issuing a search warrant, grand jury subpoena, court order, statutory authorization, certification, subpoena, or an administrative order (i.e., executing legal process) that could reasonably return congressional records. Congressional records include (1) written materials and electronic or wire communications prepared by, shared with, or obtained by a Member of Congress or congressional employee in the course of official duties; and (2) records of an electronic or wire communications service related to accounts or certain communications of a Member of Congress or congressional employee.
The bill provides exceptions to the general prohibition. Specifically, the government may execute legal process that could reasonably return congressional records if (1) the subject of the process is the target of a criminal investigation, (2) the material sought pertains to a Member of Congress or congressional employee who is the target of a criminal investigation, or (3) the records are certain electronic or wire communications.
If the government executes legal process under an exception that could reasonably return or that unexpectedly returns congressional records, then the bill generally requires the government to notify the Member of Congress or congressional employee and delay or halt review of the materials for 30 days.
If the legal process could reasonably return certain congressional records from an electronic or wire communications service provider, then the bill requires a special master to be appointed to identify materials that are constitutionally protected from disclosure.
posts.summaryLabel: Congressional Research Service, Reported to House
posts.meta: Judiciary Committee · Rep. Mike Kelly (R-PA)
posts.whatsNext: Floor scheduling (leadership decides if and when it gets a vote)

aiSummaries.text:
The Congressional Records Protection Act of 2026 generally bars the government from using legal tools such as search warrants, grand jury subpoenas, court orders, and administrative orders when those tools could reasonably produce congressional records. These records include written materials and electronic or wire communications that a Member of Congress or a congressional employee prepares, shares, or receives while doing official work. They also include records held by electronic or wire communication services that relate to the accounts or certain communications of a Member of Congress or congressional employee.

The bill makes some exceptions to this general ban. The government may still use these legal tools if the person the request is aimed at is the target of a criminal investigation, if the material sought relates to a Member of Congress or congressional employee who is the target of a criminal investigation, or if the records are certain electronic or wire communications.

When the government uses legal process under one of these exceptions and that process could reasonably produce congressional records, or unexpectedly does so, the bill generally requires the government to notify the affected Member of Congress or congressional employee. The government must also delay or stop reviewing the materials for 30 days.

If the legal process could reasonably produce certain congressional records from an electronic or wire communication provider, the bill requires a special master to be appointed. The special master's job is to identify which materials are protected from disclosure under the Constitution.

posts.title: Student Protection and University Accountability Act
posts.label: 📋 Reported by committee
posts.note: Education and Workforce, as amended, H. Rept. 119-800
posts.summary:
Student Protection and University Accountability Act
This bill requires institutions of higher education (IHEs) participating in federal student aid programs and the Department of Education (ED) to take certain actions to investigate alleged violations of civil rights under Title VI of the Civil Rights Act of 1964. (Title VI of the Civil Rights Act of 1964 prohibits discrimination based on race, color, or national origin in federally funded programs or activities.)
Specifically, the bill requires an IHE to develop specific procedures for investigating Title VI complaints and widely distribute those procedures to students and their families. Among these procedures, an IHE must designate at least one Title VI coordinator and have a system for maintaining records of complaints.
The bill makes an IHE that fails to meet the bill's requirements for two consecutive award years ineligible to participate in federal student aid programs for at least two subsequent award years. However, the IHE may regain eligibility if it demonstrates compliance with the bill's requirements.
ED's Office for Civil Rights (OCR) must give bimonthly congressional briefings on (1) the number of complaints filed with OCR, (2) how OCR plans to address those complaints and the investigations being carried out in response to those complaints, and (3) data about the length of those investigations.
The bill revises the process through which OCR investigates Title VI complaints, including by prohibiting OCR from closing a complaint due to the filing of another complaint involving the same allegations against the same IHE under certain circumstances.
posts.summaryLabel: Congressional Research Service, Reported to House
posts.meta: Education and Workforce Committee · Rep. Elise Stefanik (R-NY)
posts.whatsNext: Floor scheduling (leadership decides if and when it gets a vote)

aiSummaries.text:
This bill requires colleges and universities that take part in federal student aid programs, along with the Department of Education, to investigate alleged discrimination based on race, color, or national origin in programs that receive federal funding. Under the bill, these schools must create specific procedures for handling discrimination complaints, share those procedures widely with students and their families, appoint at least one Title VI coordinator, and keep records of all complaints.

If a school fails to meet these requirements for two award years in a row, it becomes ineligible to take part in federal student aid programs for at least the next two award years. The school can regain eligibility, however, by showing that it now complies with the bill's requirements.

The Department of Education's Office for Civil Rights must brief Congress every two months. These briefings must cover how many complaints have been filed, how the office plans to handle them and the investigations underway, and how long those investigations have taken.

The bill also changes how the Office for Civil Rights investigates these complaints. Under certain circumstances, the office may not close a complaint just because someone has filed another complaint about the same allegations against the same school.

aiSummaries.text:
The AI Tax Integrity Act of 2026 would require the Internal Revenue Service to run a pilot program that uses artificial intelligence to find federal tax returns that are wrong.

The report must cover three things: the total amount of improper tax refunds or reduced tax bills that resulted from fraud the program caught, the total amount recovered because of the program, and how accurate the artificial intelligence tools were at spotting fraudulent tax returns.

posts.title: Stop Secret Spending Act of 2025
posts.label: 📌 Presented to President
posts.summary:
Stop Secret Spending Act of 2025
This bill expands a requirement for federal agencies to report expenditures on the USAspending.gov website to include other transaction agreement expenditures. (Other transaction agreements, or OTAs, are contractual instruments other than standard procurement contracts, grants, or cooperative agreements; they are exempt from many federal procurement laws and regulations).
Under current law, federal agencies must report expenditures on federal awards to USAspending.gov with the term federal award defined as federal grants, loans, cooperative agreements, contracts, and certain other types of expenditures. This bill expands the definition of federal award to include expenditures under OTAs, and therefore such expenditures must be included on the USAspending.gov website.
The Department of the Treasury must ensure that data relating to OTAs are automatically transmitted to the website and a centralized view of this data is available on the website. Treasury must also annually post on the USAspending.gov website a report that includes (1) the total amount of federal spending on federal awards for which data has not been posted on the website, and (2) the reason why such spending data was not posted.
For 10 years after enactment, the Office of Inspector General of specified federal agencies must periodically submit to Congress and make publicly available a report assessing the agency's spending data and use of data standards.
posts.summaryLabel: Congressional Research Service, Introduced in House
posts.meta: Oversight and Government Reform Committee · Rep. Barry Moore (R-AL)
posts.whatsNext: President has 10 days (Sundays excepted): sign, veto, or it becomes law unsigned (pocket veto if adjournment prevents return)

aiSummaries.text:
This bill requires federal agencies to report their spending on other transaction agreements, a type of contract that falls outside standard procurement, grant, and cooperative agreement rules, to the USAspending.gov website. Currently, the reporting requirement covers federal grants, loans, cooperative agreements, contracts, and certain other expenditures, but not these agreements. Once this bill passes, spending under these agreements will count as federal awards and must appear on the site.

The Department of the Treasury must make sure data on these agreements is sent to the website automatically and that a single, central view of this data is available there. Each year, Treasury must also post a report on the site showing the total amount of federal spending on federal awards whose data has not been posted, along with the reason it was not posted.

For 10 years after the law is enacted, the Office of Inspector General of specified federal agencies must regularly send Congress a report evaluating the agency's spending data and its use of data standards. These reports must also be made available to the public.

posts.title: Doug LaMalfa Federal Disaster Tax Relief Certainty Act
posts.label: 📌 Presented to President
posts.summary:
Doug LaMalfa Federal Disaster Tax Relief Certainty Act
This bill extends the federal tax deduction for qualified disaster-related personal casualty losses and the exclusion from gross income of qualified wildfire relief payments.
Under current law, unreimbursed personal casualty losses arising in a qualified disaster area (qualified disaster-related personal casualty losses) are deductible (as an itemized tax deduction or as part of the standard tax deduction) if such losses exceed $500 per casualty. A qualified disaster area is an area with respect to which a major disaster has been declared during the period beginning in 2020 and ending 60 days after July 4, 2025, if the incident period begins on or after December 28, 2019, and on or before July 4, 2025.
The bill extends the federal tax deduction for qualified disaster-related personal casualty losses by defining a qualified disaster area as an area with respect to which a major disaster has been declared if the incident period begins on or after December 28, 2019, and before January 1, 2027.
The bill provides that the exclusion from gross income of qualified wildfire relief payments applies to such payments attributable to forest or range fires declared a federal disaster after 2014 and before 2027, regardless of when such payments are received. (Currently, qualified wildfire relief payments attributable to forest or range fires declared a federal disaster after 2014 and received after 2019 and before 2026 may be excluded from gross income.)
The bill also provides statutory authority for several related tax rules.
posts.summaryLabel: Congressional Research Service, Reported to House
posts.committee: Finance Committee, Ways and Means Committee
posts.meta: Finance Committee, Ways and Means Committee · Rep. W. Steube (R-FL)
posts.whatsNext: President has 10 days (Sundays excepted): sign, veto, or it becomes law unsigned (pocket veto if adjournment prevents return)

aiSummaries.text:
This bill extends two federal tax benefits for people affected by disasters. First, it extends the deduction for uninsured personal property losses in federally declared disaster areas. Under current law, those losses can be deducted, either as an itemized deduction or as part of the standard deduction, if each loss is more than $500. The current rules cover disasters with incident periods starting from December 28, 2019 through July 4, 2025. The bill would keep the deduction in place for disasters whose incident periods start on or after December 28, 2019 and before January 1, 2027.

Second, the bill extends the tax exclusion for certain wildfire relief payments. Such payments would not count as taxable income if they are tied to forest or range fires declared federal disasters after 2014 and before 2027. Under current law, that exclusion applies only to payments received after 2019 and before 2026. Under the bill, the timing of when the payment is received would no longer matter.

The bill also adds several related tax rules into federal law.

posts.title: Water Resources Development Act of 2026

posts.note: Transportation and Infrastructure, as amended, H. Rept. 119-795
posts.summary:
Water Resources Development Act of 2026
This bill authorizes and modifies certain water resource infrastructure projects and programs of the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers and makes related requirements. For example, the bill authorizes and modifies various water resources feasibility studies and projects of the Corps of Engineers, such as studies or projects to
maintain ports and harbors,
make certain waterways more navigable,
reduce flood and storm damage,
restore aquatic ecosystems and protect fish and wildlife,
protect shorelines,
address harmful algal blooms,
rehabilitate dams,
manage recreational sites and facilities,
support water supply and storage projects, and
support other water resources infrastructure.
The bill also directs the Corps of Engineers to establish an Office on Alternative Delivery Methods in order to accelerate project delivery of infrastructure.
In addition, the bill directs the Corps of Engineers to issue a rule that establishes categorical permissions for certain harbor or river improvements that will cause only minimal adverse environmental effects.
posts.summaryLabel: Congressional Research Service, Reported to House
posts.meta: Transportation and Infrastructure Committee · Rep. Sam Graves (R-MO)
posts.whatsNext: Floor scheduling (leadership decides if and when it gets a vote)

aiSummaries.text:
The Water Resources Development Act of 2026 authorizes and changes certain water infrastructure projects and programs run by the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers, and it sets related requirements. It covers a range of water-related work, including studies and projects to maintain ports and harbors, make some waterways easier to navigate, reduce flood and storm damage, restore aquatic ecosystems and protect fish and wildlife, protect shorelines, address harmful algal blooms, rehabilitate dams, manage recreation sites and facilities, support water supply and storage, and support other water resources infrastructure.

The bill also directs the Corps of Engineers to create an Office on Alternative Delivery Methods, with the goal of speeding up the delivery of infrastructure projects.

In addition, the bill requires the Corps of Engineers to issue a rule that sets up categorical permissions for certain harbor or river improvements expected to cause only minimal harm to the environment.

posts.title: Protect Economic and Academic Freedom Act of 2026
posts.label: ✅🏛️ Passed House (237-169)
posts.summary:
Protect Economic and Academic Freedom Act of 2026
This bill prohibits institutions of higher education (IHEs) that participate in federal student aid programs from engaging in boycotts against Israel. Specifically, IHEs may not engage in a commercial action intended to limit commercial relations with Israel, or with an entity licensed by, regulated by, or organized under the laws of Israel, that is not based on a valid business reason.
Further, IHEs receiving, or applying to receive, Title VI funds (federal funding for foreign language and international education programs) must annually certify that (1) students and faculty are allowed to participate in academic programs located in Israel in the same manner and under the same terms and conditions as programs in other foreign countries, and (2) students and faculty at postsecondary institutions located in Israel may participate in such IHE’s academic programs in the same manner and under the same terms and conditions as students and faculty from other foreign countries.
posts.summaryLabel: Congressional Research Service, Reported to House
posts.meta: Education and Workforce Committee · Rep. Virginia Foxx (R-NC)
posts.whatsNext: To the Senate (if and when it takes it up)

aiSummaries.text:
This bill would bar colleges and universities that take part in federal student aid programs from boycotting Israel. Under the bill, a school could not take a business action meant to limit its dealings with Israel, or with Israeli-licensed, Israeli-regulated, or Israeli-organized entities, unless there is a valid business reason for it.

The bill also adds a condition for schools that receive, or apply for, Title VI funding, which supports foreign language and international education programs. Each year, these schools would have to certify two things. First, that their students and faculty can join academic programs located in Israel in the same way, and on the same terms, as programs in other foreign countries. Second, that students and faculty from schools in Israel can join the school's own academic programs in the same way, and on the same terms, as students and faculty from other foreign countries.

posts.title: Continuing Appropriations and Extensions Act, 2027
posts.label: 📜✍️ Signed by Pres. Trump
posts.summary:
Continuing Appropriations and Extensions Act, 2027
This act provides continuing FY2027 appropriations for federal agencies through December 11, 2026, and extends various expiring programs and authorities.
DIVISION A--CONTINUING APPROPRIATIONS ACT, 2027
Continuing Appropriations Act, 2027
This division provides continuing FY2027 appropriations to federal agencies through the earlier of December 11, 2026, or the enactment of the applicable appropriations act. It is known as a continuing resolution (CR) and prevents a government shutdown that would otherwise occur if the FY2027 appropriations bills have not been enacted when FY2027 begins on October 1, 2026.
The CR funds most programs and activities at the FY2026 levels with several exceptions that provide funding flexibility or additional appropriations for various programs. For example, the CR includes exceptions for
the Special Supplemental Nutrition Program for Women, Infants, and Children (WIC);
Small Business Administration loans;
the Disaster Relief Fund;
the Indian Health Service;
the Department of Justice; and
wildfire suppression activities.
For more information on this division, see CRS Report R49353, Overview of Continuing Appropriations for FY2027 (Division A of P.L. 119-103).
DIVISION B--AUTHORIZING EXTENSIONS
This division extends various expiring programs and authorities, including certain programs related to agriculture and foreign trade.
(Sec. 2001) This section reauthorizes the United States Grain Standards Act, which authorizes the Department of Agriculture to establish official marketing standards for grains.
Specifically, this section extends the authority of the Federal Grain Inspection Service (FGIS) through December 11, 2026, to (1) collect fees for required federal supervision of official inspections and weighing services provided by designated official agencies and state agencies, and (2) maintain the Grain Inspection Advisory Committee.
The section also extends through FY2027 (1) the cap on FGIS's administrative and supervisory costs, and (2) authorization for FGIS grain standards development and maintenance activities.
(Sec. 2002) This section extends the authority for the Forest Service to use the Agriculture Conservation Experienced Services (ACES) program through December 11, 2026. The program allows the Forest Service to acquire skilled personnel (age 55 and older) from nonprofit partners to provide temporary technical and administrative services for conservation-related programs that are executed on or directly impacting National Forest System land.
(Sec. 2003) This section extends through December 11, 2026, the authority for entering into agreements to finance sales or provide other assistance through the Food for Peace program.
(Sec. 2004) This section extends certain authorities under the Defense Production Act of 1950 through December 11, 2026.
(Sec. 2005) This section extends through December 11, 2026, the authority of the Environmental Protection Agency to collect user fees under the Toxic Substances Control Act.
(Sec. 2006) This section increases Medicaid funding for FY2026 for the Northern Mariana Islands.
(Sec. 2007) This section reduces funding for the Medicare Improvement Fund beginning in FY2027.
(Sec. 2008) This section extends through December 31, 2028, trade preferences that provide duty-free access to the U.S. market for most exports from eligible countries in sub-Saharan Africa (SSA).
Specifically, the section extends through 2028 the duty-free treatment of the products of beneficiary SSA countries under the Trade Act of 1974 (specifically, the Generalized System of Preferences) and the African Growth and Opportunity Act (AGOA). (Currently, there are 32 countries eligible for AGOA.)
Additionally, the extended period applies to the following provisions of AGOA: (1) the duty-free treatment of certain apparel articles from beneficiary SSA countries; and (2) the third-country fabric provision, which allows limited amounts of apparel articles from lesser developed beneficiary SSA countries to qualify for duty-free treatment, even if the yarns and fabrics used in their production are imported from non-AGOA countries (e.g., apparel assembled in Kenya with Chinese fabrics).
(Sec. 2009) This section extends through December 31, 2028, the special duty-free rules for various apparel products imported from Haiti.
(Sec. 2010) This section extends various customs user fees through March 31, 2032, including certain rates for merchandise processing fees.
(Sec. 2011) This section extends the authorization for the Cybersecurity Information Sharing Act through December 11, 2026. The act authorizes sharing of appropriate cybersecurity information between federal and nonfederal entities, defensive cybersecurity activities, liability protections, and oversight.
(Sec. 2012) This section extends the authority for the Department of Homeland Security's (DHS’s) National Cybersecurity Protection System and related reporting requirements through December 11, 2026. The system authorizes multiple activities by DHS to help defend federal agencies from cyberthreats.
(Sec. 2013) This section extends the authority for DHS's Joint Task Forces through December 11, 2026.
(Sec. 2014) This section extends through December 11, 2026, the Technology Modernization Fund and the fund's board. The fund is administered by the General Services Administration to improve information technology and enhance cybersecurity across the federal government.
(Sec. 2015) This section extends the authority of the U.S. Patent and Trademark Office to set fees through December 11, 2026.
(Sec. 2016) This section extends the U.S. Commission on International Religious Freedom through December 11, 2026. The commission is an independent federal commission tasked with monitoring international religious freedom conditions, reviewing U.S. government policy, and making policy recommendations.
(Sec. 2017) This section extends through December 11, 2026, the authority of the Department of State to collect passport fees under the Western Hemisphere Travel Initiative.
(Sec. 2018) This section exempts the budgetary effects of Divisions B-D of this act from (1) the Statutory Pay-As-You-Go (PAYGO) Act of 2010, (2) the Senate PAYGO rule, and (3) certain budget scorekeeping rules.
(Sec. 2019) This section delays the effective date of portions of the new statutory definition of hemp until December 11, 2026. For more information, see CRS In Focus IF13136, Changes to the Statutory Definition of Hemp and Implications for Agricultural Policy.
DIVISION C--SURFACE TRANSPORTATION EXTENSION ACT OF 2026
Surface Transportation Extension Act of 2026
This division extends various expiring surface transportation programs and authorities.
TITLE I--SURFACE TRANSPORTATION PROGRAMS
(Sec. 3101) This section extends federal highway, transit, and road safety programs of the Department of Transportation through December 11, 2026.
(Sec. 3102) This section reauthorizes until December 11, 2026, the Appalachian Regional Commission, including the high-speed broadband deployment and energy hub initiatives.
(Sec. 3103) This section reauthorizes until December 11, 2026, the Sport Fish Restoration Program.
(Sec. 3104) This section extends until September 30, 2027, the deadline to use previously authorized federal highway funds for certain Federal Highway Administration programs, including the
Bridge Investment Program;
Congestion Relief Program;
Charging and Fueling Infrastructure Discretionary Grant Program;
Rural Surface Transportation Grant Program;
Promoting Resilient Operations for Transformative, Efficient, and Cost-saving Transportation Program (PROTECT) grants;
Reduction of Truck Emissions at Port Facilities Program; and
Nationally Significant Federal Lands and Tribal Projects program.
TITLE II--TRUST FUNDS
(Sec. 3201) This section extends expenditure authority through December 11, 2026, for the Highway Trust Fund, Sport Fish Restoration and Boating Trust Fund, and Leaking Underground Storage Tank Trust Fund.
DIVISION D--DEPARTMENT OF VETERANS AFFAIRS EXTENDERS
This division extends various expiring Department of Veterans Affairs (VA) programs and authorities.
TITLE I--HEALTH CARE MATTERS
(Sec. 4101) This section extends through December 10, 2026, the authority for the VA to collect copayments from certain veterans for hospital care or nursing home care.
(Sec. 4102) This section extends through December 11, 2026, the requirement that the VA provide nursing home care to certain veterans with a service-connected disability.
(Sec. 4103) This section extends through December 11, 2026, the authorization for the expansion of the VA’s Rural Access Network for Growth Enhancement (RANGE) program, which serves veterans in rural areas who are experiencing mental illness.
(Sec. 4104) This section extends through December 11, 2026, the VA’s authority to provide grants under the Staff Sergeant Parker Gordon Fox Suicide Prevention Grant Program, for purposes of providing community-based suicide prevention services and mental health care.
(Sec. 4105) This section extends through December 11, 2026, the VA grant program to provide mental health support for family caregivers of veterans who participate in the VA’s Program of Comprehensive Assistance for Family Caregivers.
(Sec. 4106) This section extends through December 11, 2026, the requirement that the VA pay or reimburse certain veterans with a service-connected disability for ambulance transport from a rural area.
(Sec. 4107) This section extends through December 11, 2026, the joint incentive program between the VA and Department of Defense to share health care resources.
TITLE II--BENEFITS
(Sec. 4201) This section extends through December 11, 2026, the authority of the VA to maintain a regional office in the Philippines.
(Sec. 4202) This section extends through December 11, 2026, the period of relief for those affected by a closure or disapproval of a course of education in regard to the individual’s educational assistance entitlement. Generally, when an individual transfers fewer than 12 credits from a program of education that is closed or disapproved, the individual is deemed to have not received those credits, and no charge from the individual's entitlement to education assistance may be made for that period of enrollment. This section extends the relief through December 11, 2026.
TITLE III--HOUSING
(Sec. 4301) This section extends through December 11, 2026, a Department of Labor grant program for programs and facilities that provide dedicated services for homeless women veterans and homeless veterans with children.
(Sec. 4302) This section extends through December 11, 2026, the VA's Health Care for Homeless Veterans program, which provides outreach, treatment, rehabilitation, and therapeutic transitional housing assistance for seriously mentally ill and homeless veterans. Additionally, the section extends the authority of the VA to operate a program to expand and improve the provision of benefits and services to homeless veterans.
(Sec. 4303) This section extends through December 11, 2026, the VA’s authority to provide housing assistance to homeless veterans and their families.
(Sec. 4304) This section extends through December 11, 2026, the Supportive Services for Veterans Families program, which provides financial assistance for supportive services for very low-income veteran families in permanent housing or transitioning from homelessness.
(Sec. 4305) This section extends through December 11, 2026, the VA program to provide grants to encourage the development of programs for homeless veterans with special needs.
(Sec. 4306) This section extends through December 11, 2026, the authority and activities of the VA’s Advisory Committee on Homeless Veterans.
(Sec. 4307) This section extends through December 11, 2026, the VA’s authority to provide assistance for housing adaptations for disabled veterans who are residing temporarily in housing owned by a family member.
(Sec. 4308) This section extends through December 11, 2026, the Specially Adapted Housing Assistive Technology (SAHAT) Grant Program, through which the VA provides grants to develop assistive technologies for use in specially adapted housing.
TITLE IV--OTHER MATTERS
(Sec. 4401) This section extends through December 11, 2026, the VA's authority to transport individuals in connection with vocational rehabilitation or required counseling or for the purpose of examination, treatment, or care.
(Sec. 4402) This section extends through December 11, 2026, the authority of the VA Office of Inspector General to subpoena the attendance and testimony of witnesses as necessary to carry out the duties of the office.
(Sec. 4403) This section extends through December 11, 2026, the authority of the VA to provide assistance for adaptive sports opportunities for disabled veterans and disabled members of the Armed Forces.
(Sec. 4404) This section extends through December 11, 2026, the authority and activities of the VA’s Advisory Committee on Minority Veterans.
(Sec. 4405) This section extends a requirement for the VA to provide a burial and funeral allowance for a veteran who dies in a home or other setting at which the veteran was receiving VA hospice care (if such care was directly preceded by VA hospital or nursing home care). The section applies the requirement to deaths occurring before December 12, 2026.
(Sec. 4406) This section extends through December 11, 2026, certain rates and procedures under the VA Vendee Loan Program, under which qualified borrowers may purchase VA real estate owned properties with little to no money down. Specifically, not more than 85% of purchases made during any fiscal year under the Vendee Loan Program shall be property marketed with VA financing.
(Sec. 4407) This section extends through December 11, 2026, the authority of the VA to transfer real property to other agencies, states, or public or private entities.

aiSummaries.text:
This act does two main things. First, it keeps the federal government funded for fiscal year 2027 through December 11, 2026, or until the regular funding bills for that year are passed, whichever comes first. This is a "continuing resolution," which prevents a government shutdown if those bills are not ready when the new fiscal year starts on October 1, 2026. Most programs continue at their 2026 funding levels, with exceptions for certain programs such as WIC (the nutrition program for women, infants, and children), Small Business Administration loans, disaster relief, the Indian Health Service, the Department of Justice, and wildfire suppression.

Second, the act extends many programs and authorities that would otherwise expire. These cover a wide range of areas. In agriculture, it continues the grain inspection and standards work of the Federal Grain Inspection Service, a Forest Service program that brings in experienced older workers, and the Food for Peace program. It also extends a Defense Production Act authority, the EPA's ability to collect fees under the Toxic Substances Control Act, and various cybersecurity programs, including information sharing, a Homeland Security cybersecurity system, and a federal technology modernization fund. Several trade benefits are extended as well. Duty-free access for most exports from eligible sub-Saharan African countries continues through December 31, 2028, and similar duty-free rules for certain apparel from Haiti also run through December 31, 2028. Customs user fees are extended through March 31, 2032. The delay of parts of the new statutory definition of hemp runs until December 11, 2026.

The act also includes Medicaid funding for the Northern Mariana Islands for fiscal year 2026, and it reduces funding for the Medicare Improvement Fund starting in fiscal year 2027. Budget rules under the Statutory Pay-As-You-Go Act and related Senate rules are set aside for the budgetary effects of the act's second through fourth divisions.

Another division extends surface transportation programs, including federal highway, transit, and road safety programs, the Appalachian Regional Commission, and the Sport Fish Restoration Program, all through December 11, 2026. It gives states until September 30, 2027, to use previously authorized highway funds for several grant programs, and it extends expenditure authority for the Highway Trust Fund, the Sport Fish Restoration and Boating Trust Fund, and the Leaking Underground Storage Tank Trust Fund through December 11, 2026.

The final division extends many Department of Veterans Affairs programs, most through December 11, 2026. These include copayment collection for certain hospital and nursing home care (through December 10, 2026), nursing home care for certain veterans with service-connected disabilities, mental health and suicide prevention programs, family caregiver mental health support, ambulance reimbursement for certain rural veterans, and a joint VA and Defense Department health resource sharing program. Benefits-related extensions cover a Philippines regional office and relief for veterans affected by school closures. Housing-related extensions cover several programs for homeless veterans, housing adaptations for disabled veterans, and assistive technology grants. Other extensions cover veteran transportation for care, the VA Inspector General's subpoena power, adaptive sports assistance, the Advisory Committee on Minority Veterans, certain burial allowances for veterans who die in VA hospice care, the Vendee Loan Program, and the transfer of VA real property. The burial allowance provision applies to deaths before December 12, 2026.

aiSummaries.text:
This bill keeps the federal government funded after the new fiscal year begins on October 1, 2026, so that a government shutdown does not occur while the full set of FY2027 spending bills is still pending. It is a continuing resolution, and its funding runs through the earlier of December 11, 2026, or the date a matching appropriations act is enacted.

Most federal programs will continue at their FY2026 funding levels. A number of programs receive special treatment, with extra funding or more flexibility. These include the Special Supplemental Nutrition Program for Women, Infants, and Children (WIC), Small Business Administration loans, the Disaster Relief Fund, the Indian Health Service, the Department of Justice, and wildfire suppression.

The bill also extends several programs and authorities that would otherwise expire. These cover agriculture, flood insurance, cybersecurity, surface transportation, veterans benefits, housing, defense production, and trade preferences for Haiti and certain countries in sub-Saharan Africa.

Finally, the bill includes several other provisions. It temporarily blocks a regulation that revises guidance for federal financial assistance. It delays certain changes to the legal definition of hemp. It extends the freeze on cost-of-living pay adjustments for Members of Congress and keeps limits on pay increases for the Vice President and certain senior political appointees. It also provides death gratuities to the beneficiaries of two Members of Congress who died while in office.

posts.title: Earned Wage Access Consumer Protection Act
posts.label: 📋 Reported by committee
posts.note: Financial Services, as amended, H. Rept. 119-790
posts.summary:
Earned Wage Access Consumer Protection Act
This bill addresses the regulation of earned wage access products. Earned wage access products provide consumers with access to their earned wages before their scheduled pay day.
The bill specifies that earned wage access products are not subject to regulation under the Truth in Lending Act (TILA). TILA requires consumer credit products to disclose borrowing costs, finance charges, and the total cost of the loan.
Under the bill, providers of earned wage access products
must provide an alternative no-cost option for receiving earned wages if the provider offers an option to receive earned wages for a fee;
are prohibited from bringing civil suits or from pursuing collection to compel repayment, except in cases of fraud; and
must reimburse the consumer for overdraft fees or penalties imposed on a consumer by their depository institution if incurred because of an error by the provider.
Providers must inform consumers of their rights under an agreement for an earned wage access product and disclose all associated fees before the consumer enters into an agreement. Providers must also inform consumers how to obtain earned wages without paying a fee or tip in a clear and conspicuous manner.
Providers are prohibited from sharing fees or tips with the consumer’s employer. The bill also limits the form of payment providers may accept from consumers and limits certain additional fees for failure to pay.
A provider may not set a default tip at an amount greater than $0 for such services.
posts.summaryLabel: Congressional Research Service, Reported to House
posts.meta: Financial Services Committee · Rep. Bryan Steil (R-WI)
posts.whatsNext: Floor scheduling (leadership decides if and when it gets a vote)

aiSummaries.text:
This bill sets rules for earned wage access products, which let workers get part of their pay before their regular payday. The bill says these products are not covered by the Truth in Lending Act, a federal law that requires lenders to clearly disclose borrowing costs, finance charges, and the total cost of a loan.

Under the bill, providers of these products must offer a free way to get earned wages if they also offer a way to get them for a fee. Providers may not file civil lawsuits or try to collect repayment from a consumer, except in cases of fraud. If a consumer is charged an overdraft fee or penalty by their bank because of a mistake made by the provider, the provider must pay the consumer back for it.

Before a consumer signs up, providers must explain the consumer's rights under the agreement and list all fees. Providers must also clearly and prominently tell consumers how to get their earned wages without paying any fee or tip.

Providers may not share fees or tips with the consumer's employer. The bill also restricts the forms of payment providers can accept from consumers and limits certain extra fees for not paying.

Finally, a provider may not set a default tip amount higher than $0.

posts.title: STOP Payments Fraud Act of 2026
posts.label: 📋 Reported by committee
posts.note: Financial Services, as amended, H. Rept. 119-792
posts.summary:
Strengthening Transaction Oversight and Preventing Payments Fraud Act of 2026 or the STOP Payments Fraud Act of 2026
This bill establishes additional grounds for banks to pause the processing of deposited checks and wire transfers. Under current law, banks are generally required to make deposited funds available in one to two business days, depending on the type of deposit and with limited exceptions.
Under the bill, receiving banks are allowed to delay the processing of checks or wire transfers that they reasonably suspect are fraudulent. The bill allows for an initial hold that is not to exceed 10 days and an extended hold that is not to exceed 45 days. If an account is overdrawn due to a hold on a wire transfer and the depositor did not receive written notice, no overdraft fees may be applied.
The bill allows the Federal Reserve Board and the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau (CFPB) to determine when to apply safeguards to accounts determined to be at greater risk of fraud. Such safeguards must not apply for more than 60 days for each occurrence.
These changes take effect 60 days after the issuance of implementing rules, which must be issued within one year of the bill's enactment.
The bill also requires (1) the board and CFPB to determine whether to remove Treasury checks and cashier’s checks from expedited classification due to material losses from fraud, and (2) the Government Accountability Office to report on issues relating to the availability of funds and fraud protection.
posts.summaryLabel: Congressional Research Service, Reported to House
posts.meta: Financial Services Committee · Rep. Young Kim (R-CA)
posts.whatsNext: Floor scheduling (leadership decides if and when it gets a vote)

aiSummaries.text:
The STOP Payments Fraud Act of 2026 gives banks more power to pause deposited checks and wire transfers they suspect are fraudulent. Right now, banks generally must make deposited money available within one to two business days, with only limited exceptions. Under this bill, a receiving bank that reasonably suspects a check or wire transfer is fraudulent may delay it. The initial hold can last no more than 10 days, and an extended hold can last no more than 45 days. If an account goes overdrawn because of a wire transfer hold and the account holder did not receive written notice, the bank cannot charge overdraft fees.

The bill also lets the Federal Reserve Board and the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau decide when extra safeguards should apply to accounts considered at greater risk of fraud. Each of these safeguards cannot last more than 60 days for each occurrence.

These changes take effect 60 days after the implementing rules are issued, and those rules must be issued within one year of the bill becoming law.

The bill further directs the Federal Reserve Board and the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau to decide whether Treasury checks and cashier's checks should be removed from the expedited availability category because of large fraud losses. It also requires the Government Accountability Office to report on how funds availability and fraud protection are working.

posts.title: Whistleblower Protection Act of 2025
posts.label: 📋 Reported by committee
posts.note: Financial Services, as amended, H. Rept. 119-786, Part I
posts.summary:
Whistleblower Protection Act of 2025
This bill expands existing whistleblower protections for employees of federal contractors or grant recipients to apply to all contracts and grants funded by the Department of Housing and Urban Development (HUD) regardless of the date of execution.
Current law protects employees of federal contractors or grant recipients from a reprisal (i.e., discharge, demotion, or discrimination) for disclosing evidence to Congress or another appropriate official of certain misconduct involving federal contracts, grants, or funds. This provision currently applies only to contracts and grants signed or modified after the law took effect in 2013. The bill expands these protections to apply to HUD contracts and grants signed before the law was enacted.
posts.summaryLabel: Congressional Research Service, Reported to House
posts.committee: Oversight and Government Reform Committee, Financial Services Committee
posts.meta: Oversight and Government Reform Committee, Financial Services Committee · Rep. Monica De La Cruz (R-TX)
posts.whatsNext: Floor scheduling - the bill went to more than one committee (leadership decides if and when it gets a vote)

aiSummaries.text:
This bill would extend whistleblower protections to more workers who are employed under contracts and grants funded by the Department of Housing and Urban Development (HUD). Under current law, employees of federal contractors and grant recipients are protected from being fired, demoted, or otherwise discriminated against for reporting certain misconduct involving federal contracts, grants, or funds to Congress or another appropriate official. However, these protections only cover contracts and grants that were signed or changed after the law took effect in 2013.

The bill would remove that date limit for HUD-funded work. Its protections would apply to HUD contracts and grants signed before the law was enacted, as well as those signed afterward.

(Sec. 2008) This section extends through December 31, 2028, trade preferences that provide duty-free access to the U.S. market for most exports from eligible countries in sub-Saharan Africa (SSA).
Specifically, the section extends through 2028 the duty-free treatment of the products of beneficiary SSA countries under the Trade Act of 1974 (specifically, the Generalized System of Preferences) and the African Growth and Opportunity Act (AGOA). (Currently, there are 32 countries eligible for AGOA.)
Additionally, the extended period applies to the following provisions of AGOA: (1) the duty-free treatment of certain apparel articles from beneficiary SSA countries; and (2) the third-country fabric provision, which allows limited amounts of apparel articles from lesser developed beneficiary SSA countries to qualify for duty-free treatment, even if the yarns and fabrics used in their production are imported from non-AGOA countries (e.g., apparel assembled in Kenya with Chinese fabrics).
(Sec. 2009) This section extends through December 31, 2028, the special duty-free rules for various apparel products imported from Haiti.
(Sec. 2010) This section extends various customs user fees through March 31, 2032, including certain rates for merchandise processing fees.
(Sec. 2011) This section extends the authorization for the Cybersecurity Information Sharing Act through December 11, 2026. The act authorizes sharing of appropriate cybersecurity information between federal and nonfederal entities, defensive cybersecurity activities, liability protections, and oversight.
(Sec. 2012) This section extends the authority for the Department of Homeland Security's (DHS’s) National Cybersecurity Protection System and related reporting requirements through December 11, 2026. The system authorizes multiple activities by DHS to help defend federal agencies from cyberthreats.
(Sec. 2013) This section extends the authority for DHS's Joint Task Forces through December 11, 2026.
(Sec. 2014) This section extends through December 11, 2026, the Technology Modernization Fund and the fund's board. The fund is administered by the General Services Administration to improve information technology and enhance cybersecurity across the federal government.
(Sec. 2015) This section extends the authority of the U.S. Patent and Trademark Office to set fees through December 11, 2026.
(Sec. 2016) This section extends the U.S. Commission on International Religious Freedom through December 11, 2026. The commission is an independent federal commission tasked with monitoring international religious freedom conditions, reviewing U.S. government policy, and making policy recommendations.
(Sec. 2017) This section extends through December 11, 2026, the authority of the Department of State to collect passport fees under the Western Hemisphere Travel Initiative.
(Sec. 2018) This section exempts the budgetary effects of Divisions B-D of this act from (1) the Statutory Pay-As-You-Go (PAYGO) Act of 2010, (2) the Senate PAYGO rule, and (3) certain budget scorekeeping rules.
(Sec. 2019) This section delays the effective date of portions of the new statutory definition of hemp until December 11, 2026. For more information, see CRS In Focus IF13136, Changes to the Statutory Definition of Hemp and Implications for Agricultural Policy.
DIVISION C--SURFACE TRANSPORTATION EXTENSION ACT OF 2026
Surface Transportation Extension Act of 2026
This division extends various expiring surface transportation programs and authorities.
TITLE I--SURFACE TRANSPORTATION PROGRAMS
(Sec. 3101) This section extends federal highway, transit, and road safety programs of the Department of Transportation through December 11, 2026.
(Sec. 3102) This section reauthorizes until December 11, 2026, the Appalachian Regional Commission, including the high-speed broadband deployment and energy hub initiatives.
(Sec. 3103) This section reauthorizes until December 11, 2026, the Sport Fish Restoration Program.
(Sec. 3104) This section extends until September 30, 2027, the deadline to use previously authorized federal highway funds for certain Federal Highway Administration programs, including the
Bridge Investment Program;
Congestion Relief Program;
Charging and Fueling Infrastructure Discretionary Grant Program;
Rural Surface Transportation Grant Program;
Promoting Resilient Operations for Transformative, Efficient, and Cost-saving Transportation Program (PROTECT) grants;
Reduction of Truck Emissions at Port Facilities Program; and
Nationally Significant Federal Lands and Tribal Projects program.
TITLE II--TRUST FUNDS
(Sec. 3201) This section extends expenditure authority through December 11, 2026, for the Highway Trust Fund, Sport Fish Restoration and Boating Trust Fund, and Leaking Underground Storage Tank Trust Fund.
DIVISION D--DEPARTMENT OF VETERANS AFFAIRS EXTENDERS
This division extends various expiring Department of Veterans Affairs (VA) programs and authorities.
TITLE I--HEALTH CARE MATTERS
(Sec. 4101) This section extends through December 10, 2026, the authority for the VA to collect copayments from certain veterans for hospital care or nursing home care.
(Sec. 4102) This section extends through December 11, 2026, the requirement that the VA provide nursing home care to certain veterans with a service-connected disability.
(Sec. 4103) This section extends through December 11, 2026, the authorization for the expansion of the VA’s Rural Access Network for Growth Enhancement (RANGE) program, which serves veterans in rural areas who are experiencing mental illness.
(Sec. 4104) This section extends through December 11, 2026, the VA’s authority to provide grants under the Staff Sergeant Parker Gordon Fox Suicide Prevention Grant Program, for purposes of providing community-based suicide prevention services and mental health care.
(Sec. 4105) This section extends through December 11, 2026, the VA grant program to provide mental health support for family caregivers of veterans who participate in the VA’s Program of Comprehensive Assistance for Family Caregivers.
(Sec. 4106) This section extends through December 11, 2026, the requirement that the VA pay or reimburse certain veterans with a service-connected disability for ambulance transport from a rural area.
(Sec. 4107) This section extends through December 11, 2026, the joint incentive program between the VA and Department of Defense to share health care resources.
TITLE II--BENEFITS
(Sec. 4201) This section extends through December 11, 2026, the authority of the VA to maintain a regional office in the Philippines.
(Sec. 4202) This section extends through December 11, 2026, the period of relief for those affected by a closure or disapproval of a course of education in regard to the individual’s educational assistance entitlement. Generally, when an individual transfers fewer than 12 credits from a program of education that is closed or disapproved, the individual is deemed to have not received those credits, and no charge from the individual's entitlement to education assistance may be made for that period of enrollment. This section extends the relief through December 11, 2026.
TITLE III--HOUSING
(Sec. 4301) This section extends through December 11, 2026, a Department of Labor grant program for programs and facilities that provide dedicated services for homeless women veterans and homeless veterans with children.
(Sec. 4302) This section extends through December 11, 2026, the VA's Health Care for Homeless Veterans program, which provides outreach, treatment, rehabilitation, and therapeutic transitional housing assistance for seriously mentally ill and homeless veterans. (Sec. 4303) This section extends through December 11, 2026, the VA’s authority to provide housing assistance to homeless veterans and their families.
(Sec. 4304) This section extends through December 11, 2026, the Supportive Services for Veterans Families program, which provides financial assistance for supportive services for very low-income veteran families in permanent housing or transitioning from homelessness.
(Sec. 4305) This section extends through December 11, 2026, the VA program to provide grants to encourage the development of programs for homeless veterans with special needs.
(Sec. 4306) This section extends through December 11, 2026, the authority and activities of the VA’s Advisory Committee on Homeless Veterans.
(Sec. 4307) This section extends through December 11, 2026, the VA’s authority to provide assistance for housing adaptations for disabled veterans who are residing temporarily in housing owned by a family member.
(Sec. 4308) This section extends through December 11, 2026, the Specially Adapted Housing Assistive Technology (SAHAT) Grant Program, through which the VA provides grants to develop assistive technologies for use in specially adapted housing.
TITLE IV--OTHER MATTERS
(Sec. 4401) This section extends through December 11, 2026, the VA's authority to transport individuals in connection with vocational rehabilitation or required counseling or for the purpose of examination, treatment, or care.
(Sec. 4402) This section extends through December 11, 2026, the authority of the VA Office of Inspector General to subpoena the attendance and testimony of witnesses as necessary to carry out the duties of the office.

(Sec. 4404) This section extends through December 11, 2026, the authority and activities of the VA’s Advisory Committee on Minority Veterans.
(Sec. 4405) This section extends a requirement for the VA to provide a burial and funeral allowance for a veteran who dies in a home or other setting at which the veteran was receiving VA hospice care (if such care was directly preceded by VA hospital or nursing home care). (Sec. 4406) This section extends through December 11, 2026, certain rates and procedures under the VA Vendee Loan Program, under which qualified borrowers may purchase VA real estate owned properties with little to no money down. aiSummaries.text:
This act does two main things. First, it keeps the federal government funded for fiscal year 2027 through December 11, 2026, or until the regular funding bills for that year are passed, whichever comes first. This is a "continuing resolution," which prevents a government shutdown if those bills are not ready when the new fiscal year starts on October 1, 2026. Most programs continue at their 2026 funding levels, with exceptions for certain programs such as WIC (the nutrition program for women, infants, and children), Small Business Administration loans, disaster relief, the Indian Health Service, the Department of Justice, and wildfire suppression.

Second, the act extends many programs and authorities that would otherwise expire. These cover a wide range of areas. In agriculture, it continues the grain inspection and standards work of the Federal Grain Inspection Service, a Forest Service program that brings in experienced older workers, and the Food for Peace program. It also extends a Defense Production Act authority, the EPA's ability to collect fees under the Toxic Substances Control Act, and various cybersecurity programs, including information sharing, a Homeland Security cybersecurity system, and a federal technology modernization fund. Several trade benefits are extended as well. Duty-free access for most exports from eligible sub-Saharan African countries continues through December 31, 2028, and similar duty-free rules for certain apparel from Haiti also run through December 31, 2028. Customs user fees are extended through March 31, 2032. The delay of parts of the new statutory definition of hemp runs until December 11, 2026.

The act also includes Medicaid funding for the Northern Mariana Islands for fiscal year 2026, and it reduces funding for the Medicare Improvement Fund starting in fiscal year 2027. Budget rules under the Statutory Pay-As-You-Go Act and related Senate rules are set aside for the budgetary effects of the act's second through fourth divisions.

Another division extends surface transportation programs, including federal highway, transit, and road safety programs, the Appalachian Regional Commission, and the Sport Fish Restoration Program, all through December 11, 2026. It gives states until September 30, 2027, to use previously authorized highway funds for several grant programs, and it extends expenditure authority for the Highway Trust Fund, the Sport Fish Restoration and Boating Trust Fund, and the Leaking Underground Storage Tank Trust Fund through December 11, 2026.

The final division extends many Department of Veterans Affairs programs, most through December 11, 2026. These include copayment collection for certain hospital and nursing home care (through December 10, 2026), nursing home care for certain veterans with service-connected disabilities, mental health and suicide prevention programs, family caregiver mental health support, ambulance reimbursement for certain rural veterans, and a joint VA and Defense Department health resource sharing program. Benefits-related extensions cover a Philippines regional office and relief for veterans affected by school closures. Housing-related extensions cover several programs for homeless veterans, housing adaptations for disabled veterans, and assistive technology grants. Other extensions cover veteran transportation for care, the VA Inspector General's subpoena power, adaptive sports assistance, the Advisory Committee on Minority Veterans, certain burial allowances for veterans who die in VA hospice care, the Vendee Loan Program, and the transfer of VA real property. The burial allowance provision applies to deaths before December 12, 2026.

posts.title: Kayleigh’s Law Act of 2026
posts.label: ✅🏛️ Passed House with amendment (voice vote)
posts.summary:
Kayleigh’s Law Act of 2026
This bill establishes a federal statutory framework to require federal courts to issue an order prohibiting contact with a victim (i.e., a no-contact order) in the case of a defendant who is convicted of certain violent crimes or sex crimes.
Specifically, in the case of a defendant convicted of a felony offense that is a crime of violence or that involves a sexual act or sexual conduct, on a motion by the victim or federal government, the court must issue a no-contact order.
Under the framework, the no-contact order must be imposed at sentencing and be in effect for the lifetime of the defendant unless it is terminated or suspended in accordance with specified procedures. Additionally, no fee may be assessed or collected from a victim in connection with the issuance of a no-contact order.
posts.summaryLabel: Congressional Research Service, Reported to House
posts.meta: Judiciary Committee · Rep. Abraham Hamadeh (R-AZ)
posts.whatsNext: To the Senate (if and when it takes it up)

aiSummaries.text:
This bill sets up a federal rule requiring federal courts to issue a "no-contact order," which bars the defendant from contacting the victim. The order applies when a defendant is convicted of a felony that is a crime of violence or that involves a sexual act or sexual conduct. The victim or the federal government can ask the court for the order, and the court must issue it when that request is made.

The order must be imposed at sentencing and stays in effect for the defendant's lifetime, unless it is ended or paused under specific procedures set out in the law. Victims cannot be charged any fee for getting a no-contact order.

posts.title: Prison Staff Safety Enhancement Act
posts.label: ✅🏛️ Passed House (376-8)
posts.summary:
Prison Staff Safety Enhancement Act
This bill establishes requirements for the Department of Justice (DOJ) and component agencies to assess and respond to incidents of sexual harassment and sexual assault by incarcerated individuals against Bureau of Prisons (BOP) staff.
Specifically, the bill requires DOJ to adopt national standards for the prevention, reduction, and punishment of sexual harassment and sexual assault by incarcerated individuals against correctional officers or other employees of the BOP.
Additionally, the bill requires the BOP to fully implement the recommendations of the DOJ Inspector General contained in the report titled Evaluation of the Federal Bureau of Prisons’ Efforts to Address Sexual Harassment and Sexual Assault Committed by Inmates Toward Staff.
posts.summaryLabel: Congressional Research Service, Introduced in Senate
posts.meta: Judiciary Committee · Sen. Marsha Blackburn (R-TN)
posts.whatsNext: Presidential review (±10 days)

aiSummaries.text:
The Prison Staff Safety Enhancement Act is meant to better protect staff at federal prisons from sexual harassment and sexual assault by people who are incarcerated. It covers the Department of Justice and the agencies under it, requiring them to look closely at these incidents and respond to them.

Under the bill, the Department of Justice must set national standards for preventing, reducing, and punishing sexual harassment and sexual assault by incarcerated people against correctional officers and other employees of the Bureau of Prisons.

The bill also requires the Bureau of Prisons to fully carry out the recommendations made by the Department of Justice's Inspector General. Those recommendations come from a report evaluating how well the Bureau of Prisons has been handling sexual harassment and sexual assault committed by inmates against staff.

posts.label: 📋 Reported by committee
posts.note: Natural Resources, H. Rept. 119-778, Part I
posts.summary:
Indian Health Service Emergency Claims Parity Act
This bill extends from 72 hours to not less than 15 days the time period to notify the Purchased/Referred Care (PRC) program of emergency medical care received from a non-Indian Health Service (IHS) medical provider or at a non-IHS medical facility. This bill does not apply to individuals who are elderly or disabled, who continue to have a 30-day notification requirement for emergency services.
The IHS provides medical and dental services directly to American Indian and Alaska Native patients whenever possible. The PRC program pays for medical or dental care that is provided away from an IHS or tribal health care facility. The PRC program must be notified of requests for authorization of payment for health care services from a non-IHS provider.
Currently in emergency cases, the patient, an individual on behalf of the patient, or the medical care provider must, within 72 hours after the beginning of treatment for the condition or after admission to a health care facility, notify a PRC authorizing official of the need for the emergency medical care. This bill instead allows the patient, other individual, or provider to notify PRC not less than 15 days of the treatment or admission.
posts.summaryLabel: Congressional Research Service, Introduced in House
posts.committee: Energy and Commerce Committee, Natural Resources Committee
posts.meta: Energy and Commerce Committee, Natural Resources Committee · Rep. Mike Kennedy (R-UT)
posts.whatsNext: Floor scheduling - the bill went to more than one committee (leadership decides if and when it gets a vote)

aiSummaries.text:
This bill gives more time to notify the Indian Health Service's Purchased/Referred Care (PRC) program about emergency medical care received outside IHS. The PRC program pays for care that IHS or tribal health facilities don't provide directly, so it has to be told about emergency care from a non-IHS provider or facility.

Right now, the patient, someone acting for the patient, or the care provider must notify a PRC authorizing official within 72 hours after treatment begins or after the patient is admitted. Under this bill, they would instead have at least 15 days from the treatment or admission to give that notice.

The longer deadline does not apply to elderly or disabled individuals. For them, the current 30-day notification requirement for emergency services remains in place.

posts.title: Safe Beaches, Safe Swimmers Act
posts.label: 📋 Reported by committee
posts.note: Natural Resources, as amended, H. Rept. 119-772
posts.summary:
Safe Beaches, Safe Swimmers Act
This bill establishes requirements to ensure an adequate staff of lifeguards at swimming areas and swimming beaches managed by the National Park Service, the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service, the Bureau of Land Management, or the Bureau of Reclamation that are typically monitored by federally employed lifeguards during normal seasonal operating hours.
If the Department of the Interior determines there is a staffing shortage of lifeguards that will leave a swimming area or beach unmonitored by federally employed lifeguards during normal seasonal operating hours, Interior may enter into an agreement with local government agencies to provide lifeguards. Interior must ensure that a local government agency providing lifeguard services is reimbursed for all reasonable costs it incurred in carrying out the agreement.
The bill does not apply to short-term staffing shortages caused by temporary absences, such as an employee taking annual or sick leave.
posts.summaryLabel: Congressional Research Service, Reported to House
posts.meta: Natural Resources Committee · Rep. Jennifer Kiggans (R-VA)
posts.whatsNext: Floor scheduling (leadership decides if and when it gets a vote)

aiSummaries.text:
The Safe Beaches, Safe Swimmers Act would require the government to keep enough lifeguards on duty at federally managed swimming areas and beaches that are normally watched by federal lifeguards during their regular seasonal hours. These areas are managed by the National Park Service, the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service, the Bureau of Land Management, or the Bureau of Reclamation.

If the Department of the Interior finds that a shortage of federal lifeguards would leave one of these swimming areas or beaches without a lifeguard during its normal season, the department may make an agreement with local government agencies to provide lifeguards instead. The department must pay the local agency back for all reasonable costs it incurs under that agreement.

The bill does not cover short-term shortages caused by temporary absences, such as an employee taking annual or sick leave.

posts.title: Enhancing Geothermal Production on Federal Lands Act
posts.label: 📋 Reported by committee
posts.note: Natural Resources, as amended, H. Rept. 119-773
posts.summary:
Enhancing Geothermal Production on Federal Lands Act
This bill exempts certain projects and activities related to geothermal development on federal land from environmental review requirements.
Specifically, the bill exempts certain geothermal exploration projects with limited impact on federal land from environmental review under the National Environmental Policy Act of 1969 (NEPA). Geothermal exploration projects are those that involve the drilling of geothermal exploratory wells, such as temperature gradient wells, monitoring wells, or calibration wells, and that are limited in size, duration, and other aspects in accordance with specified criteria.
The bill also exempts from NEPA the following activities related to the exploration, development, or production of geothermal resources: (1) geotechnical investigations; (2) off-road travel in certain existing rights-of-way; and (3) the construction, maintenance, realignment, and repair of access roads within such rights-of-way.
posts.summaryLabel: Congressional Research Service, Reported to House
posts.meta: Natural Resources Committee · Rep. Russ Fulcher (R-ID)
posts.whatsNext: Floor scheduling (leadership decides if and when it gets a vote)

aiSummaries.text:
This bill exempts certain geothermal energy work on federal land from a federal environmental review requirement, the National Environmental Policy Act of 1969 (NEPA).

First, certain geothermal exploration projects that have limited effects on federal land would not need that review. These are projects that involve drilling geothermal exploratory wells, such as temperature gradient wells, monitoring wells, or calibration wells, as long as they stay within specified limits on their size, duration, and other aspects.

The bill also exempts three other kinds of activities tied to finding, developing, or producing geothermal energy from that review. These are geotechnical investigations, which study the ground conditions at a site; off-road travel within certain existing rights-of-way; and building, maintaining, realigning, and repairing access roads within those same rights-of-way.

posts.title: Protect Economic and Academic Freedom Act of 2026
posts.label: 📋 Reported by committee
posts.note: Education and Workforce, as amended, H. Rept. 119-780
posts.summary:
Protect Economic and Academic Freedom Act of 2026
This bill prohibits institutions of higher education (IHEs) that participate in federal student aid programs from engaging in boycotts against Israel. Specifically, IHEs may not engage in a commercial action intended to limit commercial relations with Israel, or with an entity licensed by, regulated by, or organized under the laws of Israel, that is not based on a valid business reason.
Further, IHEs receiving, or applying to receive, Title VI funds (federal funding for foreign language and international education programs) must annually certify that (1) students and faculty are allowed to participate in academic programs located in Israel in the same manner and under the same terms and conditions as programs in other foreign countries, and (2) students and faculty at postsecondary institutions located in Israel may participate in such IHE’s academic programs in the same manner and under the same terms and conditions as students and faculty from other foreign countries.
posts.summaryLabel: Congressional Research Service, Reported to House
posts.meta: Education and Workforce Committee · Rep. Virginia Foxx (R-NC)
posts.whatsNext: Floor scheduling (leadership decides if and when it gets a vote)

aiSummaries.text:
This bill would bar colleges and universities that take part in federal student aid programs from boycotting Israel. Under the bill, a school could not take a business action meant to limit its dealings with Israel, or with Israeli-licensed, Israeli-regulated, or Israeli-organized entities, unless there is a valid business reason for it.

The bill also adds a condition for schools that receive, or apply for, Title VI funding, which supports foreign language and international education programs. Each year, these schools would have to certify two things. First, that their students and faculty can join academic programs located in Israel in the same way, and on the same terms, as programs in other foreign countries. Second, that students and faculty from schools in Israel can join the school's own academic programs in the same way, and on the same terms, as students and faculty from other foreign countries.
