posts.title: No Antisemitism in Education Act of 2026
posts.label: 📋 Reported by committee
posts.note: Education and Workforce, as amended, H. Rept. 119-759, Part I
posts.summary:
No Antisemitism in Education Act of 2026
This bill requires local educational agencies (LEAs) and institutions of higher education (IHEs), as a condition of receiving federal funds, to treat discrimination that is motivated by antisemitism as vigorously as the LEA or IHE treats all other forms of discrimination prohibited by Title VI of the Civil Rights Act of 1964. (Title VI of the Civil Rights Act of 1964 prohibits discrimination based on race, color, or national origin in federally funded programs or activities.)
The bill requires federal agencies, LEAs, and IHEs to consider the definition of antisemitism contained in a December 11, 2019, executive order when reviewing or investigating whether a discriminatory act or omission was motivated by discriminatory antisemitic intent. The executive order incorporates the International Holocaust Remembrance Alliance's (IHRA's) working definition of antisemitism. According to the IHRA's working definition, antisemitism is a certain perception of Jews, which may be expressed as hatred toward Jews.
posts.summaryLabel: Congressional Research Service, Reported to House
posts.committee: Judiciary Committee, Education and Workforce Committee
posts.meta: Judiciary Committee, Education and Workforce Committee · Rep. Randy Fine (R-FL)

aiSummaries.text:
This measure would require local school districts and colleges that receive federal funds to take discrimination motivated by antisemitism as seriously as they take other forms of discrimination already banned under Title VI of the Civil Rights Act of 1964, which covers discrimination based on race, color, or national origin in federally funded programs.

When federal agencies, school districts, and colleges review or investigate whether an action or failure to act was motivated by antisemitic intent, they would have to consider a definition of antisemitism from a December 11, 2019, executive order. That order adopts the working definition used by the International Holocaust Remembrance Alliance (IHRA). Under that definition, antisemitism is a certain perception of Jews, which may be expressed as hatred toward Jews.

posts.title: National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration Sexual Harassment and Assault Prevention Improvements Act of 2025
posts.label: 📋 Reported by committee
posts.note: Natural Resources, H. Rept. 119-761
posts.summary:
National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration Sexual Harassment and Assault Prevention Improvements Act of 2025
This bill expands requirements for addressing sexual harassment and sexual assault involving personnel of the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA).
The bill specifies that NOAA's sexual harassment prevention and response policy applies to personnel such as observers, at-sea monitors, and voting members and staff of regional fishery management councils.
The bill removes the requirement that certain acts, such as assault, intimidation, and sexual harassment of an observer or a data collector, be forcible in nature to be unlawful.
The bill also requires NOAA's Office of Marine and Aviation Operations to establish a policy for reporting to the Coast Guard the names of NOAA personnel involved in a sexual harassment or sexual assault claim. Specifically, such reports must identify employees or contractors who are the subject of such claim, the time and date of the incident, and the location of the vessel when the incident occurred.
The bill prohibits a person convicted of certain sexual offenses from enlisting with or being commissioned by NOAA.
Additionally, the bill directs NOAA to update its policies to develop a restricted reporting system that allows employees and other personnel to confidentially report sexual harassment or assault and receive services without triggering an investigation.
Finally, the bill also expands reporting requirements on sexual harassment, sexual assault, and equal employment.
posts.summaryLabel: Congressional Research Service, Introduced in House
posts.meta: Natural Resources Committee · Rep. Suzanne Bonamici (D-OR)
posts.whatsNext: Floor scheduling (leadership decides if and when it gets a vote)

aiSummaries.text:
This bill expands the rules NOAA, the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration, must follow when dealing with sexual harassment and sexual assault involving its personnel.

Under the bill, NOAA's sexual harassment prevention and response policy would cover people such as observers, at-sea monitors, and the voting members and staff of regional fishery management councils. It also removes the requirement that certain acts, such as assault, intimidation, and sexual harassment of an observer or a data collector, must be forcible to count as unlawful.

The bill requires NOAA's Office of Marine and Aviation Operations to set up a policy for reporting claims of sexual harassment or sexual assault to the Coast Guard. Each report must name the employees or contractors who are the subject of the claim, give the time and date of the incident, and state where the vessel was when it happened.

The bill also bars anyone convicted of certain sexual offenses from enlisting with or being commissioned by NOAA.

In addition, NOAA must update its policies to create a restricted reporting system. This lets employees and other personnel report sexual harassment or assault confidentially and receive services without that report starting an investigation.

Finally, the bill expands reporting requirements covering sexual harassment, sexual assault, and equal employment.

posts.title: 21st Century Dyslexia Act
posts.label: 📋 Reported by committee
posts.note: Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions, without amendment, without written report
posts.summary:
21st Century Dyslexia Act
This bill addresses the education of children with disabilities, with a particular focus on children with dyslexia.
Currently, dyslexia is listed as one of the disabilities under the definition of specific learning disability in the Individuals with Disabilities Education Act (IDEA). This bill instead removes dyslexia from the definition of specific learning disability and establishes a stand-alone definition for dyslexia within the IDEA.
Specifically, the bill defines dyslexia for purposes of the IDEA as an unexpected difficulty in reading for an individual who has the intelligence to be a much better reader, most commonly caused by a difficulty in the phonological processing (the appreciation of the individual sounds of spoken language), which affects the ability of an individual to speak, read, and spell.
Additionally, the bill requires a local educational agency or other agency, in determining eligibility for or providing an accommodation or service under the IDEA, to provide equal access to (1) children from low-income families, (2) children from families with low socioeconomic status, and (3) children who are limited English proficient.
posts.summaryLabel: Congressional Research Service, Introduced in Senate
posts.committee: Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee
posts.meta: Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee · Sen. Bill Cassidy (R-LA)
posts.whatsNext: Floor scheduling (leadership decides if and when it gets a vote)

aiSummaries.text:
The 21st Century Dyslexia Act changes how federal special education law, the Individuals with Disabilities Education Act (IDEA), treats dyslexia. Right now, dyslexia is listed as one example of a specific learning disability. This bill takes dyslexia out of that category and gives it its own separate definition in the law.

Under the bill, dyslexia means an unexpected difficulty with reading in a person who has the intelligence to read much better. It is most often caused by trouble with phonological processing, which is the ability to recognize the individual sounds in spoken language. That difficulty can affect a person's ability to speak, read, and spell.

The bill also requires local educational agencies, and other agencies involved, to give equal access to children from low-income families, children from families with low socioeconomic status, and children who are limited English proficient. This applies when they decide whether a child qualifies for an accommodation or service under the IDEA, and when they provide one.

posts.title: Emergency Savings Enhancement Act of 2025
posts.label: 📋 Reported by committee
posts.note: Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions, with an amendment in the nature of a substitute, without written report
posts.summary:
Emergency Savings Enhancement Act of 2025
This bill expands eligibility and increases the maximum contribution limit for pension-linked emergency savings accounts (PLESAs).
As background, PLESAs are savings accounts that are established and maintained in connection with a defined contribution retirement plan, such as a 401(k). Contributions to such accounts are subject to federal income tax, and withdrawals are allowed for any reason.
The bill expands eligibility for PLESAs by eliminating the exclusion of highly compensated employees. Thus, under the bill, individuals who meet the age, service, and other eligibility requirements of the plan, regardless of compensation, are eligible to participate in such a plan.
The bill also increases the maximum limit on the portion of a PLESA balance attributable to participant contributions to $5,000 (from $2,600 in 2026). This limit continues to be adjusted for inflation.
The bill also extends and provides additional funding for a Department of Labor program that awards grants to states to promote employee ownership and participation in businesses.

aiSummaries.text:
The Emergency Savings Enhancement Act of 2025 makes it easier to join and raises how much can be saved in certain emergency savings accounts. These accounts, called pension-linked emergency savings accounts (PLESAs), are linked to workplace retirement plans such as 401(k)s. Contributions to them are taxed as regular income, but money can be taken out for any reason.

Under the bill, highly compensated employees are no longer excluded from these accounts. Anyone who meets the plan's age, length-of-service, and other requirements can take part, no matter how much they earn.

The bill also raises the limit on the amount of a PLESA balance that can come from the worker's own contributions. The limit would rise to $5,000, up from $2,600 in 2026. The limit will continue to be adjusted for inflation over time.

Finally, the bill extends a Department of Labor program that gives grants to states to encourage employee ownership and participation in businesses, and it provides additional funding for that program.

posts.title: A bill to prohibit the transfer of certain offices and functions of the Department of Education to other Federal agencies, and for other purposes.
posts.label: 📋 Reported by committee
posts.note: Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions, with an amendment, without written report
posts.summary:
This bill prohibits the Department of Education (ED) from transferring specified offices and functions to other federal agencies.
Specifically, the bill prohibits ED from entering into or carrying out interagency agreements related to the following four offices: the Office of Special Education and Rehabilitative Services, the Office of Postsecondary Education, the Office of Indian Education, and the Office of Elementary and Secondary Education.
This prohibition applies to the transfer of functions such as administering or operating programs, making grants, carrying out technical assistance, enforcing rights and requirements (e.g., data collection requirements), conducting administrative and oversight functions, and monitoring grantees.
Additionally, ED may not transfer a function or program of one of the four offices to another ED office and then subsequently enter into an interagency agreement related to the function or program.
The bill does not apply to agreements in effect on February 1, 2025, or renewals with substantially similar terms.
ED must, within 14 days of the bill's enactment and on a quarterly basis, provide to Congress (and publish on its website) a report and cost analysis for each interagency agreement entered into on or after February 1, 2025. ED may not use specified FY2026 or FY2027 funds for travel expenses unless ED provides this required information.
(As of July 30, 2026, ED has entered into 14 interagency agreements to transfer functions of ED to other federal agencies, including the ED offices listed in the bill.)

aiSummaries.text:
This bill would stop the Department of Education from handing off work from four of its offices to other federal agencies. The four offices are the Office of Special Education and Rehabilitative Services, the Office of Postsecondary Education, the Office of Indian Education, and the Office of Elementary and Secondary Education. The ban covers moving tasks such as running programs, giving out grants, providing technical help, enforcing rules (including data collection requirements), handling administrative and oversight duties, and monitoring grant recipients.

The bill also closes a workaround. The Department could not move a function or program from one of these four offices to another Education Department office and then arrange for another federal agency to take it over.

The ban does not apply to agreements that were in effect on February 1, 2025, or to renewals with substantially similar terms.

For any new agreement made on or after February 1, 2025, the Department must send Congress a report and cost analysis within 14 days of the bill becoming law, and then every three months. It must also post these reports on its website. Until it provides this information, the Department may not use certain funds from fiscal years 2026 or 2027 for travel expenses.

As of July 30, 2026, the Department has entered into 14 agreements to move Education Department functions to other federal agencies, including functions from the offices named in the bill.

posts.title: College Transparency Act
posts.label: 📋 Reported by committee
posts.note: Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions, with an amendment in the nature of a substitute, without written report
posts.summary:
College Transparency Act
This bill requires the National Center for Education Statistics (NCES) to establish a secure and privacy-protected data system that contains information about postsecondary students.
Specifically, the data system must
evaluate student enrollment patterns, progression, completion, and postcollegiate outcomes, and higher education costs and financial aid;
provide complete and customizable information for students and families making decisions about postsecondary education;
reduce the requirements for reporting by institutions of higher education; and
periodically match with other federal systems of data.
The bill also establishes a postsecondary student data system advisory committee.
The Department of Education (ED) and NCES must (1) provide dedicated and adequate staffing at ED to implement the bill's requirements, and (2) report to Congress on a quarterly basis regarding the progress of implementing the bill's requirements.

The College Transparency Act would require the National Center for Education Statistics (NCES) to set up a secure data system with privacy protections that holds information about college students. The system is meant to track how students enroll, move through school, finish, and do afterward in their careers, as well as what colleges cost and how financial aid is used. It would be designed to give students and families complete, adjustable information when they are deciding about college. The bill also aims to cut back the amount of reporting that colleges must do, and it would regularly match this data with other federal data systems.

The bill creates an advisory committee to guide the data system. It also requires the Department of Education and NCES to provide enough dedicated staff to carry out the law. Finally, they must report to Congress every quarter on how the work is progressing.

posts.title: Southcentral Foundation Land Transfer Act of 2025
posts.label: 📋 Reported by committee
posts.note: Indian Affairs, without amendment, S. Rept. 119-131
posts.summary:
Southcentral Foundation Land Transfer Act of 2025
This bill directs the Department of Health and Human Services (HHS) to convey approximately 3.4 acres in Anchorage, Alaska, to the Southcentral Foundation (SCF) for use in connection with health and social services programs.
The conveyance must be made by warranty deed. The conveyance may not (1) require any consideration (such as payment) from the SCF for the property; (2) impose any obligation, term, or condition on the SCF relating to that property; or (3) allow for any U.S. reversionary interest in the property.
HHS must be accorded any easement or access to the property as may be reasonably necessary to satisfy any retained obligation or liability of HHS.
The bill prohibits the SCF from being liable for certain environmental contamination that occurred on or before the date on which the property is conveyed to the SCF. In turn, HHS may not be liable for any contamination that occurred after the date that the SCF controlled, occupied, and used the property.
posts.summaryLabel: Congressional Research Service, Introduced in Senate
posts.meta: Indian Affairs Committee · Sen. Lisa Murkowski (R-AK)
posts.whatsNext: Floor scheduling (leadership decides if and when it gets a vote)

aiSummaries.text:
The Southcentral Foundation Land Transfer Act of 2025 would require the Department of Health and Human Services (HHS) to transfer about 3.4 acres of land in Anchorage, Alaska, to the Southcentral Foundation (SCF). The land would be used for the foundation's health and social service programs.

The land must be transferred through a warranty deed, which is a document that gives the buyer a guarantee of clear ownership. The transfer cannot require the SCF to pay anything for the property. It also cannot place any duty, term, or condition on the SCF about the land, and it cannot give the federal government a right to take the property back later.

HHS would keep whatever easement or access rights to the property it reasonably needs to meet any obligation or liability it still has.

The SCF would not be held responsible for environmental contamination that happened on or before the date the land is transferred to it. In the same way, HHS would not be responsible for contamination that happened after the SCF began controlling, occupying, and using the property.

posts.title: EMPOWER for Health Act
posts.label: 📋 Reported by committee
posts.note: Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions, with an amendment in the nature of a substitute, without written report
posts.summary:
Educating Medical Professionals and Optimizing Workforce Efficiency and Readiness for Health Act or the EMPOWER for Health Act
This bill reauthorizes through FY2031 and revises a range of programs that provide funding and other resources to support recruiting, training, and retaining individuals to work or teach in the health professions. These programs are administered by the Health Resources and Services Administration (HRSA).
For instance, the bill revises an educational loan repayment program for certain pediatric health specialists that agree to practice in areas with shortages of such specialists. The bill (1) requires direct clinical care to comprise at least half of the required service hours, (2) broadens the eligible specialties to include any pediatric mental or behavioral health discipline HRSA determines appropriate, and (3) specifically authorizes focusing care on children enrolled in Medicaid.
Also, the bill specifically authorizes grants to entities such as states and health professions schools for supporting the nursing workforce by providing analysis, technical assistance, and best practices for alleviating nursing workforce shortages.
Finally, the bill expands grants for recruiting youth into public health careers to include outreach to middle school students (current law only includes outreach to high school students).

aiSummaries.text:
The EMPOWER for Health Act reauthorizes, through fiscal year 2031, and updates a range of federal programs that fund and support recruiting, training, and keeping people in health care jobs and teaching roles. The Health Resources and Services Administration (HRSA) runs these programs.

One change affects a loan repayment program for certain pediatric health specialists who agree to work in areas short on those specialists. Under the bill, direct clinical care must make up at least half of the required service hours. The eligible specialties are widened to include any pediatric mental or behavioral health discipline that HRSA considers appropriate. Finally, the bill extends grants that recruit young people into public health careers so they can reach middle school students, not just high school students as current law allows.

posts.title: Making America's Food Safer Act
posts.label: 📋 Reported by committee
posts.note: Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions, with an amendment in the nature of a substitute, without written report
posts.summary:
Making America's Food Safer Act
This bill expands the Food and Drug Administration’s (FDA’s) authority to require the destruction of unsafe imported foods, share food safety information, and make use of food facility audit information.
Specifically, the bill authorizes the FDA to order the destruction, without the opportunity for export, of any item that (1) is refused import into the United States; (2) violates federal law regulating food, drugs, medical devices, cosmetics, and tobacco products; and (3) presents a significant public health concern. Before issuing a destruction order, the FDA must provide an item’s owner or consignee with appropriate due process, including notice and an opportunity to appear. If an order is issued, the item’s owner or consignee must destroy it within 90 days at their own cost.
The bill also generally authorizes the FDA to share unredacted food safety information with state, local, tribal, and territorial authorities, including information related to foodborne illness tracking, recalls and outbreaks, and other topics. During a food safety incident, the FDA may disclose certain commercial information that is otherwise protected from disclosure.
Finally, the bill expands the FDA’s third-party audit system to make domestic food facilities eligible for voluntary audits. (Foreign facilities are eligible under current law.) The bill also authorizes the FDA to use audit results and related certifications to analyze risks and prioritize regulatory activities (e.g., inspections) to protect public health. (This information is currently used to determine whether specific food, or food from a specific facility, is eligible for import.)
posts.summaryLabel: Congressional Research Service, Reported to Senate
posts.committee: Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee
posts.meta: Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee · Sen. Tommy Tuberville (R-AL)
posts.whatsNext: Floor scheduling (leadership decides if and when it gets a vote)

aiSummaries.text:
The Making America's Food Safer Act lets the Food and Drug Administration (FDA) order that certain imported products be destroyed instead of sent back out of the country. This applies to an item that has been refused entry into the United States, breaks federal rules covering food, drugs, medical devices, cosmetics, or tobacco products, and poses a significant risk to public health. Before issuing such an order, the FDA must give the item's owner or buyer fair notice and a chance to appear and respond. If the order is issued, the owner or buyer has 90 days to destroy the item at their own expense.

The bill also lets the FDA share food safety information more broadly with state, local, tribal, and territorial governments. This covers information about tracking foodborne illness, recalls, and outbreaks, along with other food safety topics. The information shared is not blacked out. During a food safety emergency, the FDA may also release certain business information that would normally be kept private.

Finally, the bill extends the FDA's voluntary third-party audit program to domestic food facilities, which are now eligible to take part. Foreign food facilities already qualify under current law. The FDA may also use the results of these audits and related certifications to assess risks and decide where to focus its work, such as inspections, to protect public health. Currently, this audit information is used to decide whether particular food, or food from a particular facility, can be imported.

posts.title: Childhood Diabetes Reduction Act of 2026
posts.label: 📋 Reported by committee
posts.note: Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions, with an amendment in the nature of a substitute, without written report
posts.summary:
Childhood Diabetes Reduction Act of 2026
This bill requires health warnings on labels and in advertisements for food and beverages that are sweetened, processed, or contain a high level of certain nutrients of concern, and it prohibits specifically advertising such products to children. It also expands research and outreach on proper nutrition.
The bill requires various Food and Drug Administration (FDA) warnings on labels for (1) sugar-sweetened beverages, (2) food and beverages with non-sugar sweeteners, and (3) ultra-processed food and beverages. These warnings must contain specified information regarding the risks of developing certain health conditions (e.g., diabetes); warnings for sweetened food and beverages must specifically say that these products are not recommended for children. If a food or beverage contains a nutrient of concern (e.g., added sugar, saturated fat, or sodium) at a level that poses health risks, its label must indicate that the product is high in the relevant nutrient.
Additionally, the bill prohibits marketing or advertising these products to children under the Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act, which is primarily enforced by the FDA. Further, marketing or advertising these products to children, or without including the required warnings, is considered an unfair or deceptive trade practice that is subject to action by the Federal Trade Commission (FTC). The bill specifically restores the FTC's statutory authority to regulate advertising targeting children. (This authority was limited in 1980.)
Finally, the bill expands research on nutrition science and requires a public education campaign about nutrition and exercise.

The Childhood Diabetes Reduction Act of 2026 would require health warnings on labels and in ads for certain foods and drinks. These include sugary drinks, products sweetened with non-sugar sweeteners, and ultra-processed foods and drinks. The warnings must explain the health risks, such as developing diabetes. For sweetened products, the warnings must also state that they are not recommended for children. If a product contains a nutrient of concern, such as added sugar, saturated fat, or sodium, at a level that poses health risks, its label must say the product is high in that nutrient.

The bill also bans marketing or advertising these products to children under the Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act, which the Food and Drug Administration mainly enforces. Marketing these products to children, or advertising them without the required warnings, would be treated as an unfair or deceptive trade practice that the Federal Trade Commission can act against. The bill restores the Federal Trade Commission's authority to regulate advertising aimed at children, a power that was limited in 1980.

Finally, the bill expands research on nutrition science and requires a public education campaign about nutrition and exercise.

posts.title: Medication Affordability and Patent Integrity Act
posts.label: 📋 Reported by committee
posts.note: Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions, with an amendment in the nature of a substitute, without written report
posts.summary:
Medication Affordability and Patent Integrity Act
This bill requires applicants seeking approval of a drug or licensure of a biological product to submit certain information about relevant patents to both the Food and Drug Administration (FDA) and the U.S. Patent and Trademark Office (USPTO).
Specifically, the bill requires applicants to make certifications and disclosures related to each applicable patent on a proposed drug or biological product. An applicable patent is a patent or patent application held or sought by the applicant for the drug or biological product (including a formulation or composition, method of use, or method of manufacturing).
For each applicable patent, an applicant must submit to the USPTO any information material to patentability that the applicant submitted to the FDA and any information provided by the FDA in response. The applicant must certify that this submission is complete and consistent with the information the applicant provided to the FDA.
Further, for each applicable patent, an applicant must certify that certain information submitted to the FDA is consistent with information the applicant provided to the USPTO. This is specific to statements or characterizations that are material to patentability and related to (1) an applicable patent (including a statement or characterization of relevant publicly known information), or (2) analytical data included in a new drug or biological product application.
The bill establishes a defense to a patent infringement action if the owner of an applicable patent negligently or intentionally failed to make the disclosures required by these provisions.
posts.summaryLabel: Congressional Research Service, Reported to Senate
posts.committee: Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee
posts.meta: Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee · Sen. Maggie Hassan (D-NH)
posts.whatsNext: Floor scheduling (leadership decides if and when it gets a vote)

aiSummaries.text:
The Medication Affordability and Patent Integrity Act would require companies seeking FDA approval for a drug or a biological product to also deal with patents related to that product. Each patent the applicant holds or has applied for on the product, including patents covering its formula or composition, how it is used, or how it is made, must be reported.

For each of these patents, the applicant must send the U.S. Patent and Trademark Office any information that matters to whether the patent should be granted and that was also given to the FDA, along with any information the FDA provided back. The applicant must certify that this submission is complete and matches what was given to the FDA.

The applicant must also certify, for each of these patents, that certain information given to the FDA is consistent with what was given to the Patent Office. This applies to statements or descriptions that matter to patentability and relate either to the patent itself, including publicly known information about it, or to lab data included in a new drug or biological product application.

Finally, the bill creates a legal defense against a patent infringement lawsuit for anyone who can show that the patent owner negligently or intentionally failed to make these required disclosures.

posts.title: Title VIII Nursing Workforce Reauthorization Act of 2026
posts.label: 📋 Reported by committee
posts.note: Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions, with an amendment in the nature of a substitute, without written report
posts.summary:
Title VIII Nursing Workforce Reauthorization Act of 2026
This bill reauthorizes through FY2031, revises, and establishes programs that support recruitment, education, retention, and advanced practices of nurses and nursing school faculty.
Specifically, the bill reauthorizes programs within the Health Resources and Services Administration that provide grants to support increased enrollment in nursing education (including for individuals from disadvantaged backgrounds), advanced nursing education and specialized training, nurse retention, and enhanced patient care. The bill also reauthorizes programs that support student loan repayment and scholarships for nurses who agree to work at facilities with critical nursing shortages and nursing faculty who work at accredited schools of nursing.
Also, the bill expands certain grants to include (1) training on the use of new technologies such as telehealth and virtual resources, and (2) care for survivors of sexual assault.
Additionally, the bill temporarily establishes (1) grants to nursing schools for supplementing the salaries of eligible faculty for a period of up to three years to enhance faculty recruitment and retention, and (2) grants to state agencies, nonprofits, and nursing schools for establishing nursing workforce centers and collecting data regarding the nursing workforce.

posts.meta: Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee · Sen. Jeff Merkley (D-OR)

aiSummaries.text:
This bill extends through fiscal year 2031 and updates several federal programs that help nurses and nursing school faculty get trained, hired, and kept on the job. It also adds a few new programs.

The bill continues federal grants run by the Health Resources and Services Administration. These grants help more people enroll in nursing school, including people from disadvantaged backgrounds, and they support advanced nursing education, specialized training, keeping nurses in their jobs, and improving patient care. It also continues programs that help repay student loans and provide scholarships for nurses who agree to work at facilities with serious nursing shortages, and for nursing faculty who teach at accredited nursing schools.

Some existing grants are expanded. They can now pay for training on new technologies such as telehealth and virtual care tools, and for caring for survivors of sexual assault.

The bill also creates two temporary programs. The first gives nursing schools grants to supplement the salaries of eligible faculty for up to three years, to help recruit and keep teachers. The second gives grants to state agencies, nonprofit groups, and nursing schools to set up nursing workforce centers and to collect data about the nursing workforce.

posts.title: CLEAR LABELS Act
posts.label: 📋 Reported by committee
posts.note: Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions, with an amendment in the nature of a substitute, without written report
posts.summary:
Consumer Labeling for Enhanced API Reporting and Legitimate Accountability for Base Entity Listings Act or the CLEAR LABELS Act
This bill requires drugs and active pharmaceutical ingredients made available in the U.S. market to be labeled with the names and locations of their manufacturers.
Specifically, a finished, packaged drug product must be labeled with the name and place of business of (1) the original manufacturer (or manufacturers) of each active pharmaceutical ingredient; (2) the original manufacturer of the finished drug product; and (3) the packer or distributor, if any. This information must be printed on the product label or made available electronically. Active pharmaceutical ingredients (which are generally sold to manufacturers and researchers, not consumers) must also be labeled with the name and place of business of their original manufacturers.
Under the bill, the original manufacturer is the establishment that conducts the majority of the significant phases of manufacturing to produce the ingredient or product.
The Food and Drug Administration (FDA) has discretion to determine whether a violation of these requirements constitutes misbranding and to assess a civil fine. The FDA must consider certain factors in determining whether to assess a fine, including whether the violator was notified of their noncompliance and was provided an opportunity to correct the violation.
Finally, the FDA must coordinate with U.S. Customs and Border Protection to address any overlap between these requirements and existing requirements for imported drugs.
These provisions take effect five years after the bill is enacted.
posts.summaryLabel: Congressional Research Service, Reported to Senate
posts.committee: Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee
posts.meta: Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee · Sen. Rick Scott (R-FL)
posts.whatsNext: Floor scheduling (leadership decides if and when it gets a vote)

aiSummaries.text:
The CLEAR LABELS Act would require drugs and their active ingredients sold in the U.S. to show where they were made. Drugs for consumers would need to be labeled with the name and location of the original manufacturer of each active ingredient, the original manufacturer of the finished product, and any packer or distributor involved. This information could be printed on the label or made available electronically. Active ingredients, which are usually sold to manufacturers and researchers rather than consumers, would also need to be labeled with the name and location of their original manufacturers.

Under the bill, the original manufacturer is the company that carries out most of the important steps in making the ingredient or product.

The Food and Drug Administration would decide whether a violation counts as misbranding and could impose a civil fine. In deciding whether to fine a company, the agency must consider certain factors, including whether the company was told about the violation and given a chance to fix it. The FDA would also work with U.S. Customs and Border Protection to handle any overlap with existing rules for imported drugs.

These requirements would take effect five years after the bill becomes law.

posts.title: Expedited Access to Biosimilars Act
posts.label: 📋 Reported by committee
posts.note: Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions, with an amendment in the nature of a substitute, without written report
posts.summary:
Expedited Access to Biosimilars Act
This bill modifies statutory requirements for demonstrating that a proposed biological product (e.g., a drug or vaccine) is biosimilar to a reference (brand-name) product. Specifically, the bill eliminates the need for a clinical efficacy study unless the Food and Drug Administration (FDA) determines such a study is necessary.
Under current law, applicants seeking FDA approval of a proposed biosimilar must submit certain studies and assessments, including a clinical efficacy study demonstrating the safety, purity, and potency of the proposed biosimilar in relevant conditions of use. However, the FDA has discretion not to require studies and assessments it deems unnecessary. (For example, the FDA released draft guidance in October 2025 indicating that clinical efficacy studies may be unnecessary for a class of proposed biosimilars, known as therapeutic protein products, in some circumstances.)
The bill generally eliminates the requirement that a biosimilar applicant submit a clinical efficacy study but authorizes the FDA to require such a study if necessary. If requiring a clinical efficacy study, the FDA must provide a written determination of necessity to the applicant within a specified period.
Separately, the bill eliminates a requirement that a biosimilar application be reviewed by the same FDA division responsible for review of the reference application.
posts.summaryLabel: Congressional Research Service, Reported to Senate
posts.committee: Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee
posts.meta: Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee · Sen. Rand Paul (R-KY)
posts.whatsNext: Floor scheduling (leadership decides if and when it gets a vote)

aiSummaries.text:
This bill changes the rules for getting approval for a biosimilar, which is a biological product, such as a drug or vaccine, that is meant to work like a brand-name version of that product. Right now, companies seeking approval must usually run a clinical efficacy study, which is a study in patients showing the copy is safe, pure, and effective for the uses it is intended for. The Food and Drug Administration (FDA) can already skip studies it considers unnecessary, and in October 2025 it issued draft guidance saying such studies may not be needed for some protein-based products in certain situations.

Under the bill, companies would generally no longer have to submit a clinical efficacy study. The FDA would still be able to require one if it decides the study is necessary. If it does, it must give the applicant a written explanation of why, within a set time period.

The bill also removes a rule that required a biosimilar application to be reviewed by the same FDA division that reviews the brand-name product's application.

posts.title: Wyoming Education Trust Modernization Act
posts.label: 📋 Reported by committee
posts.note: Energy and Natural Resources, without amendment, without written report
posts.summary:
Wyoming Education Trust Modernization Act
This bill provides Wyoming with more flexibility to invest the principal of its permanent school fund by allowing the state to use earnings generated from investment of the fund rather than only interest.
By way of background, Congress created the fund when Wyoming became a state by granting certain federal lands to be held in a trust for the state. Proceeds from school trust land sales, exchanges, or disposals are deposited into the fund to support public schools.
posts.summaryLabel: Congressional Research Service, Introduced in Senate
posts.meta: Energy and Natural Resources Committee · Sen. Cynthia Lummis (R-WY)
posts.whatsNext: Floor scheduling (leadership decides if and when it gets a vote)

aiSummaries.text:
This bill gives Wyoming more freedom in how it invests the main money in its permanent school fund. Under the change, the state could use the earnings from investing the fund, not just the interest it has been limited to.

The fund dates back to statehood, when Congress gave certain federal lands to Wyoming to be held in trust for the state. Money raised when those school trust lands are sold, exchanged, or otherwise disposed of goes into the fund to support public schools.

Making National Parks Safer Act
This bill directs the National Park Service (NPS) to develop a plan to install Next Generation 911 (NG911) systems, which are certain interoperable, digital, and secure Internet Protocol-based systems for receiving 9-1-1 calls.
Specifically, the NPS must assess the implementation status and estimated costs of such NG911 systems at existing emergency communications centers in NPS units. The NPS must also develop a plan, based on the assessment, to install NG911 systems at centers.

aiSummaries.text:
This bill tells the National Park Service (NPS) to make a plan for upgrading the 911 emergency call systems used in national parks to a newer, digital, internet-based system called Next Generation 911 (NG911).

To do this, the NPS must first look at each emergency communications center in its park units that already exists. It has to find out how far along each center is in setting up NG911 and estimate what the upgrades would cost. Then, based on that review, the NPS must develop a plan for installing NG911 systems at those centers.

posts.title: Reversionary Interest Conveyance Act
posts.label: 📋 Reported by committee
posts.note: Energy and Natural Resources, without amendment, without written report
posts.summary:
Reversionary Interest Conveyance Act
This bill directs the Bureau of Land Management (BLM) to offer to sell the reversionary interest of the United States in approximately 8.43 acres of land in Sacramento, California, as generally depicted on a specified map dated November 7, 2022. Within two years of receiving a request from the owner of the land, the BLM must offer the reversionary interest and convey the reversionary interest to the buyer upon payment. The payment must be in an amount that is at least the fair market value of the reversionary interest. The buyer must also pay all costs related to the applicable conveyance of the reversionary interest, including all surveys, appraisals, and other administrative costs.
The bill subjects the conveyance to valid existing rights.
The proceeds from the sale must be deposited into Federal Land Disposal Account.
posts.summaryLabel: Congressional Research Service, Introduced in House
posts.committee: Energy and Natural Resources Committee, Natural Resources Committee
posts.meta: Energy and Natural Resources Committee, Natural Resources Committee · Rep. Doris Matsui (D-CA)
posts.whatsNext: Floor scheduling (leadership decides if and when it gets a vote)

aiSummaries.text:
The Reversionary Interest Conveyance Act would require the Bureau of Land Management (BLM) to offer to sell the United States' reversionary interest in about 8.43 acres of land in Sacramento, California. The land is shown on a map dated November 7, 2022. A reversionary interest is the government's right to get the land back under certain conditions.

If the owner of the land asks, the BLM must make the offer within two years of receiving the request. Once the buyer pays, the BLM must transfer the reversionary interest to them. The price must be at least the fair market value of that interest. The buyer also has to cover all costs of the transfer, including surveys, appraisals, and other administrative expenses.

The sale is subject to valid existing rights, meaning any rights that already legally apply to the land still hold. The money from the sale must be deposited into the Federal Land Disposal Account.

posts.title: Dolores River National Conservation Area and Special Management Area Act
posts.label: 📋 Reported by committee
posts.note: Energy and Natural Resources, without amendment, without written report
posts.summary:
Dolores River National Conservation Area and Special Management Area Act
This bill establishes the Dolores River National Conservation Area and the Dolores River Special Management Area in Colorado to protect certain natural, recreational, scenic, cultural, historical, and other values of the areas.
The conservation area must consist of approximately 52,872 acres of Bureau of Land Management land. The special management area must consist of approximately 15,452 acres of federal land in the San Juan National Forest.
A management plan must be developed for each area. The bill directs the Department of the Interior to allow for the continued use of the areas by members of Indian tribes for traditional ceremonies and as a source of traditional plants and other materials.
Additionally, Interior must manage the portions of the areas identified as Ponderosa Gorge in a manner that maintains its wilderness character, including by prohibiting (1) road construction; (2) the use of motor vehicles, motorized equipment, or mechanical transport; and (3) projects undertaken for the purpose of harvesting commercial timber.
Interior must also establish the Dolores River National Conservation Area Advisory Council.
Finally, the bill releases segments of the Dolores River inside the areas from further study for potential addition to the Wild and Scenic Rivers System.
posts.summaryLabel: Congressional Research Service, Introduced in Senate
posts.meta: Energy and Natural Resources Committee · Sen. Michael Bennet (D-CO)
posts.whatsNext: Floor scheduling (leadership decides if and when it gets a vote)

aiSummaries.text:
This bill creates two protected areas along the Dolores River in Colorado: the Dolores River National Conservation Area and the Dolores River Special Management Area. Their purpose is to protect the area's natural beauty, recreation, scenery, culture, and history, along with other important qualities.

The conservation area would cover about 52,872 acres of land managed by the Bureau of Land Management. The special management area would cover about 15,452 acres of federal land within the San Juan National Forest.

Each area would get its own management plan. Members of Indian tribes would still be allowed to use the areas for traditional ceremonies and to gather traditional plants and other materials.

A section of the areas called Ponderosa Gorge would be managed to keep its wilderness character. That means no building roads, no using motor vehicles, motorized equipment, or mechanical transport, and no commercial timber harvesting.

The Department of the Interior would also set up a council to advise on the conservation area. Finally, the sections of the Dolores River inside these areas would no longer be studied for possible inclusion in the Wild and Scenic Rivers System.

Accurately Counting Risk Elimination Solutions Act or the ACRES Act
This bill establishes requirements regarding reports about hazardous fuels reduction activities and standardized procedures for tracking data for hazardous fuels reduction. Hazardous fuels reduction activities means any vegetation management activities that reduce the risk of wildfire but excludes the award of contracts to conduct hazardous fuels reduction activities.
First, the Department of Agriculture (USDA) and the Department of the Interior must include in the materials submitted in support of the President's budget each fiscal year a report on the number of acres of federal land on which such activities were carried out during the preceding year.
Next, USDA and Interior must implement standardized procedures for tracking data related to such activities. The standardized procedures must include
regular, standardized data reviews of the accuracy and timely input of data used to track hazardous fuels reduction activities;
verification methods that validate whether such data accurately correlates to such activities;
an analysis of the short- and long-term effectiveness of such activities on reducing the risk of wildfire; and
for hazardous fuels reduction activities that occur partially within the wildland-urban interface, methods to distinguish which acres are located within and which located outside the wildland-urban interface.
Finally, the Government Accountability Office must (1) conduct a study on this bill's implementation, and (2) submit a report to Congress with the results of the study.

aiSummaries.text:
The ACRES Act (Accurately Counting Risk Elimination Solutions Act) is meant to make the federal government's wildfire-prevention work easier to measure and check. "Hazardous fuels reduction" means vegetation management that lowers the risk of wildfire, but it does not include awarding contracts to carry out that work.

Each year, the Department of Agriculture and the Department of the Interior would have to include in their budget submissions a report on how many acres of federal land received this kind of work in the previous year.

The two departments would also have to set up standard procedures for tracking the data on this work. Those procedures would include regular reviews to check that the data is accurate and entered on time, methods to confirm that the data matches the work actually done, and an analysis of how well the work reduces wildfire risk in both the short and long term. For work that happens partly inside the wildland-urban interface, the procedures would also need methods to separate the acres inside that area from those outside it.

Finally, the Government Accountability Office would study how the bill is carried out and report the results to Congress.

posts.title: Establishing the congressional budget for the United States Government for fiscal year 2027 and setting forth the appropriate budgetary levels for fiscal years 2028 through 2036.
posts.label: 📋 Reported by committee
posts.note: Budget, original measure, H. Rept. 119-754
posts.summary:
This concurrent resolution establishes the congressional budget for the federal government for FY2027, sets forth budgetary levels for FY2028-FY2036, and provides reconciliation instructions for legislation that increases the deficit.
The resolution recommends levels and amounts for FY2027-FY2036 for
federal revenues,
new budget authority,
budget outlays,
deficits (on-budget),
debt subject to limit,
debt held by the public, and
the major functional categories of spending.
The resolution includes reconciliation instructions that direct the House Agriculture Committee, the House Armed Services Committee, the House Permanent Select Committee on Intelligence, and the House Administration Committee to submit recommendations for legislation that will increase the deficit over FY2027-FY2036 by not more than specified amounts. Each committee must submit the recommendations to the House Budget Committee by September 11, 2026.
(Under current law, reconciliation bills are considered by Congress using expedited legislative procedures that prevent a filibuster and restrict amendments in the Senate.)
In addition, the resolution establishes a reserve fund that allows certain adjustments to committee allocations and other budgetary levels to accommodate reconciliation legislation.
Finally, the resolution sets forth budget enforcement procedures that address issues such as
adjustments to committee allocations and other budgetary levels;
the budgetary treatment of the discretionary administrative expenses for the Social Security Administration and the U.S. Postal Service;
emergency spending; and
additional adjustments for disaster relief, wildfire suppression, health care fraud and abuse control, continuing disability reviews and redeterminations, and reemployment services and eligibility assessments.

posts.meta: Budget Committee · Rep. Jodey Arrington (R-TX)
posts.whatsNext: Floor scheduling (leadership decides if and when it gets a vote)

aiSummaries.text:
This resolution sets Congress's budget plan for the federal government for fiscal year 2027, and it lays out spending and revenue targets for fiscal years 2028 through 2036. It sets goals for federal revenue, new spending authority, actual spending, the deficit (on-budget), the debt limit, debt held by the public, and the major categories of federal spending, all covering fiscal years 2027 through 2036.

The resolution also gives instructions for a type of bill called reconciliation, which is used for legislation that would increase the deficit. It directs four House committees (Agriculture, Armed Services, Intelligence, and Administration) to recommend such legislation, with each increase in the deficit capped at specified amounts over fiscal years 2027 through 2036. Each committee must send its recommendations to the House Budget Committee by September 11, 2026. Under current law, these reconciliation bills move through Congress under special rules that prevent a filibuster in the Senate and limit amendments.

The resolution further creates a reserve fund that allows certain changes to committee spending allocations and other budget levels so that reconciliation legislation can fit within the plan.

Finally, it sets out rules for enforcing the budget. These cover adjustments to committee allocations and other budget levels, how the administrative costs of the Social Security Administration and the U.S. Postal Service are counted, and how emergency spending is treated. It also allows additional adjustments for disaster relief, wildfire suppression, health care fraud and abuse control, continuing disability reviews and redeterminations, and reemployment services and eligibility assessments.

posts.title: Accelerating Access to Critical Therapies for ALS Reauthorization Act of 2026
posts.label: 📋 Reported by committee
posts.note: Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions, with an amendment in the nature of a substitute, without written report
posts.summary:
Accelerating Access to Critical Therapies for ALS Reauthorization Act of 2026
This bill reauthorizes through FY2031 and revises programs that support research and development of drugs and other therapies to address amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (also known as ALS or Lou Gehrig's disease) and other neurodegenerative diseases.
The bill reauthorizes
grants from the National Institutes of Health (NIH) for scientific research on investigational drugs to prevent or treat ALS for individuals not otherwise eligible for clinical trials,
grants from the Food and Drug Administration (FDA) for research and development of therapies to prevent and treat ALS and other neurodegenerative diseases, and
a Public-Private Partnership including the FDA and NIH that supports development and regulatory review of treatments for neurodegenerative diseases.
Also, the bill revises the NIH grants to require (1) the NIH, in considering grant renewal, to assess available information on the safety and efficacy of the investigational drugs; (2) grantees to promptly report available safety data from ongoing clinical trials; and (3) the NIH to determine the timeframe for enrollment in clinical trials for the investigational drugs.
Additionally, every five years, the FDA must publish a plan describing actions it will take over a five-year period to foster development of safe and effective drugs, and facilitate access to investigational drugs, for ALS and other rare neurodegenerative diseases. Each plan must include the FDA's previous actions and recommendations for improvements.
Finally, the Government Accountability Office and the Department of Health and Human Services must report on the impacts of these grants.

aiSummaries.text:
This bill extends, through fiscal year 2031, several federal programs that fund research into treatments for amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS, also called Lou Gehrig's disease) and other brain and nerve diseases that worsen over time. The programs cover three areas: grants from the National Institutes of Health (NIH) for research on experimental drugs to prevent or treat ALS for people who would not otherwise qualify for clinical trials; grants from the Food and Drug Administration (FDA) for developing therapies for ALS and other neurodegenerative diseases; and a public-private partnership involving the FDA and NIH that supports developing and reviewing treatments for these diseases.

The bill also changes the NIH grant rules. When deciding whether to renew a grant, the NIH must look at the available information on how safe and effective the experimental drugs are. Grant recipients must promptly report any safety data they have from ongoing clinical trials. In addition, the NIH will set the timeframe for enrolling people in clinical trials of these drugs.

Every five years, the FDA must publish a plan describing what it will do over the next five years to encourage the development of safe and effective drugs for ALS and other rare neurodegenerative diseases, and to make experimental drugs easier to access. Each plan must include the actions the FDA took in the past and recommendations for improvement.

Finally, the Government Accountability Office and the Department of Health and Human Services must each report on the effects of these grants.

posts.title: To amend the Research and Development, Competition, and Innovation Act to support nucleic acid screening, and for other purposes.
posts.label: 📋 Reported by committee
posts.note: Science, Space, and Technology, H. Rept. 119-751
posts.summary:
Nucleic Acid Standards for Biosecurity Act
This bill explicitly requires the National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) to support the development of best practices and technical standards for nucleic acid synthesis.
Nucleic acids, including deoxyribonucleic acid (DNA) and ribonucleic acid (RNA), carry genetic information within cells. Nucleic acid synthesis is the process of designing and creating custom nucleic acids; it is used in the development of medications and agricultural products. However, this technology also poses a risk of misuse (e.g., the intentional or unintentional creation of dangerous biological agents).
The bill requires NIST to carry out measurement research to support the development and improvement of biosecurity best practices and technical standards related to nucleic acid synthesis. This effort must address specified topics including nucleic acid synthesis screening, operational security, and conformity assessment. (A 2023 executive order titled Safe, Secure, and Trustworthy Development and Use of Artificial Intelligence directed NIST to develop and refine similar specifications and best practices for use by synthetic nucleic acid providers. NIST's work on this topic is ongoing.)
In carrying out this effort, NIST must convene stakeholders to develop and periodically update consensus priorities and best practices for synthetic nucleic acid screening mechanisms. Within a specified period, NIST must submit a summary of the stakeholder group’s findings to Congress.
NIST must also take steps to advance risk management best practices and technical standards for engineering biology and biomanufacturing, including with respect to risks associated with the use of artificial intelligence.

aiSummaries.text:
The Nucleic Acid Standards for Biosecurity Act would require the National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) to help develop best practices and technical standards for nucleic acid synthesis. Nucleic acids, such as DNA and RNA, carry genetic information in living cells. Custom-making them is useful for medicines and farm products, but it also carries a risk of misuse, such as the creation of dangerous biological agents, whether on purpose or by accident.

To address this, NIST would carry out measurement research to improve biosecurity practices and standards in this area. The work must cover specified topics, including screening of nucleic acid synthesis, operational security, and conformity assessment. This builds on a 2023 executive order on artificial intelligence, which had already directed NIST to develop similar standards for companies that provide synthetic nucleic acids. NIST's work on this is still ongoing.

NIST would also bring stakeholders together to agree on priorities and best practices for screening synthetic nucleic acids, and to update them periodically. Within a set period, NIST must send Congress a summary of what this stakeholder group has found.

Finally, NIST would take steps to advance risk management practices and technical standards for engineering biology and biomanufacturing. This includes addressing risks linked to the use of artificial intelligence.
